caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 93 of 2003
lawyer:
Abdul Baset Majumder, Senior Advocate, instructed by Md Shahidur Rahman Khoshnabish, Advocate-on-Record -For the Petitioners. 	
Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, Senior Advocate, instructed by Chowdhury Md Zahangir, Advocate-on-Record -For Respondent No. 1. 	
Not represented-Respondent Nos. 2-4.
parties:
Anwara Begum and others ------ Petitioners
Vs.
Shah Newaj ------ Respondent
full_judgment:
Syed J.R. Mudassir Husain, J: The defendant-petitioners are seeking leave to appeal against the judgment and order dated 10-12-2002 passed in Civil Revision No. 4285 of 2002 by a Division Bench of the High Court Division discharging the Rule by affirming the judgment dated 18-7-2002 in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 241 of 2001 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka who rejected the Miscellaneous Case No. 39 of 1985 under Order IX rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restoring the Title Sit No. 491 of 1981 upon setting aside the ex parte decree dated 1-10-1984 passed therein by the learned Subordinate Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka.

2. The plaintiff-respondent instituted the aforesaid title suit in the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka for Specific Performance of Contract against the defendant-petitioners, who contested the suit by filing written statement but the suit was however decreed ex parte on 1-10-1984. Against the aforesaid ex parte decree the petitioners as defendants filed Miscellaneous Case No. 39 of 1985 on 28-11-1984 under Order IX rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restoring the above suit to its original file and number. The said Miscellaneous Case was contested by the plaintiff-respondent by filing written objection.

3. Upon hearing the parties, the learned Subordinate Judge dismissed the said Miscellaneous Case on 17-10-2001 and against which the defendant-petitioners preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No. 241 of 2001 and the same was dismissed by the learned Additional District Judge, Dhaka, who affirmed the decision of the learned Subordinate Judge, Dhaka.

4. Against the aforesaid judgment of affirmance, the petitioners moved the High Court Division and the Rule obtained in the aforesaid Civil Revision was discharged.

5. Mr. AB Majumder, the learned Advocate, appearing for the petitioners, has placed before us the judgments of the courts below as well as the impugned judgment of the High Court Division. It is contended that the learned Judges of the High Court Division failed to consider that the illness of the defendant-petitioner No. 1, Anowara Begum has been proved by filing a medical certificate as well as by examining the corroborating witness PW 2, Sahida Begum and thereby committed an error of law in not holding that the petitioner was prevented by sufficient cause from appearing in court on the date when the suit was fixed for peremptory hearing and the ex parte decree ought to have been set aside and it ought not to have discarded the medical certificate only due to non-examination of medical officer and, in such view of the matter, the findings and decisions as arrived at by the High Court Division are liable to be set aside.

6. Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Senior Counsel, entering Caviat for the respondent No. 1, on the other hand, contended that the courts below as well as the learned Judges of the High Court Division considered the respective cases of the parties and considered the decisions in the case of Kutubuddin Ahmed Siddiky vs East Pakistan Industrial Development Corporation, reported in 27 DLR 433, the decision in the case of Khalada Roushan Ara vs Md Nurul Hoque, reported in 1990 BLD (AD) 242 and another decision in the case of Jaidurga Industries, Joypur and another ...... vs Union Bank of India reported in AIR 1988 (Orissa) 104 and he argued that the learned Judges of the High Court Division rightly decided the case finding to the effect, "Medical Certificate about the illness of a certain person and his inability to move is not admissible in evidence without the examination of the Medical Officer giving the certificate in court".

<u>7. We have heard the submissions made on behalf of both sides. It appears that the learned Joint District Judge on assessment of evidence on record found that the petitioner's application under Order IX rule 13 was barred by limitation as she could not prove the fact of her illness and which fact has been concluded by concurrent finding of the appellate Court as a final court of fact.</u>

<u>8. Having regard to the aforesaid premises, we are of the view that the learned Judges of the High Court Division considered the facts and circumstances of the case and the decisions cited before them and rightly held that without examination of the doctor, the medical certificate granted by him is inadmissible in evidence and we are fully in agreement with the findings and decisions as arrived at by the High Court Division.</u>

<u>For the above reasons, this application merits no consideration. Accordingly, it is dismissed.</u>

End.

Vs
Ashrafun Nessa Bibi and others ----- Respondents.
case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated 26-2-1968, passed by the  Dacca High Court in F.M.A. No. 59 of 1967)
full_judgment:
The Judgment of the Court was delivered by

Ahsanuddin Chowdhury, J.—This appeal by special leave is from a judgment passed by a Division Bench of the Dacca High Court affirming an order of the Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dacca in Miscellaneous Case No. 50 of 1967.

2. The appeal arises in the following circumstances. Appellant Haji Md. Shariatullah filed, in the 3rd Court of the Subordinate Judge, Dacca, an application under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (hereinfater referred to as the Act) for pre-emption of certain land purchased on 19-3-66 by respondent No. 2 Rehana Begum. An objection petition against the said application for pre-emption was filed by Rehena Begum but ultimately the parties, namely, the pre-emptor Haji Shariatullah and the pre-emptee Rehena Begum compromised the matter and they filed a compromise petition on 5-9-66. The case was disposed of on 5-11-66 in terms of compromise. Thereafter on 5-12-66 the pre-emptor, namely, the appellant filed an application under section 96(9)(c) of the Act for delivery of possession with the help of a Pleader Commissioner. The said prayer was opposed by Respondent No. 1 Ashrafun Nessa and an application purported to be under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure (hereinafter referred to as the Code) was filed by her and it was registered a Miscellaneous Case No. 50 of 1967. It was stated therein that, in terms of the solenama, the pre-emptee Rehena Begum delivered vacant possession of the purchased land as per description mentioned in her sale deed to the pre-emptor who in his turn entered into possession thereof on the date of filing the solenama and that he has been in peaceful possession of the pre-empted land. It was alleged that the delivery of possession through Court with the help of a Pleader Commissioner was sought only to encroach upon the land which Ashrafun Nessa got by way of gift from Habibullah, the vendor of the pre-emptee on 1-6-64 i.e., long before the sale under the pre-emption. Having heard the parties the Subordinate Judge allowed Respondent No. l's objection and rejected appellant's application for possession through Court. His decision was upheld by the High Court.

3. In the leave application the appellant contended that (i) an application purported to be under section 47 of the Code filed by Respondent No. 1 Ashrafun Nessa was not maintainable as she was not a party to the pre-emption proceeding and (ii) that in the absence of a fielding that Respondent No. 1 Ashrafun Nessa was claiming in good faith to be in possession of the property on her own account, the execution case should not have been dis-missed. Leave was granted to consider the above question.

4. Mr. Golam Rabbani, the learned Counsel for the appellant submitted that the compromise order of pre-emption which was sought to be executed being not a decree passed in a suit and respondent No. 1 who resisted the execution of the said order of pre-emption being not a party to the proceeding in which the said order was passed, the application purported to have been made under section 47 of the Code of Civil procedure was not maintainable and as such, the order allowing the said application was passed without jurisdiction.

<u>5. On this question arguments of counsel of both sides were heard. Besides, Mr. Ranadhir Sen, the learned Deputy Attorney-General was heard as amicus curiae. In course of the argument a question was raised as to the applicability of the-provisions of Order XXI of the Code in execution of an order of pre-emption passed under section 96 of the Act. It should first be considered whether an order passed under section 96 of the Act is executable under the provisions of Order XXI of the Code. The order of pre-emption has been made under section 96(7) of the Act. Section 96(9)(c) of the Act provides that an order of pre-emption is executable for the purpose of placing the pre-emptor in possession of the pre-empted land. Section 96(9)(c) is in the following terms .—</u>

<u>"The court on further application of such applicants may place him or them, as the case may be in possession of the property vested in him or them."</u>

<u>6. It is obvious that in view of the above provisions of law a court may, on the application of the pre-emptor, put him into possession of the property vested in him by virtue of an order of pre-emption passed in his favour. Similar provisions were made under section 26F(7)(c) of the Bengal Tenancy Act,. On a comparison of the provisions stated above, it appears that section 96(9)(c) of the Act is a replica of section 26F(7)(c) of the Bengal Tenancy Act. The question now arises as to whether the decision in a case under section 96 of the Act may be deemed to be a decree within the meaning of section 2(2), or an order within the meaning of section 2(14) of the 'Code or it is an order having the effect of a decree. It is therefore necessary first to determine the character of the order passed under section 96 of the Act. The Act, it is evident, did not use the expression 'decree' or ‘order having the effect of a decree'. The word 'order' has been defined' in section 2(14) of the Code. in the following terms :</u>

<u>'order' means the formal expression of any decision of a Civil Court which is not a decree."</u>

<u>7. Order, as defined above, is analogous to a decree and generally has the essential attributes of a decree but as it arises out of a proceeding not being a suit, it does not amount to a decree. There is no doubt, however, that an order allowing pre-emption under section 96 of the Act is an adjudication finally determining the rights of the parties as to the claim of pre-emption and is a decision formally expressed by a Civil Court: As the proceeding in which the said order had been passed did not arise out of a suit instituted on the basis of a plaint, but of a proceeding on the basis of an application, such a decision did not amount to a decree. An order of pre-emption passed under section 96 of the Act is, therefore, an order within the meaning of section 2(14) of the Code and as such the provisions of section 36 of the Code will apply in its term in respect of execution of such an order. The said section is in the following terms :—</u>

<u>"36 Application to order : "The provisions of this Code relating to the execution of decree shall, so far as they are applicable, be deemed to apply to the execution of orders."</u>

<u>8. The expression "so far as they are applicable" refers to the limitation as to the applicability of any particular provision of the Code as may be necessary from the nature of the order in execution.</u>

<u>9. Order XXI of the Code has codified all the rules for execution of decrees and by virtue of section 36 of the Code they shall be equally applicable for the execution of the orders of Civil Court which come under the definition as laid down in section 2(14) of the Code. It is significant to note that the heading as has been given to Order XXI is "Execution of decrees and orders" although all the rules of the said order specifically refer to decrees of Civil Court. We have already seen that an order of pre-emption passed under section 96 of the Act is an order within the meaning of section 2(14) of the Code and as such the provisions of section 36 of the Code will apply in terms to the execution of such an order for delivery of possession as contemplated in section 96(7) read with section 96(9)(c) of the Act and it comes under rule 35 of Order XXI for the said purpose.</u>

10. We now proceed to consider some decisions cited from the Bar. The decision in the case of Jogendra Chandra Sen Vs. Bibee Wasidunnessa Khatun in 11 C.W.N. 856 is one on the earlier Civil Procedure Code. The Calcutta High Court held that when the Division Bench of the High Court made an order dismissing an application for leave to appeal to His Majesty in Council with costs, the order as to costs, is to be enforced by execution in the court which passed the order originally. It was observed that the Code is not exhaustive and that there is an inherent power in the court to have the order for costs passed by it to carry into effect. In the case of Parvathammal Vs. Chokalinga Chetty A.I.R. 1918, Madras, 389 it has been held that the order passed under section 34(e) of the Guardian and Wards Act is not an order under section 2(14) of the-Code in that it is not a final adjudication of any dispute and so not executable in terms of section 36 of the Code. In the case of Mohammad Baqar Vs. Md. Casim A.I.R. 1932, Oudh 210 the Full Bench has held that if an Act by necessary implication authorises an inquiry, it is immaterial that no Specific procedure is prescribed by the Act itself. In the absence of any specific provisions to the contrary in any special or local law, the ordinary rules of procedure would apply. This decision refers to' the application of section 141 of the Code and so relates to the proceeding of the pre-decree stage but in the instant case we are concerned with post-decree stage. In Kilehand Devachand Vs. Ajodhyaprasad Sukhanand, (A.I.R. 1934 Bom. 452) Kania, J. has held that an order made on a notice of motion of the original Side of the Bombay High Court falls within the meaning of section 2(14) and could therefore be executed under section 36 of the Code. In Ramgopal Raghunath Das Bhaagde Vs. Ram Chandra Krishnarao Sigaru (A.I.R. 1949 Nagpur, 359) a Single Judge of the Nagpur High Court has held that an order for costs passed by the Debt Relief Court cannot be executed by the Civil Court as in the Act there is no provision for the transfer of business to the Civil Court from the Debt Relief Court. The view taken was that the Debt Relief Court was not a Civil Court though presided over by a Civil Judge and as such section 36 read with section 38 of the Code was not applicable. In Tarapada Mishra Vs. Hare Krishna Das A.I.R. 1957 Cal. 335, a Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court has held that an order of pre-emption passed under West Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act will be leviable by execution in a Civil Court in view of section 36 of the Code. In Ram Taran Vs. Sukumari Debi, 5 D.L.R. 351, Guha J. held that an order of division of lands of a tenure or holding under section 88 of the Bengal Tenancy Act is an order of a Civil Court within the meaning of section 2(14) of the Code, and as such, executable under the provisions of the Code by virtue of section 36. Guha, J's decision so far it purports to hold that second appeal lies has not been rightly decided inasmuch as only one appeal as the parent order is appealable is allowable. Another decision of the Dacca High Court, namely, Ranjit Singh Hazari Vs. Juman Meab, 13 D.L.R. 105, may be noted here. In the said case in execution of an order directing restoration of possession under Order-XXI Rule 101 of the Code, certain persons, who were alleged to have been ousted from certain land, applied under Order XXI Rule 100 of the Code for restoration of possession and a Division Bench of the Dacca High Court consisting of Murshed and Khan JJ held that such-an application was maintainable in the proceeding in execution of an order passed under Order XXI Rule 101 of the Code by virtue of section 36.

11. It has been submitted by the learned counsel for the appellant that the application of respondent No. 1 raising an objection to the execution of the compromise order of pre-emption under section 47 of the Code is not maintainable, inasmuch as the order under execution is not a decree within the meaning of section 47 of the Code nor Respondent No. 1 who objected to the execution of the said order appears to have been a party to the proceeding in which the said order had been passed.

12. It is no doubt true that neither the order of pre-emption under execution is a decree nor has the dispute arisen between the parties to a suit. There has, however, been a conflict of judicial views in respect of applicability of the provision of section 47 of the Code to the execution of an order in view of the provision of section 36 of the Code. A Division Bench of the High Court of Madras in the case of Ankala Venkata Reddy Vs. Manchala Venkata Reddy in A.I.R. 1915 Madras 1222 held that the provision of section 47 would not be applicable to the execution of such an order. The High Court of Calcutta (Suhrawardy and Duval JJ), on the other hand, held in the case of Chandra Kumar De Vs. Kusum Kumary Roy, in I.L.R. 52 Calcutta 269 that an order granting costs to a Pleader Commissioner is executable in the same way as a decree in view of section 36 of the Code and as such section. 47 would apply to such a case and that the order dealing with an objection to the execution of such an order being under sec. 47, an appeal would necessarily lie from the said order. In a latter Calcutta case, Viz. Dharani Dhar Chose Vs. Phanibhusan Mukherjee 50 C.W.N. 837, another Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court (Nasim Ali, A.C.J. and Hindley, J) did not follow the earlier decision and held the an objection to the execution of an order awarding costs to a Pleader Commissioner was not covered by sec. 47 of the Code as the question did not relate to the execution, discharge or satisfaction of a decree and also that a the question did not arise between the parties to suit, and that as such no appeal lay against the order disposing of such objection. In the case of Ramkeshawar Prasad Vs. Babu Girja Prasad A.I.R. 1957 Patna 501, the Patna High Court expressed a similar-view and held that an order directing payment of sum of money to a Pleader Commissioner was no doubt executable by virtue of sec. 36 of the Code but as the Pleader Commissioner was not a party to the suit and the question raised were not questions in regard to the execution, discharge or satisfaction of a decree", section 47 had therefore no application.

<u>13. It can hardly be disputed that the order of pre-emption under execution is not a decree. It cannot also be denied that the dispute as to the execution of the said order has not arisen between the parties to a suit. But the question is whether by virtue of the provisions of section 36 of the Code, the provisions of section 47 of the Code has been made applicable to a proceeding in execution of an order in the same way as the provisions of Order XXI of the Code. There appears to be patent difficulty in invoking the provisions of section 47 of the Code in respect of such a proceeding, as section 36 of the Code merely makes the provisions of the Code relating to the execution of decrees applicable to the execution of orders, and it does not proceed further to the extent of making the order under execution a decree nor the proceeding in which the said order was passed a suit.</u>

<u>14. We are, therefore, of opinion, that having regard to the terms of section 47 of the Code, the said provision is not attracted to the instant case, although the order of pre-emption is executable under the provisions of Order XXI of the Code, by virtue of section 36 thereof.</u>

15. Nevertheless, such a view as to non-applicability of section 47 of the Code would not make the application of respondent No. 1 raising objection to the execution of the order of pre-emption non-maintainable, although the said application was wrongly described as under section 47 of the Code.

16. The question of appealability of the order disposing of the said application is, of course, very important, but in the instant case it has little practical significance. It is no doubt true that such an order cannot be deemed to be a decision under section 47 of the Code and appealable as a decree. But the said order refusing the appellants prayer for delivery of possession can be taken to be an order under section 96(9)(c) of the Act, and as such appeal-able under section 96(13) thereof and no further appeal will lie in terms of the said section.

17. It appears that the appellant sought to make out a case in the executing court as well as before the High Court that Respondent No. 1 dispossessed the appellant, the pre-emptor, from the pre-empted land, and as such she was liable to be evicted from the said land in the execution case. The executing court and also the High Court have taken the view that it having .been admitted in the petition of compromise dated 5-11-66 that possession of the land had already been made over to the appellant, there was no scope of further delivery of possession. The executing court also pointed out that the question of dispossession could not be gone into in the said execution case, whether the alleged dispossession took place before or after 5-11-66.

18. It has been strenuously contended by the learned counsel for the appellant that Respondent No. 1 having been found to be in possession of a part of the land in respect of which an order of pre-emption was made in favour of pre-emptor appellant, Respondent No. 1 is liable to be evicted from the said land in execution of the order of pre-emption, and the said respondent has no locus standi to come to the court to object to his eviction from the pre-empted land. This contention is absurd on the face of it. If a person who is sought to be ousted by an order of a court from a piece of land in which he claims to be in possession in exercise of a valid right, is not given an opportunity to represent to the court, by whose order he has been directed to be removed, that he is not liable to be so removed according to law, it will be a mere travesty of law and clearly violative of the basic principle of equity and justice. If his right of representation in the said circumstance is not provided under a specific provision of any law, he will undoubtedly be entitled to the said right under the general principle of natural justice. But the provisions of Order XXI being applicable to the execution .of the order of pre-emption in view of section 36 of the Code, as we have already so held, the position of Respondent No. 1 claiming independent title to the pre-empted land is, however, covered by some positive provisions of the said Order.

19. Having regard to the allegations made by the appellant against Respondent No. 1 before the executing court, rule 97 of Order XXI, is attracted in the circumstances of the case. The appellant complained of some resistance and obstruction by Respondent No. 1 to the delivery of possession of the pre-empted land and prayed for police help to the executing court for enforcing delivery of possession in pursuance of the order of pre-emption. Respondent No. 1 thereupon appeared and filed an application purporting to be under section 47 of the Code alleging that she was in occupation of the land in exercise of her own right and had not encroached upon any portion of the pre-empted land, which had already been taken possession of by the appellant, and prayed that the application for delivery of possession should be dismissed. The provision of order XXI, rule 97 of the Code provides that the Court shall investigate the matter after summoning the persons against whom the complaint of some resistance or obstruction has been made and this provision necessarily implies that such a person should be given some opportunity to represent his case to the executing court before the said court decides the question of the correctness and validity of the said complaint. The application which was filed by Respondent No. 1 defending her possession and opposing the execution of the order of pre-emption in respect of the land claimed to have been in her rightful possession, though wrongly described to be under section 47 of the Code may well be taken to have been made under Order XXI, rule 97 of the Code and there seems to be nothing irregular in such an application, it being a case of mere misdescription of the cause title.

20. The next question which arises in this appeal is whether the executing court rightly dismissed the execution case at the instance of. Respondent No. 1 without coming to a fin-ding that the said respondent was claiming in good faith to be in possession of the property on her own account, that is to say, whether the application of Respondent No. 1 dated 9-3-67 which may be taken to have been one under Order XXI, rule 97 of the Code had been properly disposed of according to law. In order to find out the correct answer to the said question we shall have to examine the facts of the case in the light of the relevant provision of the Code applicable to the instant case. Order XXI, rule 98 of the Code provides that if after the investigation contemplated in sub-rule (2) of rule 97 of Order XXI, the Court is satisfied that the resistance or obstruction was occasioned without any just cause by the judgment debtor or by some other person at his instigation it shall direct that the applicant (i.e., the pre-emptor appellant in the instant case) be put into possession of the property, and Order XXI, rule 99 of the Code provides that where the court is satisfied that the resistance or obstruction was occasioned by any person other than the judgment debtor claiming in good faith to be in possession of the property on his own account or on account of some person other than the judgment debtor, the court shall make an order dismissing the application.

21. In her application dated 9-3-67, Respondent No. 1 stated that Habibullah, the vendor of the pre-empted land transferred, by means of an oral gift more or less 11 kathas of land from the southern portion of Chitta Dag No. 5 measuring 51 kathas, which had been allotted to him by the final decree passed in an earlier partition suit, to Respondent No. 1 on 1-6-64 and delivered possession thereof to her, that the said Habibullah also executed a deed of gift to facilitate mutation proceeding and retained the remaining 4 kathas of the said chitta dag with some pucca structures thereon, which was separated from the gifted 11 kathas of land by a pucca boundary wall, that the appellant was in possession of the pre-empted land as covered by the schedule to the kabala and that the appellant was trying to encroach upon the land in which Respondent No. 1 had been in possession in good faith on her own account.

22. An objection was filed on behalf of the appellant to the aforesaid application of Respondent No. 1 in which the allegations as to oral gift and delivery of possession were denied and the alleged deed of gift in writing was characterised as "a false forged and fabricated document' and also as maliciously false and concocted story manufactured by the Respondent No. l's son Ashrafuddin in collusion with some designing persons of his camp."

<u>23. It is significant to notice that no averment was made in the said petition of objection to the effect that Respondent No. 1 had been trying to resist or obstruct the execution on behalf of or at the instigation of Respondent No. 2, the purchaser. The entire case of the appellant, as sought to be made out in the executing court, was that the compromise order or pre-emption having been made after service of necessary notice upon Respondent No. 1, as required under section 96(2) of the Act, was binding upon Respondent No. 1 and was also executable against her for the purpose of affecting delivery of possession of the land in respect of which the order of pre-emption had been made. This case of the appellant was rightly rejected by the executing court on the view that in a pre-emption case, delivery of possession would be effected against the purchaser alone and not against the other co-sharers of the holding who were made parties only to afford them an opportunity for applying for joint or proportionate pre-emption. Learned counsel for the appellant has repeated this contention before this court and has submitted that as Respondent No. 1, was a party to the pre-emption proceeding, (`it is interesting to notice that in one part of his argument dealing with the question of the applicability of section 47 of the Code it was contended that she was not a party to it) and an order of pre-emption has been made in respect of some lands, a part of which is in possession of Respondent No. 1, the said respondent would be bound to deliver possession of the said lands in execution of the order of pre-emption in the same way as the purchaser, Respondent No. 2.</u>

<u>24. This view is totally misconceived. It should be understood that a pre-emption proceeding is no substitute for a suit for partition or for possession. It is a summary proceeding in which the right of a co-sharer or a contiguous owner to buy off a holding or a share or part thereof from a stranger to whom it has been transferred by another co-sharer is determined. In case an order of pre-emption is made in favour of a co-sharer or a contiguous owner under section 96(9)(a) of the Act, the right, title and interest in the holding or the portion or share thereof accruing to the transferee shall be deemed to have vested, free from all encumbrances which may have been created after the date of transfer, in the co-sharer tenant, or the contiguous owner, as the case may be, whose application to purchase has been allowed and under clause (c) of the said sub-section the court may place the pre-emptor in possession of the property vested in him. It is clear from the provisions referred to above that the pre-emptor, by virtue of an order of pre-emption becomes entitled to be placed in the same position as that of the pre-emptee transferee, and can claim so much of the right, title and interest in the land as the said transferee had and was capable of conveying at the date of the transfer. It is only the transferee or anybody claiming through him after the said date of transfer, who can be regarded as the judgment debtor under an order of pre-emption and such an order can be executed only against the said transferee or successor-in-interest for effecting delivery of possession of the pre-empted land to the pre-empting co-sharer or continguous owner. Respondent No. 1 being not such a person, the order of pre-emption is not obviously executable against her.</u>

<u>25. Respondent, No. 1 can be evicted in execution of the order of pre-emption, if the appellant could make out a case under Order XXI, Rule 97 of the Code and satisfy the court as required under Rule 98 of the said Order that she was resisting the execution at the instance or instigation of the judgment-debtor, the transferee. On the other hand, the execution case shall be dismissed if it can be shown that Respondent No. 1 was claiming a bona-fide right to the land in her possession on her Own account. Although the correctness of the Respondent No. l's assertion as to her claim of title was disputed by the appellant; but it was nowhere stated that she was not claiming on her own account or that she was set up by the Judgment-debtor, i.e., the purchaser Respondent No. 2, to resist or obstruct the execution of the pre-emption order. In the circumstances it appears to us that having regard to the Provisions of Order XXI, Rules 98 and 99 of the Code it has been rightly held that the execution case was liable to be dismissed as against Respondent No. 1.</u>

<u>Having regard to the considerations made above we find no substance in this appeal. It is accordingly dismissed with costs.</u>

End.
