case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated June 10, 2002 passed by the High Court, Division in Civil Revision No. 728 of 2001)
full_judgment:
Md Ruhul Amin J: This petition for leave to appeal is directed against the judgment and order, June 10, 2002, of a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 728 of 2001 making the Rule absolute upon setting aside the order of November 8, 2000 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, in charge, 1st Court of Additional District Judge, Dhaka dismissing the Miscellaneous Case No. 1 of 1999.

<u>2. Facts, in short, are that respondent No. 1 filed 3 suits in respect of the self-same subject matter. The petitioners herein also filed one suit in respect of subject matter of suits of the respondent No. 1 All the suits were heard analogously by the Court of Subordinate Judge and the said Court by the judgment and decree of February 8, 1995 dismissed the suits filed by the respondent No. 1 and decreed the suit filed by the petitioners herein. Respondent No. 1 preferred appeals. The appeals were heard by the learned Additional District Judge, 9th Court, Dhaka analogously and by the judgment and decree of March 25, 1999 dismissed the appeals filed against the judgment and decree passed in the respondent No. 1's suits and allowed the appeal filed against the judgment and decree passed in the suit of the petitioners herein and dismissed the suit filed by them. Thereupon the respondent No. 1 filed Miscellaneous Case No. 1 of 1999 seeking review of the judgment and decree passed in the appeals filed against the judgment and decree dismissing his suits. The Miscellaneous Case was fixed for hearing on November 8, 2000. On that date on the ground of illness of the learned Advocate for the respondent No. 1 an application was filed seeking adjournment. The learned Additional District Judge upon rejecting the application seeking adjournment dismissed the Miscellaneous Case for default. As against the said order of the learned Additional District Judge, respondent No. 1 moved the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction. The High Court Division upon observing.... "the application for adjournment was made not on any ground other than the ailment of the learned Advocate I have noticed from the order sheet of the case that on each of the previous occasions, the petitioner appeared and took proper steps in the case. The learned Additional District Judge was absolutely unjustified in rejecting the prayer for time in failing to appreciate that the learned Advocates are the officers of the Court and the Bar and the Bench are complementary to each other and that the learned Advocates are integral part of the Court. Therefore, they deserve some privilege from the Courts in respect of adjournment of any case on their personal ground" made the Rule absolute and set aside the order of dismissal of the Miscellaneous Case and further directed the learned Additional District Judge to "dispose of the Miscellaneous Case within 60 days from the date of receipt of the order without fail."</u>

<u>3. Learned Counsel for the petitioners submits that one Miscellaneous Case has been filed against the judgment and decree in 3 appeals and the same being not maintainable the learned Additional District Judge did not commit any error in dismissing the said Miscellaneous Case with the observation that the Miscellaneous Case so filed was not maintainable and, as such, the High Court Division was in error in setting aside the order of the learned Additional District Judge without considering the fact that Miscellaneous Case so filed was not maintainable. The learned Counsel also submits that application upon which Miscellaneous Case has been registered does not disclose any ground for review of the judgment dismissing the 3 appeals filed by the plaintiff respondent No. 1 and, as such, the High Court Division was in error in not considering the said aspect of the Miscellaneous Case and that also in not considering the fact that the Miscellaneous Case has been filed only to harass the petitioner herein. The submissions of the learned Counsel for the petitioners as to maintainability of the Miscellaneous Case are the matter for consideration by the Court before which the Miscellaneous Case has been filed. In the instant case the only consideration whether the Court was justified in dismissing the Miscellaneous Case in spite of seeking adjournment on the ground of illness of respondent No. 1's learned Advocate. The High Court Division on perusal of the record was of the view that the respondent No. 1, as the petitioner in the Miscellaneous Case, was diligently prosecuting the Miscellaneous Case and that almost on the previous all dates he took steps for hearing of the Miscellaneous Case and that only on one date ie, November 8, 2000, an application was filed seeking adjournment of hearing of the Miscellaneous Case on the ground of illness of the learned Advocate. The learned Counsel for the petitioners failed to point out any infirmity in the findings of the High Court Division upon making which said Division set aside the order dismissing the Miscellaneous Case for default.</u>

4. In the afore state of the matter we find no substance in the petition.

Accordingly, the petition is dismissed.

End.

lawyer:
Md Rabiul Alam Chowdhury, Advocate—For the Petitioners. 
Md Asadullah, Advocate—For the Opposite Party.
parties:
Government of Bangladesh represented by the DC and others ----- Defendants-Respondents-Petitioners 
Vs. 
Anjum Nahar Khatun ----- Plaintiff-Appellant-Opposite Party
full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party No. 1 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 14-10-97 and 21-10-97 respectively passed by the learned District Judge, Satkhira, in Title Appeal No. 188 of 1995 allowing the appeal and decreeing the suit and setting aside the judgment and decree dated 29-10-95 and 6-11-95 respectively passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Satkhira Sadar, in Title Suit No. 415 of 1990 dismissing the suit should not be set aside.

2. The brief fact of the case is that the opposite party as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 415 of 1990 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Satkhira against the present petitioner and others for declaration of title of the suit lands and for further declaration that the vested property list relating to suit lands is illegal, void and not binding upon the plaintiff, which was dismissed on contest.

3. The case of the plaintiff-appellant-opposite party, in short, is that, the suit land along with other lands appertaining to CS plot No. 247 originally belonged to Murali Dhar Chattapadhya who settled the land by postdated 11-8-39 in favour of Ashalata Das and others who sold the same by the registered kabala dated 26-4-47 to Hari Sadhan and this Hari Sakhan sold 1.87 acres of land including the suit land to plaintiff by a registered kabala dated 2-9-70 and delivered the possession.

4. The further case of the plaintiff-appellant-opposite party is that she mutated her name vide Mutation Case No. 1060/74 and has been owning and possessing by paying rents but was SA record wrongly prepared in the name of Hari Sadhan and on the basis of his wrong record the suit lands were enlisted as vested property.

5. The further case of plaintiff-appellant-opposite party is, that she, in Miscellaneous Case No. 24 of 1981 applied for release of the property from the vested property list and the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) by his order dated 10-8-81 recommended for release of the property and the defendant No. 3 (Assistant Commissioner of Land) the present preformed opposite party No. 2 released the suit lands granting DCR to defendant No. 4 (the present proforma opposite party No. 3) illegally on 5-8-90 and threatened to dispossess the plaintiff-appellant-opposite party from the suit land. Hence the instant suit.

6. The defendant Nos. 1-3, 4 and 6 contested the suit by filing almost identical written statement alleging that the suit land belonged to Hari Sadhan who left for India permanently after 1965 war and thus the suit land was vested in the government by operation of law which has been duly enlisted in the list as vested property and duly processed and leased out to the defendant No. 4 by granting DCR.

7. The further case of the petitioner is that plaintiff has no title and possession over the suit land but filed the instant false suit by creating a forged and fabricated kabala which is liable to be dismissed with costs.

8. The learned trial Court framed as many as five issues and considering the evidence on record, documents and other connected papers dismissed the suit by his judgment and decree dated 29-10-95 and 6-11-95 respectively.

9. The plaintiff-appellant-opposite party being aggrieved by the judgment and decree preferred an appeal before the learned District Judge, Satkhira being Title Appeal No. 188 of 1995.

10. The learned District Judge, Satkhira after hearing both the parties allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment and decree passed by the learned trial Court by his judgment and decree dated 14-10-97 and 21-10-97 respectively.

11. The defendant-respondent-petitioner being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree passed by the learned District Judge, Satkhira preferred the instant revisional application before the High Court Division stating, inter alia, that the judgment of the lower appellate Court is manifestly perverse which is liable to be interfered by this court.

12. The learned Counsel Mr Md Rabiul Alam Chowdhury, appearing on behalf of the defendant-respondent-petitioner, submits that the learned lower appellate Court without considering the material evidence on record affecting the merit of the case passed the judgment and decree which is manifestly perverse. The learned District Judge, Satkhira came to this finding on the basis of the recommendation made by the ADC (Revenue) and recommended to release the property from the list of the vested property. The learned District Judge, Satkhira failed to appreciate the evidence on record. The plaintiff examined as many as 6 witnesses in this case to prove the case.

14. Abdul Haque Dhali, the husband of the plaintiff Anjum Nahar Khatun, was examined as PW 2 who stated in his evidence that the suit property was purchased by his wife Anjum Nahar Khatun by a registered kabala dated 2-9-70 from one Hari Sadhan and produced the certified copy of the purchase deed which was exhibited as Exhibit 4. He further stated in his evidence that as the original deed was lost he could not produce the original deed.

15. Mostab Ali Halder, a permanent Moharar of Sub-Registry office was examined as PW 1 who brought the volume from Sub-Registry office to prove the genuineness of the certified copy of the purchase deed. The learned Counsel for the petitioner submits that the plaintiff claims her right and title over the suit land on the basis of the title deed. Next he submits that mere producing a certified copy of a deed and calling for the volume from Sub-Registry office does not necessarily mean to prove the execution of a deed. The PW 2 stated in his evidence that Hari Sadhan is still living in Bangladesh and they are living in the same village and the distance of the house of Hari Sadhan and the plaintiff is about 10/12 cubit hands, as such, to prove the genuineness of the document, the plaintiff ought to have produced Hari Sadhan as witness but plaintiff failed to produce Hari Sadhan to prove the execution of the deed. The learned Counsel for the petitioner further submits that as a matter of fact Hari Sadhan left for India long before, as such, his property was treated as enemy property and subsequently, vested property by operation of law. In support of his contention the learned Counsel relying on the case of Abani Mohan Saha vs Assistant Custodian Vested Property, Chandpur, reported in 39 DLR (AD) 223 wherein it has been held that :

"A person relying on a document is bound to prove its execution. The fact that it is registered makes no difference. It is true that no document is registered unless the Registrar is satisfied on such enquiry as the Registration Act authorizes that it was executed by the alleged executants. But he is not a Court and has no judicial function. The object of his enquiry is to enable him to do his departmental duty, and the opinion formed in such an enquiry, though good for departmental purpose has no value in judicial enquiry as evidence of its execution."

16. The learned Counsel next submits that it is the duty of the plaintiff to prove his case beyond all reasonable doubt. The initial onus lies on the plaintiff to prove his title according to his claim over the suit land. In this connection, the learned Counsel cited another decision in the case of Abani Mohan Saha vs Assistant Custodian, Vested Property, Sandspur reported in 39 DLR (AD) 224 wherein it is stated that:

"The plaintiff is claiming his title to the suit land on the basis of a deed of gift. I have got no doubt in my mind that the initial onus was on him to prove his title. The observation made in 32 DLR (AD) 29 would be of no avail to the appellant, as he failed to discharge his initial onus by proving his document of title. Had he succeeded to do so then the onus would have shifted on the enemy property authority to prove that the executants of the plaintiff's document, the sons of Surendra Mohan Saha, were residing in an enemy country at the relevant time."

17. The learned Counsel further submits that the plaintiff has got no title and possession over the suit land and the plaintiff miserably failed to prove his title and also possession. Although the plaintiff claims that she is in possession of the suit land and produced two rent receipts, one of 1986 and another of 1990, that is not the proof of his possession. Next he submits although the plaintiff claims that he has mutated his name by Mutation Case No. 1060/74 but the plaintiff could not produce any certified copy of mutated khatian or any rough paper of mutated khatian. Finally, the learned Counsel submits that the Enemy Property (Continuance of Emergency Provisions) (Repeal) Act, 1974 which is known as Act No. XLV of 1974 wherein section 3 savings-(1) reads as follows :

"Notwithstanding the repeal of the said Ordinance and anything contained in any other law for the time being for such repeal; (a) all enemy property vested in the Custodian of Enemy Property appointed under the provisions of the Defence of Pakistan Rules continued in force by the said Ordinance shall vest in the Government"

Amendment of section 3, Act XLV of 1974, this shall be inserted in both the places, namely,

"And shall be administered, controlled, managed and disposed of by transfer or otherwise, by the government or by such officer or authority as the Government may direct."

18. So the question of treating a property as enemy property after the repeal of Ordinance No.1 of 1969 on 23-3-74 does not create any legal bar at all. In support of his contention the learned Counsel cited the case of Privates Talukder vs Assistant Custodian, Vested and Non-Resident Property, Chittagong and others reported in 39 DLR (AD) 178 wherein it has been held that—

"The contention is one interpretation of the effect of the provisions of section 3 of the Act of 1974 which repealed the Enemy Property (Continuance of Emergency Provisions) Ordinance, 1969. Clause 1 of section 3 containing the 'savings' says that in spite of the repeal of the Ordinance all enemy properties which have vested in the Custodian of Enemy Property shall vest in the Government. Once such property stands vested in the Government under this clause, it cannot, in my opinion, be divested except in due course of law. If no exceptions have been made in the law itself, either simultaneously or even subsequently, such vesting confers fully ownership of the property in the Government or in whomsoever is mentioned in the Act".

19. The learned lower appellate Court while allowing the appeal did not take into consideration all the legal aspects of the case and material facts and evidence affecting the merit of the case. The learned District Judge simply banked upon the recommendation made by the ADC (Revenue) to the Ministry of land for releasing the property from the list of the vested property, as such, committed an error of law as well as on facts which is liable to be interfered with by this court.

20. On the other hand, the learned Counsel Mr Md Asadullah, appearing on behalf of the defendant-respondent-opposite party submits that the suit property is not an enemy property, because the plaintiff by a registered kabala dated 2-9-70 purchased the suit property from Hari Sadhan, the original owner of the suit property. The plaintiff since the purchase was owning and possessing the suit property but abruptly the vested property authority treated the said property in the list of vested property vide VP Case No. 1 600 (Kali)/ 8081. The learned Counsel next submits that the plaintiff has mutated his name vide Mutation case No. 1060/74 and paid rent upto 1387 BS. Hari Sadhan, the vendor of the plaintiff, is a permanent citizen of Bangladesh who never went to India and is still living in Bangladesh, as such, his property cannot be treated as vested property in the year 1980. The plaintiff thereafter submitted a prayer before the ADC (Revenue) for releasing the property from the list of the vested property. On the prayer of the plaintiff, the ADC (Revenue) after perusing the record and connected papers recommended to the Ministry of Land that the property does not come within the purview of vested property list, as such, the suit property may be released from the list of the vested property. The learned Counsel further submits that after the repeal of Ordinance No. 1 of 1969 no property could be declared as enemy or vested property. This suit property was declared as vested property in the year 1980 which is absolutely illegal and without jurisdiction and ultra virus to the Enemy Property Repeal Act of 1974. The learned Counsel in support of his contention cited the case of Saju Hosein and others vs Bangladesh and another reported in 58 DLR (AD) 177 wherein it has been held that:

"Since the law of enemy property itself died with the repeal of Ordinance No.1 of 1969 on 23-3-74 no further vested property case can be started thereafter on the basis of the law which is already dead. Accordingly, there is no basis at all to treat the case land as vested property upon starting VP Case No. 210 of 1980."

21. The learned Counsel next submits that vested property authority without any jurisdiction and without any cogent reason treated the property as vested property. The learned lower appellate Court rightly observed that the case land was not vested property and the trial Court without considering the recommendation made by the ADC (Revenue) dismissed the suit of the plaintiff. The learned Counsel Mr Md Asadullah finally submits that the finding and observation made by the lower appellate Court is absolutely justified because finding of facts of the lower appellate Court should not be disturbed unless and until it is manifestly perverse. The learned District Judge after considering the evidence on record as well as the registered kabala, exhibits and other connected papers allowed the appeal which is not liable to be interfered with by this Court.

22. On a meticulous examination of the evidence on record, certified copy of the registered deed, the judgments of both the courts below and other connected papers, it transpires that the learned trial Court in his judgment discussed the evidence and also perused the certified copy of the registered deed produced by the plaintiff and made his clear observation that the certified copy of the registered deed by the plaintiff dated 2-9-70 which was exhibited as Exhibit 1 (ka) was not the original deed. The PW 2, the husband of the plaintiff, stated in his evidence that the original deed by which the plaintiff purchased the suit land from Hari Sadhan was lost, as such, the certified copy of the original deed as secondary evidence was produced and exhibited as Exhibit 1 (ka).

<u>23. The plaintiff examined as many as 6 witnesses in this case to prove the case. Shahamat Ali Karikar was examined as PW 3 who was said to be an attesting witness. The learned trial Court observed that since the original deed was not produced his signature could not be compared with original deed. PW 2 stated in his evidence that the vendor of the plaintiff Hari Sadhan never went to India and still he is living in Bangladesh and Hari Sadhan has been living in the same village of the plaintiff and in that case the plaintiff ought to have examined Hari Sadhan to prove the genuineness of the registered kabala dated 2-9-70. The recommendation made by the ADC (Revenue) to release the property from the list of the vested property has got no basis because although the plaintiff claimed that she was possessing the suit land by mutating her name by Mutation Case No. 1060/74 but the plaintiff could not produce any certified copy of the mutation khatian or any rough mutation khatian. The plaintiff produced 2 rent receipts, one of 1986 and another of 1990, but the claim of the plaintiff is that he purchased the land in the year 1970 but no rent receipt except in 1986 and 1990 could be produced by the plaintiff. The trial Court rightly observed that the plaintiff had no continuous possession over the suit land. The plaintiff's case has got two phases: first phase of the plaintiff's case is that the plaintiff purchased the suit land from Hari Sadhan by a registered kabala dated 2-9-70 and the second phase is to treat the property as vested property. Thereafter, while the plaintiff was enjoying the property, abruptly in the year 1980 the vested property authority treated this property as vested property and enlisted the property in the vested property list and thereafter, leased out the suit property to one Nur Mohammad vide VP Case No. 600 (kali)/ 8081. Now the question is, whether the plaintiff has been able to prove his title over the suit property by the certified copy of the kabala dated 2-9-70. In this connection, I like to rely on the case of Sova Rani Guha alias Sova Rani Gupta vs Abdul Awal Miah and others reported in 1994 BLD (AD) 257 wherein it has been held that section 63—Secondary evidence —"The production of the certified copy of a sale deed does not by itself warrant the presumption of due execution of the original document A party producing the Secondary evidence of a document is not relieved of the duty of proving the execution of the original. Even in a case where a document has been exhibited without objection the court is to be satisfied as to the execution of the document." In the instant case, to prove the genuineness of the document onus is upon the plaintiff to produce Hari Sadhan who executed the deed in absence of the original one but the plaintiff could not produce Hari Sadhan before the court as witness. The lower appellate Court while reversing the judgment of the trial Court ought to have assigned in his judgment justifying the reason in reversing the judgment of the trial Court, particularly in respect of the title deed. But the lower appellate Court in reversing the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court did not assign any cogent reason and also did not consider the evidence on record, particularly the evidence of PW 2 affecting the merit of the case. In this connection, I like to rely on the decision in the case of Most Mohsina Khatun vs Ms Habib Knitting Mills reported in 1997 BLD (AD) 47 wherein it is stated that while reversing the judgment of the trial Court the appellate Court is required to reverse the material findings of the trial Court with reference to evidence on record. The judgment of the trial Court transpires that in arriving at its finding the said Court carefully considered the material facts and circumstances of the case and evidence on record, both oral and documentary, and the certified copy of the original title deed of the plaintiff. The learned trial Court did not commit any error of law and illegality in arriving at its finding because the plaintiff could not be able to prove his case. The lower appellant Court without considering the evidence on record and without proper assessment of the evidence and also without considering the title deed was not proved and came to an erroneous finding which is liable to be interfered by this Court. In this connection, I rely on the decision in the case of Hasan Ahmed Chowdhury vs Md Nurul Amin and others reported in 47 DLR (AD) 162 wherein it has been held that—</u>

<u>"If there is misreading of evidence and non-consideration of some material evidence then it was incumbent on the provisional Court to consider the same and to arrive at a proper finding on the material evidence on record and to finally dispose of the case."</u>

24. In view of the facts and legal position of the case I find that the lower appellate Court is absolutely wrong in reversing the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court which is liable to be set aside.

25. From the discussion made above and the facts and circumstances of the case and also the legal position, the impugned judgment and decree dated 14-10-97 and 21-10-97 respectively passed by learned District Judge, Satkhira, in Title Appeal No. 188 of 1995 allowing the appeal and reversing the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court is hereby set aside and the Judgment and decree of the trial Court is affirmed.

26. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to the costs.

Lower Court's record be sent down at once with a copy of the judgment.

End.

lawyer: HSD Brahman, Advocate — For the Petitioner.
parties:
Nur Nahar Begum ------ Petitioner 
vs
Din Mohammad and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This application is directed at the instance of the plaintiff of Other Suit 46 of 1994, which was filed for declaration of her title in the suit land comprising an area of 0.28 acre land of plot of 58.

2. Trial Court decreed the suit by its judgment dated 18-2-96. The appellate Court in Other Appeal 135 of 1996 preferred by the defendant found that without the prayer for partition, since the title of the plaintiff is disputed by the admitted co-sharers the suit for simple declaration of title cannot be allowed, by the impugned judgment and decree dated 9-9-97.

3. Plaintiffs averments leading to the suit are that, the suit land along with other lands belonged to four brothers, namely Meher Ali, Ala Meah, Abdul Aziz and Abdul Hakim, Accordingly, they were in possession. The RS Khatian was also prepared in their favour ihowing 4 annas share against each of them. Plaintiff is the daughter of Khalilur Rahman who was a son of said Meher Ali. Plaintiff has filed the suit for declaration of her title in eight annas share in the suit land as described in the schedule of the plaint. Ala Miah mortgaged his 4 annas share on 4-11-47 with one Abul Khair, Khalilur Rahman later on redeemed the mortgage and got the said land freed. Khalilur Rahman thus became owner to the extent of 4 annas of the lands after death of his father in the suit holding of said 4 brothers.

4. Subsequently, Khalilur Rahman gifted his entire 4 annas share to the plaintiff who is his daughter. Defendants 1-4 contested the suit by filing written statement. They admit that the land of the suit Khatian originally belonged to the aforesaid four brothers. But during their life time and after their death many inter transfers have commenced. As a result, according to the defendants the plaintiff is not entitled to get 0.28 decimals of land as claimed specific case of the defendants is that since the suit land in party ejmali land without prayer for partition no decree can be passed in respect of 0.28 acres land for declaration of title.

5. Both the Courts below have dismissed the suit finding that without a prayer for partition, simple suit for declaration of title cannot be decreed.

6. Mr Brahman, the learned Counsel for the petitioner, submits that since all the co-sharers are parties in the suit, the present suit for declaration of title is maintainable. Mr Brahman in support of his argument cities the decision. In the case of 46 DLR 419. It is held as under:

"In a case of original co-ownership the plaintiff and defendant being in joint possession of the suit property suit for declaratory relief in respect of the share of the plaintiff in a specified land without seeking partition is maintainable".

<u>7. The decision is not applicable in this case because of the fact that the title as well as possession are disputed in this case between co-sharers. It is also not clear by the findings and decisions of the Courts below in the instant case whether all the co-sharers have been made parties. Moreover, the point of law raised in this litigation troubles my mind. Because if without a prayer for partition declaration of title is made in favour of one person even if he is a co-sharer in respect of certain land out of the ejmali land and if a suit for partition is filed later on by any of the co-sharers the decision of the suit relating to declaration of title only can be pleaded as a res-judicata against the subsequent partition suit. Partition suit is only a full fledged suit as provided under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act for a giving final and adequate relief to the parties in respect of their right and title in the suit land which is under their joint possession and ownership as co-sharers.</u>

<u>8. Here in this case, title of the plaintiff is not admitted. It is rather disputed seriously by the defendant. Therefore, the appellate Court has rightly and legally found that without a prayer for partition, a decree in respect of certain portion of land cannot be passed declaring title of a particular co-sharer.</u>

9. However, the plaintiff may file a suit for partition because a dispute must be decided once and for all and between all the persons. The plaintiff may have some title but that cannot be decided in the present suit. In case the plaintiff files a suit for partition the declaration in the suit shall not be a bar or res-judicata.

The judgment and decrees of the appellate Court does not suffer from any illegality and it has not invited any error of law in the decision occasioning failure of justice. So the present revisional application having no merits is rejected summarily.

End.

lawyer:
PC Guha, Advocate—For the Petitioner. 
Syed Ziaul Karim, Advocate—For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Moinab Bibi and others ------ Petitioners
VS. 
Abdur Rashid Mridha and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Rule arises out of an application filed under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and is directed against the Judgment and decree of affirmance dated 31-1-91 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Barguna in Title Appeal No. 89 of 1987 dismissing the suit.

2. The plaintiffs-petitioners instituted Title Suit No. 52 of 1986 in the court of the Assistant Judge, Batagi, District Barguna for declaration of title in respect of "Ka" schedule land for a further declaration that the deed obtained in favour of the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 as described in the schedule "Ga" in respect of the "Kha" schedule land is illegal, fraudulent and null and void and not binding upon the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs case is, that the suit land originally belonged to Lalu Forazi and from him the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs got the property and thereafter he was in enjoyment of the said property on payment of the rent to the Government for well over 12 years but the SA and RS Khatian has been wrongly recorded in the name of defendant No. 3 along with the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs and, as such, the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs Erfan Farazi filed Title Suit No. 16 of 1955 in the court of the then Munsif, 3rd Court Patuakhali for correction of the record of right and the said suit was decreed ex parte on 27-1-1956 in favour of the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs. The further case of the plaintiff-petitioners is that the defendant opposite party No. 3 had no right, title and interest in the suit land and the deed in question by which she had transferred the suit land to the defendant opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 did not create any right, title and interest in favour of the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 and they are also not in possession of the suit land.

3. The defendant-opposite parity Nos. 1 and 2 entered appearance and contested the suit by filing a written statement wherein they have denied the material allegations as made in the plaint and the positive case of the defendant opposite parties Nos. 1 and 2 is that defendant No. 3 Amena Khatan as heir of Lalu Farazi got the suit property through inheritance after the death of her father Lalu Farazi along with the prodecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs Erfan Farazi and their mother Soleman Bibi and since then she had been possessing the suit land and while she was in possession of the same she transferred the suit land to the defendant opposite parties No. 1 and 2 through sale deed No. 231 dated 29-1-86 of Betagi Sub-Registry office Exhibit "Ka" in favour of defendant opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 and since their purchase they are in possession of the suit land within the knowledge of all including the plaintiffs.

4. The trial Court on consideration of the evidence and materials on record dismissed the suit. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree of the trial Court the plaintiffs preferred appeal before the learned District Judge, which was an appeal before the learned District Judge, which was registered as Title Appeal No. 89 of 1987 and the said appeal on transfer was heard and disposed of by the learned Subordinate Judge who by the impugned judgment and decreed date 20-2-1991 dismissed the appeal and affirmed the judgment of the trial Court and being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree of the appellate Court below the plaintiff petitioners obtained the instant Rule.

5. Mr. PC Guha, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiffs-petitioners, submitted only two points. His first point of attack against the impugned judgment is that admittedly the plaintiffs-predecessor filed Title Suit No. 16 of 1955 against the vendor of the defendant opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 for correction of record of right and that suit was decreed ex parte on 27-1-1956 but neither the vendor of the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 nor the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 ever took any steps to challenge the legality and propriety of the aforesaid decree passed in Title Suit No. 16 of 1955 and in that view of the matter both the courts below found that the plaintiffs have failed to prove that the aforesaid decree was not obtained by the predecessor of the plaintiffs properly and without suppressing the process of the court. The second grievance of Mr. Guha is that both the courts concurrently found that the plaintiffs petitioners are not in possession of the suit land but neither of the court below did at all discuss the evidence adduced of the plaintiffs-petitioners before the trial Court in support of their case on possession and that there is overwhelming evidence from the side of the plaintiff-petitioners through which they have successfully proved their possession in the suit land and the appellate Court below without, adverting to those evidence on record and without re-assessing the same afresh as is required by Order 41 rule 31 of the Code in a slipshod manner affirmed the findings of the trial Court and, in that view of the matter, the impugned judgment is liable to be set aside.

6. Mr. Syed Ziaul Karim, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2, on the other hand, submits that both the courts below on proper assessment of the materials and evidence on record rightly arrived at concurrent finding that the plaintiff petitioners have failed to prove their case and both the courts below concurrently found that the defendant opposite party No. 3 namely, the vendor of the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 had valid right, title, interest and possession in respect of the suit land before the transfer made by her in 1986 to the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 and the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 after their purchase are in possession of the same and these findings of facts of both the court below are based on materials and evidence on record and, as such, there is no scope for this court to interfere with the concurrent findings of facts based on materials on record. The learned Advocate finally submits that it is true that an ex parte decree dated 27-1-1956 was obtained by the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs petitioners but it is crystal clear from the evidence and material on record that the decree was never acted upon and both the SA and RS Khatian in respect of the suit land stands in the name of the vendor of the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 and in that view of the matter both the defendant opposite parties Nos. 1 and 2 did not challenge the legality and validity of the ex parte decree dated 27-1-1956 passed in Title Suit No. 16 of 1955 and the same will not stand in their way.

7. On perusal of the impugned judgment as well as the judgment of the trial Court it appears that both the courts concurrently found that the suit land originally belonged to one Lalu Farazi, the father of the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs and the defendant-opposite party No. 3 and after his death the said property devolved upon one Soleman Bibi wife of Lalu Farazi and to Erfan Farazi and Amena Khatun, son and daughter respectively of said Lalu Farazi and, as such, it is established beyond any shadow of doubt that Amena Khatun inherited the suit property as heir of Lalu Farazi. Both the courts below also concurrently found that both SA and RS Khatian in respect of the suit land stand in the name of the defendant opposite party No. 3 and both the courts below on scrutiny of evidence both oral and documentary arrived at a concurrent finding that the defendant opposite party No. 3 after inheriting the suit property as described in the schedule "Ga" to the plaint was in continuous possession. After her inheritance and while she was so seized with the suit property, she transferred the same to the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 through deed No. 231 dated 29-1-86 and after their purchase the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 are in possession of the same and, in that view of the matter, both the courts below concurrently observed that the suit as framed for a declaration simpliciter is not maintainable. It further appears from a perusal of the judgment of the courts below that they have rightly noticed the fact that the ex parte decree was obtained on 27-1-58 in Title Suit No. 16 of 1955 against the defendant opposite party No. 3 but after the passing of the aforesaid decree till the transfer of the suit property made by the defendant-opposite party No. 3 in favour of the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 the plaintiffs or their predecessor-in-interest had never taken any steps whatsoever to correct the record of rights in pursuance of the decree passed in Title Suit No. 16 of 1955 and taking this aspect of the case into consideration both the courts concurrently found that the plaintiff-petitioners have failed to show that the decree passed in Title Suit No. 16 of 1955 was validly obtained by the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiff-petitioners.

<u>8. On a perusal of the impugned judgment as well as the judgment of the trial Court it is crystal clear that the predecessor-interest of the plaintiff-petitioners obtained the decree in Title Suit No. 16 of 1955 but neither the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs nor the plaintiffs did take any steps to correct the record of rights. It is not clear who paid rent in respect of the suit land for these long 30 years, yet it has been frankly admitted by Mr. Guha in reply to a question posed to him by the court that rents have been paid by the plaintiffs in respect of the suit in the name of the defendant-opposite party No. 3 beside, there is no denial of the fact that both the SA and RS khatian in respect of the "Ka" schedule property stand in the name of the defendant opposite party No. 3. These two factors that rent had been paid for the suit land by the plaintiffs in the name of the defendant-opposite party No. 3 and that suit land stands recorded in the name of the defendant opposite party No. 3 show that the defendant opposite party No. 3 was in possession of the suit land prior to the transfer made by her in 1986 and in that view of the matter, I am of the view that both the courts below rightly observed that in the instant case the plaintiff-petitioners have miserably failed to show that the decree in Title Suit No. 16 of 1955 was validly obtained by the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiff-petitioners and also failed to show that the decree had been acted upon. The omission on the part of the plaintiff-petitioners to prove that the decree passed in Title Suit No. 16 of 1955 had been acted upon and that the concerned record of rights had been corrected stare at the face of the plaintiff-petitioner and taking this aspect of the case into consideration it appears to me that the courts below rightly arrived at a finding that the ex parte decree dated 27-1-1956 passed in Title Suit No. 16 of 1955 will not stand in the way of the defendant-petitioners to acquire their valid title in respect of suit land. Besides, on a perusal of the records it appears that the plaintiff petitioners have miserably failed to show that they are in possession of the suit land through his father who was the owner of the suit property. Rather it appears from the evidence of the PWs themselves that they had admitted that defendant-opposite party No. 3 got the suit property through inheritance from her father late Lalu Forazi and it is also found from the evidence of PW 4 that the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 are in possession of the suit land since their purchase. It further appears that the evidence of PWs 2 and 3 is not worthy of credence and no reliance could be put on them on the point of possession as they have admitted in their cross examination that they do not know the suit land. It further appears that though PW 1 in his examination-in-chief did not specifically assert that their vendor opposite party No. 3 was is in continuous and uninterrupted possession of the suit land for more than 12 years prior to the date of transfer made on 19-1-1986 yet it appears from the evidence of DW 2 that he has testified to the effect that the defendant-opposite party No. 3, after getting the suit property through inheritance was in possession of the same and using the usufruct thereof through bargader and it further appears from the evidence of PW 3 that even Erfan Farazi the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs, was also for some time bargader of the defendant-opposite party No. 1 prior to the sale of the same to the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 In that view of the matter it appears that the appellate Court below rightly observed that the plaintiffs-petitioners have failed to prove their possession in respect of the suit land and that the defendant-opposite party No. 1 and 2 successfully proved that they are in possession of the suit land since their purchase and their vendor defendant No. 3 was in possession of the suit land prior to the transfer made by her and since there are materials and evidence on record to arrive at such a finding mere non discussion of the evidence by the appellate Court below is not fatal. In this connection it may further be mentioned that the trial Court elaborately discussed the evidence of both the parties in great detail and on proper assessment of the same arrived at a positive finding on the point of possession by referring to the evidence adduced by PWs 1, 2, 3 and 4 vis-a-vis the evidence of the DWs 1-3 that the plaintiff petitioners have failed to prove their possession in the suit land and the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 have been successful in proving their possession in the suit land. It is true that Order 41 rule 31 imposes a duty upon the appellate Court to re-assess the evidence afresh to arrive at a finding, in respect of each and every issue framed in the suit but it is now well settled that in case of affirmance if the appellate Court below failed to discuss the evidence in detail that would not stand in the way of the successful party if it is found that the trial Court has discussed the evidence in detail and there are, in fact, materials on record to arrive at such findings. I have already found that there are sufficient evidence on record for the Courts below to disbelieve the plaintiffs'' case and in view of the settled principles of law that the burden lies on the plaintiff to prove his case and he must succeed on his own strength only and not at the weakness of the adversary, the courts below took the correct view that since the plaintiff-petitioners have failed to prove their case they are not entitled to get any relief as prayed for.</u>

<u>9. The suit has been filed for the paramount declaration that the deed No. 231 dated 29-1-1986 of the Betagi Sub-Registry Office is fraudulent, null and void, inoperative and not binding upon the plaintiffs inasmuch as the vendor of the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 had no right, title and interest and possession in the suit land but it has been found on the admission of PW 1 himself that the defendant-opposite party No. 3 had right, title and interest in the suit land and both the courts below on scrutiny of the evidence both oral and documentary found that defendants are in possession of the suit land and the plaintiffs are not in possession of the suit land. It is now well settled that record of rights are documents of possession and in the instant case both SA and RS khatian stand in the name of defendant-opposite party No. 3. This documentary evidence coupled with the oral evidence of both the parties conclusively prove that defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 are in possession of the suit land and in that view of the matter the trial Court rightly observed that the instant suit as framed is not maintainable for declaration simpliciter without any prayer for consequential relief as it has been found that the plaintiffs are not in possession of the suit land and the cases relied on by Mr. Syed Ziaul Karim aptly supports the view.</u>

10. It is found by both the courts below that the plaintiffs-petitioners did not disclose the source of their title and it has been found as a matter of fact by the courts below that defendant-opposite party No. 3, in fact, inherited the suit property from her gather Lalu Farazi. Thus her title to the suit land is established beyond any doubt and in that view of the matter also the decree passed in Title Suit No. 16 of 1955 will have no bearing in the instant case because the plaintiffs have miserably failed to show how and when they have acquired the suit property.

11. In the result the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

Send down the records at once.

End.

lawyer:
Habibul Islam Bhuiyan, Advocate — For the Petitioners.
Kh Mahbubuddin Ahmed, with Sahabuddin Foez, Advocates — For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Chittagong Development Authority, represented by its Chairman and others ------ Petitioner
Vs. 
Rokeya Anwar and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule is directed against the judgment and decree dated 15-3-90 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Chittagong in Other Appeal No. 109 of 1989 affirming the judgment and decree passed by the learned Assistant Judge, 2nd Court, Chittagong in other Suit No. 96 of 1978 decreeing the suit.

2. Opposite Party No. 1 as plaintiff instituted a suit in the Court of the Assistant Judge, 2nd Court, Chittagong, being Other Suit No. 96 of 1978, praying for declaration of title and mandatory injunction alleging, inter alia, that suit plot No. 489 in Agrabad Residential Area, Chittagong was settled with Mofazal Ahmed and Fazal Hoque, defendant Nos. 7 and 8 respectively and they owned and possessed the same. Subsequently on taking permission from the Chittagong Development Authority (CDA) defendant Nos. 7 and 8 transferred the suit land to plaintiff No. 1 and in the lease deed in question 4.666 kathas of land was mentioned. In course of time the plaintiff constructed pucca buildings in the said premises and since then she has been residing therein. It has been further contended that at the time of construction of the house it was detected that the suit land actually comprises more than 4.666 kathas as mentioned in the deed of lease, following which the plaintiff filed an application before the CDA for granting her lease of the excess land in terms of the conditions embodied in the deed of agreement but the CDA instead of allowing the said prayer for lease of the excess land directed the plaintiff by letter dated 27-11-88 to surrender the excess land to the CDA and this necessitated the filing of the suit.

3. Defendant Nos. 1-5 contested the suit by filing written statements denying the material allegations of the plaint and contended, inter alia, that suit plot No. 489 with an area of 4.696 kathas only was leased out to the vendors of the plaintiff and the area of the land settled was specifically mentioned in the lease deed as 4.696 kathas of land and, as such, the plaintiff''s claim for more than 4.696 kathas of land cannot be entertained. It was further contended that the quantum of land allotted to the settle was clearly and specifically mentioned in the lease deed in terms of the lease agreement and the site-map and the sketch-map appended thereto are mere indications for the purpose of identification of the land settled and these by no means indicate the actual quantum of land demised. It was further contended that the plaintiff illegally encroached upon the land of schedule No. 2 to the plaint, in which she has no title and interest. Since the suit land as described in Schedule No. 2 to the plaint is admittedly the land of the Chittagong Development Authority, which fact has not been denied by the plaintiff or her predecessors-in-interest, the plaintiff cannot claim this excess land as a matter of right and, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed.

4. On the pleadings of the contending parties the trial Court framed four issues which are as follows:

1) Is the suit maintainable in its present form?

2) Has the plaintiff any cause of action to file the present suit?

3) Whether the plaintiff has any title, interest and possession in the suit property? and

4) To what relief, if any, the plaintiff is entitled to?

5. At the trial the plaintiff examined two witnesses and the contesting defendant examined four witnesses and exhibited documents in support of their respective cases. The learned Assistant Judge by the impugned judgment dated 31-1-89 decreed the suit and directed defendant Nos. 1-5 for giving settlement of the land of Schedule 2 to the plaint to the plaintiff within 60 days of the decree. Against the aforesaid judgment and decree the defendant petitioners took an appeal before the District Judge, Chittagong, who was pleased by the impugned judgment dated 15-3-93 to dismiss the appeal and affirmed the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court. It is to be noted in this connection that the trial Court while decreeing the suit did not declare the plaintiff''s title in the suit land, which tantamount to rejection of the plaintiff's prayer for declaration of her title in the suit land. It appears from the record that the plaintiff did not prefer any cross-objection against it after defendant-petitioners preferred Other Class Appeal No. 109 of 1989 before the District Judge, Chittagong and, as such, the plaintiff is deemed to have accepted the said refusal to declare her title in the suit land gracefully.

6. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree passed by the Additional District Judge, Chittagong the defendant-petitioners moved this Court and obtained the present Rule.

7. Mr. Habibul Islam Bhuiyan, the learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the defendant-petitioners, submits that the learned Courts below erred in law in decreeing the suit without noticing and considering that the suit was clearly barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and the same has occasioned failure of justice. Mr. Bhuiyan further submits that the learned Courts below seriously erred in law in holding that the boundaries of the suit land shall prevail over the area of the land mentioned in the lease agreement Ext. 2 and Ext. A, which clearly show that only 4.96 kathas of land in suit plot No. 489 was settled with the allotees, who are the vendors of the present plaintiff, and possession of the said land was made over to them and the same has resulted in error in the impugned decision occasioning failure of justice. Mr Bhuiyan further submits that in the face of the admitted fact that 4.966 kathas of land in suit plot No. 489 was settled with the plaintiff by lease agreement Ext. 2, and the plaintiff prayed for settlement of lease of the excess amount of land measuring 4.80 square feet and for a declaration of title over the excess amount of land than originally settled, the suit for declaration of title and permanent injunction relating to the said excess land is not contemplated in law and, as such, the learned Courts below misdirected themselves to decree the suit on an erroneous view of law and the same has occasioned failure of justice. Mr Bhuiyan further submits that the lay-out plan, site-map, etc. merely indicate the location and identification of the suit land and not the quantum of land settled with the allottees, which was specifically mentioned in the lease deed as 4.966 kathas of land only, and the plaintiff accepted the same and acted upon the same taking it to be so, as has been specifically admitted in paragraph 9 of the plaint, and consequently, the plaintiffs claim of title in the excess land is not contemplated in law and the learned Courts below clearly erred in law in decreeing the suit completely ignoring the scope of the suit and the same has occasioned failure of justice. Mr. Bhuiyan further submits that in view of the admitted fact that no vested right was created in favour of the plaintiff for getting settlement of Schedule 2 land and there was no corresponding legal obligation on the part of the CDA to grant lease of the said land in favour of the plaintiff, the learned Courts below erred in law in decreeing the suit completely ignoring this material aspect of the case and the law bearing on the subject and the same has occasioned failure of justice.

8. Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-opposite party, on the other hand, submits that the learned Courts below concurrently found that the plaintiff is entitled to get settlement of Schedule 2 land and the impugned judgment thus being concluded by concurrent findings of fact is not to be interfered with by this Court exercising power under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure. Mr. Khondker further submits that although the trial Court and, as a matter of fact, the appellate Court did not declare the plaintiff's title in the suit land, nevertheless there was a prayer for declaration of plaintiff''s title in the suit land and, as such, in the facts and circumstance of the case and the evidence on record, the plaintiff''s title in the suit land can be declared by this Court exercising revisional power under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure. Mr. Khondker further submits that since the plaintiff was successful in proving her case the suit has rightly been decreed and the said decree cannot be interfered with in revision as it has not occasioned any failure of justice.

9. Mr. Habibul Islam Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, has taken me through the impugned judgment. I also heard the learned Advocates of the contending parties extensively. In the impugned judgment of the trial Court the learned Assistant Judge found, as has been specifically mentioned in paragraph No. 9 of the plaint, that the plaintiff took settlement of 4.966 kathas of land and she acted on the same premises without any reservation but at the time of physical measurement it transpired that the suit land actually measured 5.666 kathas and not 4.966 kathas of land as mentioned in the lease deed Ext. 2 and for the excess land measuring 4.80 sqft she promptly prayed for settlement from the CDA on usual terms and conditions but on refusal of the defendants to settle the excess land to the plaintiff, she was constrained to file the present suit.

10. It appears that the learned trial Court without discussing and considering the oral evidence of the two PWs and four DWs and without considering the exhibited documents decreed the suit directing the defendants to settle the excess land measuring 4.80 sqft to the plaintiff on usual terms and conditions without spelling out anything as to how the plaintiff acquired a vested right in the said land and the CDA was under a legal obligation to grant lease of the said land to the plaintiff.

11. While disposing of the appeal the learned Additional District Judge also failed to discuss and consider any evidence of the 6 witnesses examined by the contending parties and dismissed the appeal on the finding that the plaintiff being in possession of Schedule 2 land as an integral part of Schedule 1 land has become the rightful owner of the scheduled land and, as such, she was entitled to get lease of Schedule 2 land on payment of proportionate premium to the CDA. The learned Additional District Judge further held that the boundary of the suit land will prevail over the area mentioned in the lease deed Ext. 2. From the impugned judgments it appears that neither the trial Court nor the appellate Court took the pains of discussing and considering the material evidence of the 6 witnesses examined by the contending parties.

12. The principle of law relating to appreciation of evidence is well settled. The Court has a right to believe or disbelieve a particular witness or a number of witnesses on assigning reasons but it has no right to ignore the evidence, particularly the material evidence, either oral or documentary, while deciding a case. It appears that both the Courts below clearly erred in law in completely ignoring the oral evidence of the six witnesses examined by the contending parties and in considering the legal incidence that flows therefrom in coming to their conclusions. The way in which the learned Courts below opted to keep the oral evidence of the 6 witnesses, examined by the contending parties in support of their respective cases, out of their consideration is grossly illegal and highly deplorable as it stands out prominently against the established principle of law for appreciation of evidence.

13. The moot question in this case is as to whether the plaintiff has any vested legal right in claiming the settlement of Schedule 2 land and whether the defendant CDA was under any legal obligation to grant lease of the excess land contained in Schedule 2 of the plaint in favour of the plaintiff. In the absence of any vested legal right on the part of the plaintiff and a corresponding legal obligation on the part of the CDA to grant lease of the excess land in favour of the plaintiff, the plaintiff's claim for settlement cannot be entertained. Neither the trial Court nor the lower appellate Court appeal's to have addressed itself to this vital question nor has it drawn any conclusion on it on the basis of the evidence on record. Nowhere in the impugned judgments it is found that the learned Courts below held that the plaintiff is entitled to get settlement of the suit land as of right and the CDA is under a legal obligation to make such settlement. The plaintiff did not make out any case of adverse possession, establishing any claim for life.

14. In paragraph No. 9 of the plaint it has been specifically mentioned that the plaintiff bona fide believed that she took the settlement of only 4.999 kathas of land from the CDA and acting on the said premises she owned and possessed the suit land but while taking actual measurement of the suit land at the time of construction of her house it was detected that the suit land actually measured 5.666 kathas and not 4.966 kathas as mentioned in the lease deed. In the facts and circumstances of the case the trial Court as well as the appellate Court rightly did not find plaintiff's title in the suit land described in Schedule 2 of the plaint.

<u>15. Admittedly, the CDA is the owner of Schedule 2 land, as such, in the absence of a definite proof of acquisition of title or interest by the plaintiff in Schedule 2 land and a corresponding legal obligation on the part of the CDA to grant lease of the Schedule 2 land to the plaintiff, there cannot be any direction by the Court upon the CDA to grant lease of the excess land in favour of the plaintiff. In the frame of the suit the prayer for a direction upon the defendant CDA to grant lease of Schedule 2 land to the plaintiff appears to be barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The Courts below seriously erred in law in decreeing the suit on a casual view of the matter and without considering this vital legal question and the law bearing on the subject and the same has occasioned failure of justice.</u>

<u>16. For a proper appreciation of the term ''obligation'' as defined in section 3 of the Specific Relief Act, we may profitably refer to the provision of section 54 of the said Act. The expression ''obligation'' as defined in section 3 of the Specific Relief Act means and includes every duty which is enforceable by law while the word ''obligation'' occurring in section 54 of the said Act may be treated as a tie or bond which constrains a person to do or suffer something. It implies a right in another person to which it is co-related and it restricts the freedom of the obligee with respect to definite act or acts and forbearances. At any rate such an obligation must be a legal obligation, and not merely a moral obligation having reference to a legal enforceable right in the opposite party. In our case under review, I am unable to find any such legal enforceable right in the plaintiff and a corresponding legal obligation on the defendant CDA for grant of lease of Schedule 2 land as mandated by the learned Courts below. We get support of this view in the case of Aftabuddin vs. Mahfuzus Sobhan & ors., reported in 42 DLR (AD) 78 relied by the petitioners.</u>

17. Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Counsel for the opposite parties, has referred to me the case of S Zafar Ahmed vs. Abdul Khaliq,, reported in 16 DLR (WP, Karachi) 49. In this case their Lordships explained the scope of section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Mr. Khondker next referred to me the case of Alamgir & others vs. Jainal Abedin, reported in 34 DLR 325. In this case also their Lordships explained the scope of section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure in giving relief to the aggrieved party under given circumstances. There is no dispute to the proposition of law enunciated by their Lordships that a Court exercising power under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure is competent to correct any error of law committed by any subordinate Court occasioning failure of justice. But the reported cited decisions appear to have no relevance to the facts of the present case and, as such, the cited decisions are of no assistance to the plaintiff-opposite party.

<u>18. In this case the plaintiff filed the suit praying for getting lease of Schedule 2 land from the CDA. Subsequently, of course, the plaint was amended adding a prayer for declaration of title. Nowhere from the record it is found as to how the plaintiff acquired title in Schedule 2 land. It has been clearly admitted in paragraph No. 9 of the plaint that the plaintiff got settlement of 4.999 kathas of land on the basis of lease deed Ext. 2 and she acted on the same premises bona fide believing that the acquired title and interest in that quantum of land only and it never occurred to her that she got interest in 5.666 kathas of land till before the physical measurement of the suit land at the time of construction of her house thereon. It is thus evident that the additional 4.80 sqft of land was clearly beyond the contemplation and comprehension of the contending parties while concluding the lease deed Ext. 2. This excess land measuring 4.80 square feet thus clearly falls outside the purview of the lease agreement in question and consequently, the plaintiff cannot claim the same as a matter of right and the defendant CDA cannot be compelled to give settlement of the same to the plaintiff. It is thus crystal clear that the plaintiff did not acquire any title in Schedule 2 land. The only material question that remained for consideration by the Courts was whether the plaintiffs claim for getting lease of excess land contained in Schedule 2 of the plaint could be entertained and a direction from the Court to the CDA for granting such lease of the same in favour of the plaintiff could lawfully be made. Since I have already found that there is nothing on record to prove that the plaintiff has acquired any right and title in Schedule 2 land admittedly the CDA is the owner of Schedule 2 land, and there being no corresponding legal obligation on the part of the CDA to grant lease of the same to the plaintiff, the Court cannot give a mandate compelling the defendant CDA to grant lease of the suit land to the plaintiff. Such a direction could be given only if a clear case was made out in favour of the plaintiff establishing a definite legal right for her for the enforcement of which the Court could come to her rescue in a properly constituted suit for Specific Performance of Contract. But, in the instant case, in the light of the case made out in the plaint and the evidence adduced at the trial I do not find any such legal right in favour of the plaintiff and a corresponding legal obligation on the part of the defendant CDA for granting lease of the Schedule 2 land to the plaintiff and, as such, the impugned decree passed by the learned Assistant Judge and subsequently affirmed by the learned appellate Court cannot be sustained in law. The impugned judgment is thus found to be neither legal nor proper and the same has occasioned failure of justice. The concurrent findings of fact arrived at by the learned Courts below are not supported by the evidence on record and the law bearing on the subject and, as such, the same are not sustainable. For the reasons stated above the submissions made by the learned Counsel for the petitioners are sustained and those made by the learned Counsel for the opposite party are repelled.</u>

19. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and decree passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Chittagong in Title Appeal. No. 109 of 1989 affirming the judgment and decree passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Sadar, Chittagong in Other Suit No. 96 of 1978 are set aside and Other Suit No. 96 of 1978 of the 2nd Court of the Assistant Judge, Chittagong is hereby dismissed.

Send down the lower Court records at once.

End.
