full_judgment:
This Rule, calls in question the legality and propriety of the judgment and decree dated 24101989 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, First Court, Barisal, in Title Appeal No. 64 of 1978, dismissing the appeal and affirming the judgment and decree dated 30-11-1977 passed by the learned Munsif, First Court, Barisal, dismissing the suit.

2. Short facts leading to this Rule are that on 5-3-1974, the petitioners as plaintiffs, instituted Title Suit No. 175 of 1974, in the First Court of Munsif, Barisal, impleading the opposite parties as defendants for declaration of title in respect of land described in Schedule "Ka" of the plaint and for further declaration that the auction proceedings as described in Schedule Kha of the plaint is illegal, ultra vires and not binding upon the plaintiffs.

3. The plaintiff's case, put in a nutshell, is that the suit land measuring an area 1.52 acres, appertaining to plot Nos. 3541, 3554 and 1770 of RS Khatian No. 95 and SA Khatian No. 198 of Mouza Solak, the area of CS Khatian No. 1027 having 7.84 acres of land, originally belonged to Edel Sharif who died leaving behind two sons namely, Abdul Aziz and Abdul Kader, two daughters namely, Sonabaru @ Shams-unless and Pakhi Bibi @ Fakirunnessa; that they having been interested in the suit property as heirs of Edel Sharif made a transfer there-of to one Abdul Jabbar by a registered kabala dated 31st Chaitra, 1340 BS corresponding to 14-6-1933 AD; that Abdul Jabbar possessed the suit land and after his death his heirs i.e. the plaintiffs, have been possessing the same; that RS. and SA record of the suit land had been wrongly prepared in the names of the defendants; that in the first part of Aswin, 1381 BS they came to know about the erroneous record of rights of the suit land; that they came to know that the deceased defendant No. 1 Syed Abdus Sattar purchased the suit land including other lands in auction; subsequently, defendant Nos. 2 and 3 (herein opposite party Nos. 9 and 10) purchased the suit land from Syed Abdus Sattar and by dint of that purchase, the defendant Nos. 2 and 3 have got no possession over the suit land; that the plaintiffs are in possession in the suit land on cultivation and by transferring some portion thereof to South Solak Free Primary School by a registered kabala. Hence, the suit.

4. The defendant. Nos. 2 and 3 (hereinafter opposite party Nos. 9-10 contested the suit by filing a, written statement, denying all the material allegations made in the plaint, contending inter alias, that the suit is not maintainable in the present form and the same is barred by limitation; that RS and SA record were prepared in the names of defendants on consideration of their right, title, interest and possession; that the processes of Rent Suit No. 4781 of 1934 and Rent Execution Case No. 1350 of 1935 were duly served upon the debtors; that Syed Abdus Sattar, predecessor of the contesting defendants owned the suit land by dint of purchase in auction on 15-11-1935; that the auction sale was confirmed on 7-1-1936 and delivery of possession was made on 26-5-1936; that the heirs of Edel Sharif filed a case under section 173(3) of the BT Act for setting aside the auction sale held in the aforesaid Rent Suit and the suit was dismissed on contest on 21-7-36; that the name of Abdul Jabbar was not mutated in the office of the superior landlord; that no notice under section 26C of the BT Act was given to the landlord informing of transfer made in favour of Abdul Jabbar that the heirs of Abdul Jabbar were not necessary parties in the rent suit; that the deceased Syed Abdus Sattar instituted Title Suit No. 251 of 1939 in the Sixth Court of Munsif, Barisal for the purpose of evicting the heirs of Edel Sharif from the suit land; that the suit was decreed; that the plaintiffs have got no right, title, interest and possession in the suit land; and that the suit is liable to be dismissed.

5. On the pleadings, following issues were settled :

(a) Whether the suit was maintainable in its present form ?

(b) Whether the suit was barred by limitation?

(c) Whether the impugned auction sale was forged and can be declared as void and not binding upon the plaintiffs? (d) Whether the plaintiffs have right, title, interest and possession in the suit land?

(e) To what relief, if any, the plaintiffs were entitled to?

6. In course of trial the plaintiffs in all examined three witnesses and the defendants examined four witnesses in support of their respective case.

7. Eventually, after hearing the learned Judge of the trial Court by the judgment and decree dated 30-11-1977 dismissed the suit. Against which the plaintiffs as appellants preferred Title Appeal No. 64 of 1978 in the Court of District Judge, Barisal, which was ultimately heard by the learned Subordinate Judge, First Court, Barisal who by the judgment and decree, dated 24-10-1989 dismissed the appeal.

8. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgments and decrees the plaintiffs as petitioners obtained the present Rule.

9. Mr Abdul Quayum, the learned Advocate appearing with Mr Md Ali Reza on behalf of the petitioners, supports the Rule and submits that the learned Judges of the Courts below misconstrued the provisions of sections 12(2), 26C and 146A(3) of the BT Act, thereby came to an erroneous finding causing serious miscarriage of justice. The learned Counsel adds that the Courts below committed an error of law in holding that the plaintiffs' suit was barred by limitation, inasmuch as the suit was not filed within six years from the date of knowledge of the auction sale. The learned Counsel further submits that the Courts below committed an error of law in not considering the presumption of service of notice of the plaintiffs' kabala dated 14-6-1933 upon the superior landlords under section 12 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. He adds that the Courts below committed an error of law in not finding that the entire tenancy was not represented under section 146A of the Bengal Tenancy Act.

10. The learned Counsel submits that the auction sale was held on 15-11-1935 i.e. but the kabala was executed on 14-6-1933, i.e. prior to the auction sale and, as such, by the said kabala the plaintiffs' right, title and interest will not be extinguished. He adds that the Courts below relied upon certain documents wherein the predecessors of the plaintiffs were not a party, so the same are not binding upon them. In support of his contention, the learned Counsel referred the provisions of law prescribed in sections 12(2), 26C and 146A,(3) of the BT Act and also refers the case of Monoranjan Dutta Choudhury vs Sandhyarani Devi Choudhurani and others reported in 5 DLR 288 wherein it is held—

"Bengal Tenancy Act (VIII of 1885)

Sections 15, 146A.

Failure to give notice of succession as provided by section 15, if exonerates the Landlord, to make the successor a party to a rent suit, if the landlord otherwise gets notice of succession.

The failure to give notice of the succession as directed by section 15, Bengal Tenancy Act, does not exonerate the land lord from making the tenant a party to the suit for rent, if the landlord otherwise comes to know of the succession. The third clause of sub-section (3) of section 46A speaks of notice under section 15; but that does not mean that if the landlord other-wise gets the notice, he is not bound to make him a party. The general rule is that in a suit for rent all the landlords and all the tenants should be made parties. Section 146A comes as an exception to that general rule to meet cases where it may be difficult for the landlord to find out all the co-sharer tenants. "

11. The learned Counsel further submits that the learned Judge of the Court of appeal below wrongly relied upon the case of Jullfu Mona vs Noab Ali Sarkar and others reported in 27 DLR 441 wherein it is held—

"Bengal Tenancy Act (VIII of 1885)

Section 146A

In case of a transfer if the landlord has not been notified as required in clause (iii) of subsection (3) of section 146A the landlord is not bound to make him a party in a rent suit and if sale takes place in his absence, the tenancy shall in terms of sub-sections (2) and (3) be deemed to have been represented and the sale will be a rent sale.

Section 146A of the Bengal Tenancy Act the provision of which is applicable in this particular case, says that there must be relationship between the landlord and tenant and it further provides how the tenancy is represented, transferee who has gone to the extent that even has not notified in terms of section 26C or who has not noticed in terms of section 15 and whose name does not appear in the land-lord's rent roll need not be made a party in a rent suit and minus them the tenancy will still be represented."

12. The learned Counsel lastly submits that the learned Judges of the Courts below failed to weigh and sift the evidence on record as required by law and evidently fell in an error in coming to his ultimate decision occasioning failure of justice.

13. Mr Mohammad Ullah, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of Mrs. Rowshan Ara Begum, Advocate for the opposite party Nos. 9-10, opposes the Rule and submits that the suit itself is not maintainable in its present form, inasmuch as the plaintiffs could not prove their right, title and possession in the suit land. He adds that both the Courts below categorically, held that without praying for any consequential relief the suit is barred by law. He lastly submits that the judgments and decrees of the Courts below are just and proper which call for no interference by this Court.

14. In order to appreciate the submissions advanced by the learned Counsels, I have gone through the revisional application, plaint, deposition of the witnesses, all exhibits, judgments and decrees of the Courts below, other materials on record and given my anxious consideration to the submissions advanced by the learned Counsels of both sides.

15. Now the question that calls for my consideration is, whether the learned Subordinate Judge, First Court, Barisal, committed any error of law, resulting in an error in the decision, occasioning failure of justice in passing the impugned Judgment and decree dated 24-10-1989 affirming the judgment and decree dated 30-11-1977 passed by the learned Munsif, First Court, Barisal, in Title Suit No. 175 of 1974.

16. Admittedly, the suit land originally be-longed to Edel Sharif. The plaintiffs, on the basis of a registered kabala deed dated 14-6-1933 (Exhibit 1), claim right, title over the suit land. Exhibit 1 is the certified copy of the aforesaid registered kabala. Exhibits 2-2(b) are CS, RS and SA khatians purported to have been proved that the suit land was recorded in the CS, khatian in the name of Edel Sharif. RS and SA khatians prove that the record of the suit land had been made in the name of Syed Abdus Sattar, predecessor of defendants. Exhibit 3 is plot Index of the suit property appertaining to some plots as mentioned in the Schedule of the plaint.

17. The defendants claimed their right, title, interest and possession over the suit land on the basis of auction purchase made in the rent suit and subsequent transfer has been made to them by the auction purchaser Syed Abdus Sattar on 12-1-1973 by registered kabala, marked as Exhibit A. It appears that on behalf of the defendants a series of documents have been filed and marked as Exhibits A-G(4).

18. On critical analysis of the evidence on record, I find that both the Courts below concurrently held that the suit land was actually sold in auction and the auction purchaser Syed Abdus Sattar purchased it in open auction. It further appears that both the Courts below concurrently relied upon the Exhibit B Sale certificate of the land by which Syed Abdus Sattar purchased the suit land on 15-11-1935. Exhibit C, Miscellaneous Case No. 298 of 1996 under section 174(3) of the BT Act for setting aside the auction sale and the case was dismissed on contest. Exhibit C(1) writ of the delivery of possession on which that possession of the suit land was handed over to the auction purchaser on 29-6-1936.

<u>19. It further appears that the plaintiffs claiming their right, title and interest only upon the Exhibit 1, save and except the said document they have no other supporting papers to show that after purchase the plaintiffs tried to pay rent and to get necessary right over the suit land. Furthermore, it has come to notice that the defendants' predecessors possessed the suit land by purchasing the same in auction and the defendants also got possession over the same. On perusal of the documentary and oral evidence on record, the defendants are found in possession as such the plaintiffs' suit for declaration without having prayer for recovery of khas possession in the suit land, the suit is not maintainable in the present form. Having regard to the facts I am in agreement with the concurrent finding of facts arrived at by the Courts below.</u>

<u>20. It appears that the findings arrived at by the Courts below having been rested  upon consideration and discussion of legal evidence and materials on record and also on a correct and proper analysis of the legal aspects involved in the case and the findings being findings of fact are not liable to be disturbed by the High Court Division in exercise of power under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure.</u>

21. In the cases of Shambu Nath Poddar vs Bangladesh Railway and others reported in 43 DLR (AD) 82 wherein it is held:

"A revision court acts beyond its jurisdiction in setting aside concurrent finding of fact, when there is no misreading and misappreciation of the evidence on record."

22. In the case of Kochi Mia @ Khocha Mia vs Surly Mia being dead his heirs Md Fazlur Rahman and others reported in 51 DLR (AD) 57 wherein it is held:

"Code of Civil Procedure

Section 115

The High Court Division as a revisional court had hardly any jurisdiction to set aside the findings of fact by the appellate Court and that also without discussing any fault in the factual finding by the said Court."

23. In the case of Abdul Matin Chowdhury vs Chapala Rani Sen and others reported in 37 DLR (AD) 205, it is held that concurrent finding of facts arrived at by the trial Court and the First Appellate Court is binding upon the High Court Division in a second appeal unless it could be shown that the said finding had been vitiated by an error of law or of procedure which had affected the merit of the case. Similar views were taken in the cases of Abdul Mutaleb vs Md Mustakim Ali and others reported in 1999 BLD (AD) 156 and Abdul Mannan Khan and others vs Bangladesh and others reported in 38 DLR (AD) 201.

I have gone through the Provisions of sections 12(2), 26C and 146A,(3) of the BT Act and gone through the facts of the case reported in 5 DLR 288 as referred by the learned Counsel for the petitioner. The facts leading in reference to the above provisions of the above case are distinguishable with that of the instant case and, as such, the same has no manner of application in this particular case. Moreover, the learned Judge of the Court of appeal below rightly considered and relied upon the principle enunciated in the case reported in 27 DLR 441.

24. Having regard to the facts, I find that all the issues involved in the suit have rightly been framed, considered and decided by the trial Court with reference to the evidence and materials on record. Moreover, I do not find any misreading or non consideration of the evidence on record. The impugned judgment and decree passed by the Court of appeal below are well reasoned backed by sufficient oral and documentary evidence, which cannot be interfered with. Therefore, I failed to discover any merit in the submissions advanced by the learned Counsel for the petitioners.

25. Having considered the facts and circumstances of the case and foregoing narrative, I am of the view that the judgments and decrees of the Courts below suffer from no illegality and impropriety, which call for no interference by this Court. Thus the Rule having no merit fails.

26. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to cost. The impugned judgment and decree dated 24-10-1989 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, (now Joint District Judge) First Court, Barisal, in Title Appeal No. 64 of 1978 affirming the Judgment and decree dated 30-11-1977 passed by the learned Munsif (now Assistant Judge), First Court, Barisal, in Title Suit No. 175 of 1974 dismissing the suit is hereby affirmed.

Send down the lower Court's record at once with a copy of judgment for information.

End.

full_judgment:
Hasan Foez Siddique J: This Rule is directed against the order dated 8-7-2001 passed by the Subordinate Judge, First Court, Moulavi Bazar in Title Execution Case No. 1 of 2001 rejecting the application for staying of the further proceeding in the said execution case.

2. The opposite party No. 1 filed Title Suit No. 22 of 1992 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Moulavi Bazar for declaration of his title in the suit land and recovery of khas possession alleging, inter alia, the suit property Rangi Chara Tea Garden originally belonged to Ext-Jaminder of Protimpasha Nababjada Ali Askar Akha. Record of right was prepared in his name. He died leaving behind only son Ali Laor Khan as his heir who appointed one Imtiaz Ali as his attorney to maintain the garden. The defendant No. 1 was Head Clerk of the said tea garden and used to live in a staff quarter of the tea garden. He was released from service in 1985 and was directed to vacate the staff quarter but claiming title of said Tea Garden he denied to vacate the quarter. Hence the plaintiff filed the instant suit for declaration of title and for possession. Defendant Nos. 1 and 2 appeared in the suit and filed written statement. The suit was decreed on 19-9-2000 on contest against defendant No. 2 and ex parte against the defendant No. 1 on 5-11-2000. The defendant No. 1 filed an application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code for setting aside the said ex parte decree which was registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 17 of 2000. In the meantime, the said decree was put in execution in Title Execution Case No. 1 of 2001. Then the defendant-petitioner filed an application for staying the further proceeding of said Execution Case. The learned Subordinate Judge by the impugned order dated 8-7-2001 rejected the said application for stay. Against which the defendant moved revisional application before this Court and obtained Rule and ad-interim order of stay of further proceeding of said Execution Case.

<u>3. We have heard the learned Advocate, perused the revisional application and other materials on record. It appears that earlier opposite party No. 1 instituted aforesaid suit for declaration of title and recovery of possession and obtained ex parte decree against the petitioner on 19-9-2000. Thereafter, on 5-11-2000 the petitioner filed an application for setting aside the said ex parte decree under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code. In the meantime the said decree was put in execution. Accordingly, he filed an application for further stay of the proceeding of the said Execution Case which was rejected by the learned Subordinate Judge.</u>

<u>4. Mr M Khaled Ahmed, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, relying upon the decision of the case of Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Dhaka vs Abdul Rab reported in 4 BLC (AD) 92 submits that as the ex parte decree is under challenged so, for the ends of justice till the disposal of the said application, further proceeding of the execution case was liable to be stayed. In the cited case it appears that a suit was decreed ex parte. Thereafter, appellant before the Appellate Division filed a regular Title for setting aside the ex parte decree on the ground of fraud and prayed for stay of the further proceeding of the execution case arising out of said ex parte decree. High Court Division refused to stay the further proceeding of the execution case but their Lordships of Appellate Division stayed further proceeding of the execution Case till disposal of the said Title Suit for setting aside the decree.</u>

<u>5. In view of the aforesaid decision and considering the facts and circumstances of the case, we are of the opinion that the Executing Court has failed to exercise its discretion properly and thereby erroneously rejected the prayer for stay.</u>

6. Consequently, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to cost. The impugned order is set aside. The further proceeding of Title Execution Case No. 1 of 2001 pending in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Moulvibazar be stayed till disposal of the Miscellaneous Case No. 17 of 2000 and the learned Subordinate Judge, First Court, Moulvibazar is directed to hear and dispose of the said Miscellaneous Case as early as possible preferably within four months from the date of receipt of this order.

Communicate the order.

End.

full_judgment:
By this application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the judgment and decree dated 31 August, 1987 passed in a suit under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act has been called in question whereupon a Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party No. 1 to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 31-8-87 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Madarganj, Jamalpur in Other Class Suit No. 81 of 1984 should not be set aside.

2. When the plaintiff brings a suit under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act based on possession, the question of title of the plaintiff or defendant is relevant or not is the question involved in this Rule.

3. For the purpose of answering to the question posed, the factual canvass of the matter may be adverted to which are summarised as follows :

The opposite party No. 1 as plaintiff instituted Other Class Suit No. 398 of 1981 in the Second Court of Munsif, Jamalpur under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act for recovery of khas possession. The suit on transfer to the court of Munsif, Madarganj was renumbered there as Other Class Suit No. 81 of 1984.

4. Sadar Akanda, Riazuddin, Ayenuddin and Moyanuddin had been the owners to the extent of 8 annas, 4 annas, 2 annas and 2 annas share respectively. The superior landlord Brojendra Kishore Roy auction purchased the suit land along with other land in execution of decree of Money Suit No. 786 of 1929. The said landlord, thereafter, settled 2.72 acres of land to Mohammad Ali Akand by a registered deed of settlement dated 12-4-1947. Mafizuddin Pramanik, also, took settlement with respect to .52 acres of land by a registered deed of settlement dated 26-4-1947 who subsequently transferred the said 0.52 acres of land by a sale deed dated 4-10-1984 in favour of plaintiff and Amezuddin. Mohammad Ali sold 0.17 acres of land to defendant No. 10, Md Shahabuddin. Mohammad Ali transferred 0.52 acres of land by a sale deed to Sibaruddin, the predecessor-in-interest of the defendant Nos. 1-9. Mohammad Ali died leaving behind the plaintiff and Amejuddin as the only legal heirs. Amejuddin subsequently died leaving behind his 4 sons, defendant Nos. 10-13 and 2 daughters defendant Nos. 14 and 15. The plaintiff while in possession of the suit land covering 0.51 acres, the same was wrongly recorded in the name of the defendant Nos. 1-9 and Shahabuddin, the defendant No. 10. The plaintiff grew jute in the month of Baishak, 1388 BS and took the jute and cultivated the land for growing Aman paddy. The defendant Nos. 1-4 taking the advantage of the wrong record in their names, on 13th Sraban, 1388 BS corresponding to 15-8-1981 being armed with deadly weapons entered into the suit land and dispossessed the plaintiff therefrom. The plaintiffs, thus, had been constrained to file the suit.

5. The defendant Nos. 1-4 contested the suit by presenting written statement taking the stand that Sadar Akanda was the rightful owner of the suit land. Sadar Akanda died leaving behind 4 sons namely Mahmud Ali, Akbar Ali, Nayebullah and Kabaj Ali and one daughter. During the lifetime of Sadar Akand, Nayebullah died leaving son Reazul. Kabaj Ali, thereafter, died leaving two sons Mayezuddin and Ayenuddin. Sadar Akanda, Reazuddin, Moizuddin and Ayenuddin had 8 annas, 4 annas, 2 annas and 2 annas share respectively in the suit CS Khatian No. 142. Further pleading is that the heirs of Sadar Akand and Reazuddin, Moizuddin and Ayenuddin used to enjoy their properties amicably. Akbor died leaving a son Efazuddin and the said Efazuddin transferred 0.85 acres of land by way of sale deed dated 20-3-1943 AD to Siberuddin, the predecessor-in-interest of the defendants. It is also pleaded that Mofizuddin transferred the share inherited by him from his mother to the plaintiff and Amejuzzin on 4-10-1984. The plaintiff and Amejuddin, also, transferred 0.52 acres of land in favour of the father of the defendant Nos. 1-4, Siberuddin by way of a deed of transfer. It is also averred that Mahmud Ali transferred 0.52 acres of land in favour of Siberuddin, the predecessor father of the defendant Nos. 1-4 by way of sale deed dated 11-5-1957. It is further stated that the suitland had been correctly recorded in the name of Siberuddin, the predecessor father of the defendants. It is asserted that plaintiff had no possession on the suit land and, as such, the question of dispossession did not at all arise.

6. The pleadings of the parties gave rise to the following issues:

১। বর্তমান আকারে ও প্রকারে মোকদ্দমা আনয়ন করার অধিকার বাদীর আছে কি না?

২। বাদীর মোকদ্দমা তামাদি আইনে বারিত কিনা?

৩। বাদীর মোকদ্দমা পক্ষ দোষে দষিত কিনা?

৪। নালিশী ভূমিতে বাদীর কোন দখল ছিল কিনা?

৫। বাদী পক্ষ পূর্ণ দখল পেতে পারে কিনা?

৬। আদালতের ন্যায় বিচারে বাদী অন্য কোন প্রতিকার পেতে হকদার কিনা?

7. Both the parties adduced evidence both oral as well as documentary in support of their respective contentions/pleas.

8. Three PWs including the plaintiff himself had been examined from the side of the plaintiff and equal number of witnesses had been examined by the defendants.

9. The learned trial Judge held that the suit is maintainable in its present form. Learned trial Judge further held that the plaintiff filed the suit within prescribed period of time from the date of dispossession. The learned trial Judge further found that the suit is not bad for defect of parties. The learned trial Judge ultimately recorded the finding that the plaintiff through legal evidence could prove his possession and subsequent dispossession and he was entitled to get a decree of recovery of khas possession. With the above findings and deciding all the issues in favour of the plaintiff, the trial Judge decreed the suit.

10. Feeling aggrieved by the aforesaid decision of the trial Judge, the defendants approached this Court in an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule raising the contention that the learned Assistant Judge erred in law in not deciding the title of the property in dispute in favour of the defendant and also in not holding that the presumption of the correctness of the record of right standing in the name of the defendants had not been rebutted by the plaintiff and also that the learned Judge misapprised and misread the evidence on record and by this misreading and misappraisal, the merit of the decision of the case has been seriously affected.

11. The plaintiff-opposite-party No. 1 resisted the Rule by filing an affidavit-in-opposition controverting all the material averments made in the Revision petition and raised the contentions that in a suit under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act the question of title is irrelevant and the court will not adjudicate upon the title of the parties and the plaintiff-opposite-party through legal evidence proved his previous possession and subsequent dispossession by the defendant-petitioners and the learned trial Judge did not commit any error of law warranting interference in the exercise of the power under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

12. The defendant-petitioner is represented by the learned Advocate Mr Abdul Hamid. The plaintiff-opposite-party No. 1 is represented by the learned Advocate Mr Md Muzammel Hossain.

13. It is canvassed vigorously from the side of the petitioner that the record of right having been prepared in the name of the defendants, there is presumption of the correctness of the entries of the record of right and also a presumption of possession in favour of the defendants and the said presumption attached to the record of right has not been rebutted by the plaintiff. The case of Aminuddin Biswas vs Miajan Biswas and others 12 DLR 103 has been referred to in support of the contention raised.

14. In repelling the said contention it is submitted from the side of the opposite party that the presumption of the correctness of the entry in the record of right and the presumption of possession is kept beyond the purview of a suit under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act.

15. In order to appreciate the contentions raised, it is appropriate to look at the provision of section 9 of the Specific Relief Act which runs as follows :

"9. Suit by Person Dispossessed of immoveable Property :

If any person is dispossessed without his consent of immoveable property otherwise than in due course of law, he or any person claiming through him may, by suit, recover possession thereof, not with-standing any other title that may be set up in such suit.

Nothing in this section shall bar any person from suing to establish his title to such property and to recover possession thereof.

No suit under this section shall be brought against the Government.

No appeal shall lie from any order or decree passed in any suit instituted under this section, nor shall any review of any such order or decree be allowed".

16. From a plain reading of the said provision, it becomes manifestly clear that if a person, who has without his consent, been dispossessed of immoveable property otherwise than in due course of law, he is entitled to recover possession thereof by filing a suit within the period of 6 months of dispossession.

17. Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act has been enacted to prevent persons from ousting men from possession except by due course of law. It is a section the object of which is to drive persons who want to dispossess persons and prevent them from going with a high hand and dispossessing such persons. The object of this section is to provide speedy remedy for that class or classes of case or cases where person/persons in physical possession of property is forcibly dispossessed from it against his/their will and consent. This section is more than a reproduction of the provisions of Roman Law by which the Praetor was entitled to possession to a person forcibly dispossessed. The only question, therefore, in a case under this section is whether a person while in physical possession of an immovable property has been dispossessed of the same otherwise than in due course of law and if so dispossessed he can be restored to such possession under the decree of the court if the suit is instituted within the period stipulated in the section.

18. In Yar Mohammad vs Lakshmi Das AIR 1959 Allahabad 1 the objects and purposes of section 9 have been detailed. The Full Bench of Allahabad High Court observed thus :

"No question of title either of the plaintiff or of the defendant can be raised or gone into under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act. The plaintiff will be entitled to succeed without proving any title on which he can fall back upon and the defendant cannot succeed even though he may be in a position to establish the best of all titles. The restoration of possession in such a suit is, however, always subject to a regular title suit and the person who has the real title or even the better title cannot therefore be prejudiced in any way by a decree in such a suit. It will always be open to him to establish his title in a regular suit and to recover back possession".

The High Court further observed :

"Law respects possession even if there is no title to support it. It will not permit any person to take the law in his own hands and to dispossess a person in actual possession without having recourse to a court. No person can be allowed to become a judge in his own cause". As observed by Edge, CJ, in Wall Ahmed Khan vs Ayudhia Kundu ILR 13 Allahabad at page 558

"The object of the section was to drive that person who wanted to eject a person into the proper court and to prevent them from going with a high hand ejecting such persons".

19. Similar view was expressed by a Division Bench of the Patna High Court in the case of Akal Ahir vs Baijnath Das AIR 1924 Patna 709 Dawson Millar, CJ who agreed to the main judgment which was delivered by Mallick J. laid down the possession of law in she following guidelines:

"There is abundant authority for the proposition that if a person is in possession of land even without title thereto he cannot be successfully turned out by another person".

20. The law on the subject had been dealt with by the High Court of Bombay in KK Verma vs Narain Das C Malkani AIR 1954 Bombay 358, Chagla, CJ observed as under:

"Under the Indian law the possession of a tenant who has ceased to be a tenant is protected by law. Although he may not have a right to continue in possession after the termination of the tenancy his possession is juridical and that possession is protected by statute. Under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act a tenant who has ceased to be a tenant may sue for possession against his landlord if the landlord deprives him of possession otherwise than in due course of law".

21. A similar question came up for consideration before their Lordships of the Supreme Court of India in Lallu Jaswant Singh vs Raojagadish Singh AIR 1968 SC 620. Their Lordships quoted with approval the observation made by Chagla CJ in K K Verma vs Narain Das C Malkani AIR 1954 Bombay 358 and also the observation made by the Full Bench of the Allahabad High Court in Yar Mohammad and another vs Lakshmi Das AIR 1959 Allahabad 1. After reviewing the case law enunciated by the Privy Council and different High Courts, the Supreme Court ruled that law on the scope of section 9 of the Specific Relief Act had been correctly stated by the Privy Council, by Chagla CJ and by the Full Bench of the Allahabad High Court.

22. In the case of Dr Kudrot Ali vs Md Munsur Ali, 16 DLR 599 as referred to from the side of the opposite party, a Division Bench consisting of SM Morshed, CJ and Abdullah, J held that in a suit under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act, the court will not adjudicate upon the title of the parties. In the said case good number of authorities has been discussed and considered.

<u>23. The law, thus, stands is that, when a plaintiff brings a suit for recovery of possession based on possession under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act he will be entitled to get a decree for possession against a defendant without proving his title. The remedy under this section being a summary one is intended to restore the status quo ante on all questions of title whether of the plaintiff or the defendant are out of place and cannot be allowed either to be raised or to be considered. This remedy does not in any way preclude the successful assertion of a possessory title in the ordinary way in a proper case. The restoration of possession is, however, always subject to a regular Title suit and the person who has the real title or even better title cannot be prejudiced in any way by a decree in such a suit. It will be always open to him to establish his title in a regular suit and recover back possession.</u>

24. In Amiruddin Biswas vs Miajar Biswas and others 12 DLR 102 referred to from the side of the petitioner the presumption of the correctness of the entry in the record of right was the question that fell for determination. I am afraid the said case is of no assistance for answering to the question involved in the instant Rule. The contention so advanced on behalf of the petitioner is, thus, devoid of any substance.

25. It has already been stated that section 9 of the Specific Relief Act provides for a summary and speedy remedy through the medium of Civil Court for the restoration of possession of party dispossessed by another person. Previous possession and dispossession without the consent of the plaintiff or otherwise than in due course of law having been the issue in the suit—let me see whether the plaintiff could prove that before dispossession he was in possession of the suit property and the suit was filed within 6 months of the alleged date of dispossession.

26. In the plaint it is stated that one Mohammad Ali and others remained the owner and possessor of the suit land on the basis of a registered deed of settlement from the Superior landlords who auction purchased the land in execution of a decree in a money suit and the plaintiff and his father acquired the said property by way of purchase from the said Mohammad Ali and others. It is also stated that the plaintiff remained in possession of the suit land and while in possession on 13th Sraban, 1388 BS corresponding to 15-8-1981 he was dispossessed from the suitland by the defendants. The allegation made by the plaintiff in the plaint had been denied by the defendants setting up their claim that the suitland was never put to auction and was also never purchased by the superior landlords and the plaintiff had no possession at all on the suitland and the defendants had been in possession of the same. Both the parties adduced evidence in support of their claims. The parties also produced documentary evidence to have their claim established and those documents were also exhibited as Exhibits. On perusal of the impugned judgment it appears that the learned trial Judge considered the evidences of the PWs and DWs and made a comparative study/analysis of the evidences adduced from both the parties and came to the decision that the plaintiff could prove by legal evidence his possession on the suit land and his dispossession by the defendants. The finding of the Court is quoted thus:

“উভয় পক্ষের স্বাক্ষীগনের মধ্যে তুলনামূলক ভাবে পর্যালোচনা করিলে দেথা যায় য়ে, বাদী তাহার মামলার বর্ণিত বেদখলের ঘটনা তাহার স্বাক্ষী দ্বারা প্রমান করিতে পারিয়াছেন। অর্থাৎ বাদীর স্বাক্ষীগনের স্বাক্ষ্য অত্র বিজ্ঞ আদালতের নিকট গ্রহনযোগ্য। কেন না বাদীর স্বাক্ষ্যীগন নিরপেক্ষ ঘটনার প্রত্যক্ষ দর্শী এবং নালীশী দাগের জন্য  অংশের দখলকার। নাঃ জমিতে বাদীর দখল ছিল এবং বিবাদীরা বেদখল করিয়াছে এই কথা বাদী তাহার স্বাক্ষী দ্বারা প্রমান করিতে সমর্থ হইয়াছে। বাদীর বর্তমান আকারে এই মামলা করার অধিকার আছে। কাজেই বাদী তাহার দাবী অনুযায়ী নাঃ জমির পুনঃদখল হকদার বটে”।

The learned trial Judge, with the above decisions decreed the suit and granted the relief of recovery of khas possession.

<u>27. Let me now turn to another aspect of the case. It is noticed that the plaintiff along with the relief of recovery of khas possession on the suit land also prayed for recording his name along with the names of the defendants in the record of right. The learned trial Judge refused to grant the said relief taking the view that granting of the said relief was beyond the scope in a suit under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act. The learned trial Judge is well founded on law in refusing to grant the said relief which is not at all permitted in a summary proceeding under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act.</u>

28. It has been streneously argued from the side of the petitioner that the learned trial Judge misread and misappraised the evidences on record in coming to the decision. Reliance has been also placed in support of the said contention on Khondker Mohiuddin vs SM Ahmed 28 DLR (AD) 85. In the said case it has been held by the Appellate Division that misreading or misrepresentation of evidence may be kind of error or defect in the procedure because it is reading or representing something as evidence which, in reality, is not on record or is not evidence at all and the decision of a case on such misreading or misrepresentation is contrary to the well-recognised judicial procedure according to which the decision of a court must be based on the evidence on record. In respectful obedience to the principles of law enunciated in the said decision I also express the view that misreading or misrepresentation of evidence is always an error of law which warrants interference by the High Court Division. But on examination of the evidences on record, it does not appear that the learned trial Judge misread or misappraised any evidence on record. The cited decision is of no help to the question debated from the side of the petitioner.

29. The court in disposing of a suit under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act is also a court of fact and the finding of fact arrived at by a court of fact on a due consideration of the evidences on record is immune from attack in exercising jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code. This Court in exercising Revisional Jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code can only interfere if it is shown that the finding is based on gross misreading or non-consideration of material evidence or it has been founded on misconception or misapplication of law or misinterpretation of any material document or otherwise it is perverse being contrary to the evidences on record. In the instant case before me the impugned decision cannot be said to have been based on misreading of evidence nor it has been founded on a misconception or misinterpretation of law or otherwise contrary to the weight on evidence on record. The said decision cannot be said to have suffered from perversity.

30. In view of the discussion made hereinbefore I am of this considered view that there is no merit in the Rule and the same, thus, fails.

31. In the result, the Rule is discharged. The judgment and decree passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Madarganj, Jamalpur is maintained.

32. Having regard to the facts and circumstance of the case I direct the parties to bear their respective cost.

33. Stay granted stands vacated.

LCR be sent down at an early date.

End.

lawyer: M Hafizullah with SK Siddique and Md Al-Amin Sarker, Advocates — For the Petitioner.
parties:
Black Sea Shipping Company (Blasco) ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Continental Traders  ------ Opposite Party
full_judgment:
Qazi Shafiuddin J : This application under section 115 CPC is directed against the order dated 13-8-87 passed by the Additional District Judge, 6th Court, Dhaka in Title Execution Case No. 1 of 1997 rejecting the application under section 13(b) and 44A CPC and for sale of the vessel MV SOKOL.

2. The opposite party filed execution case being Title Execution Case No. 1 of 1997 under section 44A CPC on the basis of a judgment passed by a High Court of Justice, Queen''s Bench Division, Commercial Court UK against the judgment debtor. By an order dated 14-7-97 the learned Judge ordered for attachment of the vessel MV SOKOL now berthed at Chittagong Port, Chittagong. The petitioner thereafter filed an application under section 13(b) and 44A read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejection of the execution case and also filed an application for vacating the order of attachment dated 14-7-97. In the aforesaid application it is stated that the decree-holder did not file the certified copy of the judgment and decree in the execution case and the judgment was passed ex parte as such the same is not conclusive and the execution case is not maintainable. Furthermore the judgment was not passed on merit. It has also been stated in the aforesaid application that no summons was issued upon the defendant-petitioner and the Court had no jurisdiction to pass such decree. In that view of the matter the execution case is liable to be rejected and the vessel is liable to be released from attachment forthwith.

3. The opposite party decree-holder had filed a reply to the application for rejection of the execution case and stated that the allegations of the petitioner are not at all correct. It is stated that summons were issued twice. First of all on 8-1-96 and then on 14-8-96. The defendant after receiving the writ amended the points of claim but they did not appear as such under the law in UK. The default judgment was passed on merit of the case after considering the points of claim and therefore it does not fall within the scope of section 13(b) CPC. As to the jurisdiction it is stated that Continental Traders and Black Sea Shipping Company by an agreement signed between them submitted themselves to the jurisdiction of English Court and the law prevailing. It also shows that the Court has jurisdiction to execute the said foreign judgment. Section 44A CPC reads as follows:

"44A—(1) Where a certified copy of decree of any of the superior Courts of the United Kingdom or any reciprocating territory has been filed in a District Court, the decree may be executed in Bangladesh as if it has been passed by the District Court.

(2) Together with the certificated copy of the decree shall be filed a certificate from such superior Court stating the extent, if any, to which the decree has been satisfied or adjusted and such certificate shall, for the purpose of proceedings under this section, be conclusive proof of the extent of such satisfaction or adjustment.

(3) The provisions of section 47 shall as from the filing of the certified copy of the decree apply to the proceeding of a District Court executing a decree under this section, and the District Court shall refuse execution of any such decree, if it is shown to the satisfaction Of the Court that the decree falls within any of the exceptions specified in clauses (a) to (f) of section 13.

Explanation 1—"Superior Courts", with reference to the United Kingdom, means the High Court in England, the Court of Session in Scotland, the High Court in Northern Ireland, the Court of Chancery of the County Palatine of Lancaster and the Court of Chancery of the County Palatine of Durham.

Explanation 2—"Reciprocating territory" means the United Kingdom and such other country or territory as the Government may, from time to time by notification in the official Gazette, declare to be reciprocating territory for the purposes of this section and "Superior Courts", with reference to any such territory, means such Courts as may be specified in the said notification.

Explanation 3—"Decree", with reference to a superior Court, means any decree or judgment of such Court under which a sum of money is payable, not being a sum payable in respect of taxes or other charges of a like nature or in respect of a fine or other penalty."

<u>4. Mr M Hafizullah, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, argues vehemently that section 44A CPC lays down the law that a certificated copy of a decree of any of the superior Courts of the United Kingdom or any reciprocating territory is to be filed. Together with the certified copy of the decree shall be filed a certificate from such superior Court stating the extent to which the decree has been satisfied or adjusted. It is stated in this application that no certified copy has been filed before the Executing Court. Only a photocopy of the same has been filed which cannot satisfy the requirement of the certified copy as embodied in section 44A CPC. The learned Additional District Judge has held that the copy can very well be treated as certified copy because it bears the seal and signature of the Court concerned. Moreover, the same carried Notorial Certificate which has been authenticated by the High Commission of Bangladesh in UK. In this application photocopy of the certified copy of the Judgment is shown to have been annexed at page 30 of this petition but it appears that only the first page has been annexed and the remaining pages are totally absent. The petitioner ought to have annexed the judgment as a whole. This sort of practice we do not approve. The point raised before the learned Additional District Judge that the requirement of section 44A CPC having not been complied with strictly the learned Additional District Judge ought to have rejected the execution case in terms of section 13(b) CPC. Section 13 CPC reads as follows:</u>

<u>"13. A foreign judgment shall be conclusive as to any matter thereby directly adjudicated upon between the same parties or between parties under whom they or any of them claim litigating under the same title except—</u>

<u>(a) where it has not been pronounced by a Court of competent jurisdiction;</u>

<u>(b) where it has not been given on the merits of the case;</u>

<u>(c) where it appears on the face of the proceedings to be founded on an incorrect view of international law or a refusal to recognise the law of Bangladesh in cases in which such law is applicable;</u>

<u>(d) where the proceedings in which the judgment was obtained are opposed to natural justice;</u>

<u>(e) where it has been obtained by fraud;</u>

<u>(f) where it sustains a claim founded on a breach of any law in force in Bangladesh."</u>

<u>5. Mr M Hafizullah, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, submits that the impugned judgment has not been pronounced by a Court of competent jurisdiction. He has further submitted that the judgment has not been passed on merit of the case. The learned Additional District Judge in his judgment has observed that the District Judge has authority to proceed with the execution case under section 44A CPC and that the decree-holder Continental Traders and the judgment-debtor Black Sea Shipping Company (petitioner) by signing an agreement submitted themselves to the jurisdiction of English Court and the learned Judge also referred to the Article 12 of the agreement in support of the jurisdiction. The learned Judge observed that the judgment was passed upon following the Supreme Court Rules in UK and on the face of the judgment and procedure the learned Judge continued to hold that the case has been decided on merit. Therefore the exceptions as enumerated in section 13 CPC do not attract the present case as the judgment was pronounced by the Court of competent jurisdiction and the same has been passed on merit although the defendant did not appear. Section 44A sub-section (3) provides that the provision of section 47 shall apply and the District Court shall refuse execution of any such decree, if it is shown to the satisfaction of the Court that the decree falls within any of the exceptions specified in clauses (a) to (f) of section 13 but section 47 CPC has been omitted by Ordinance No. XLVIII of 1983 as such the aforesaid section 47 is not at all applicable as enumerated in section 44A CPC. Therefore sub-section (3) of section 44A requiring that a decree falls within the purview of clauses (a) to (f) of section 13 the executing Court will refuse to execute such decree does not arise.</u>

<u>6. As to the attachment of the ship in question the executing court has already passed the order for sale of ship MV SOKOL. Since the executing Court is invested with the power to execute the decree the order passed is well within full jurisdiction. The learned Additional District Judge appears to have committed an error of law in passing the impugned order, as such, the aforesaid order does not call for any interference by this Court.</u>

Accordingly this application is rejected summarily.

End.

lawyer:
Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, Additional Attorney-General (Sharifuddin Chakladar, Assistant Attorney-General with him) instructed by Mvi Md Wahidullah, Advocate-on-Record — For the Appellants.
