parties:
Government of Bangladesh and another ------ Appellant
Vs.
Hosne Ara Begum and others ------ Respondents
case_source: (From the Judgment and order dated 8-5-94 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 384 of 1994)
full_judgment:
Latifur Rahman J: This appeal by leave at the instance of the defendant-appellants is against the judgment and order dated 8-5-94 passed by a Division Bench, High Court Division in Civil Revision No 384 of 1994, discharging the Rule thereby upholding the judgment dated 30-9-93 passed by the Additional District Judge, 6th Court, Dhaka in Title Appeal No 169 of 1991 affirming the judgment and decree dated 23-3-91 and 30-3-91 respectively passed by the Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 471 of 1990.

<u>2. The plaintiff-respondent brought the aforesaid suit in 1982 on the averments, inter alia, that the predecessor-in-interest of defendant Nos. 1-4, Syed Abdul Ali, got the suit properly as permanent lessee of the Government; that upon his death defendants No 1-4 inherited the suit, property; that they entered into an agreement with the plaintiff on 6-7-73 for selling the suit property at a price of Taka 80,000.00 which was paid in its entirety at the time of execution of the deed of agreement; that it was stipulated that they (defendant Nos. 1-4) would retain possession of the disputed property for 8 years and if within that period they could return the consideration money, the purchaser (plaintiff) would take back the same and in case of their failure to return the consideration money within the stipulated time the defendants would be bound to execute and register a deed of sale in favour of the plaintiff; that on their failure to do so the plaintiff would be at liberty to get the kabala executed and registered through court within the next one year; that defendants Nos. 1-4 in fact, failed to perform their part of the contract and as a result the cause of action for the suit arose on 5-8-82 Hence the suit.</u>

<u>3. Defendant Nos. 1-4 did not contest the suit. It was contested by the appellants ie  defendant No. 5-8 (Government of Bangladesh and Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka). They filed a written statement denying the assertion made by the plaintiff and asserted further that the suit property belonged to a non-Bengali who during the liberation war in 1971 left the country and as a result the suit property became an abandoned property under President''s Order No. 16 of 1972. The suit property was leased out to Shahid Family, namely, Mrs Nazma Majid, who was the wife of late Abdul Majid, the then SP Rajshahi and that since 12-1-76 Mrs. Nazma Majid has been living there with her children on payment of regular rent to the Government. Defendant Nos. 1-4 were not the owners of the suit property and that the alleged agreement for sale was concocted and fraudulent and that the suit itself was not maintainable.</u>

<u>4. The trial Judge decreed the suit ex parte against defendant Nos.1-4 and decreed the suit on contest against the present appellants. On appeal and revision by the contesting defendant- appellants the suit was decreed all through.</u>

<u>5. Leave was granted to consider whether the learned Judges of the High Court Division erred in law in not holding that the alleged deed of agreement Ext. 3 was a deed of mortgage by conditional sale which required registration under section 59 of the Transfer of Property Act and the same not being a registered instrument did not create any right, title and interest in favour of the plaintiff and the same was not admissible in evidence in view of the provision of section 49 of the Registration Act. Leave was also granted to consider whether the alleged death certificates, Ext 2 and 2(a) of the predecessor-in-interest of defendant Nos. 1-4 having not been legally proved, and being authenticated by Bangladesh High Commission in Calculate, the learned Judges of the High Court Division erred in law in not holding that the plaintiffs'' alleged vendor, namely, defendant Nos. 1-4 had no authority to enter into the alleged agreement for sale during the lifetime of the original owner the suit property. Leave was further granted to consider whether in view of the assertion of the contesting defendants that the disputed house is an abandoned property and the same admittedly is in possession of a member of a Shahid Family, the alleged agreement was void being hit by Article 6 of the President's Order No. 16 of 1972 and consequently, the decree for specific performance of contract could not be passed in respect of an abandoned properly in view of Article 14 of the President's Order No. 16 of 1972.</u>

<u>6. In this case, a concise statement was filed on behalf of respondent No.3, namely, Rana  Ali, daughter of lala Hakim Syed Abdul Ali, the original owner of the suit property. In the concise statement it has been clearly stated that the suit for specific performance of contract was decreed ex parte against defendant Nos.1-4 and the addresses of defendant Nos. 1-4 were shown at House No. 40, Road No. 6, Dhanmondi Residential Area, Dhaka although they were living at 11, Barin Bari Lal Lane, Calcutta. In view of the addresses given in the plaint the service of summons upon them was effected under Order 9 rule 5 of the Code by hanging at, Dhaka address. Respondent No. 3 having come to know of the ex parte decree passed in Title Suit No. 471 of 1990 (renumbered as Title Suit No. 286 of 1992) filed Miscellaneous Case No. 50 of 1994 under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the ex parte decree was set aside and subsequently the suit itself was dismissed on 23-4-96. In this appeal, leave was granted on    3-11-94 and during the pendency of the appeal the main suit out of which the present appeal arose had already been dismissed on 23-4-96. In view of this factual position, the present decree passed in suit for specific performance of contract is no longer in existence. Thus the present decree passed in the suit cannot exist in view of dismissal of the original suit. Two conflicting decrees cannot co-exist in the same suit.</u>

In view of the above observation, it is needless for us to enter into the controversies on which leave was granted. Consequently, the appeal is allowed without any order as to costs and the decree passed in the suit is set aside.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 760 of 1997
lawyer:
Nazmul Huda, Advocate, instructed by Md. Aftab Hossain, Advocate-on-Record—For the Petitioner. 
Tofailur Rahman, Advocate, instructed by Sharifuddin Chaklader, Advocate-on-Record—For the Respondents.
parties:
Gold Coin Textile and Garments ------- Judgment debtor-Petitioner
Vs.
Gul Ahmed Jute Mills Ltd ------- Decree-holder Respondents
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated May 27, 1997 passed by the High Court Division, Dhaka in Civil Revision No. 1896 of 1995)
full_judgment:
ATM Afzal CJ: The respondent as plaintiff filed Other Suit No. 70 of 1987 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong for ejectment of the defendant-petitioner from the suit premises, realization of arrear rent and compensation for illegal occupation of the suit premises. The suit was decreed for eviction of the defendant-petitioner and also for recovery of Taka 32,18,132.00 from the defendant after adjusting Taka 7,03,156.00 which was already paid during the pendency of the suit. The defendant-petitioner was directed to pay the decretal amount (Taka 32,18,132 Taka 7,03,156 Taka 25,14,976.00) to the plaintiff and to vacate the suit premises within 60 days from the date of the judgment and decree dated 30-11-91, failing which the defendant was liable to pay compensation at the rate of Taka 2,000.00 per day. The plaintiff-respondent put the decree in execution on 9-3-92 in the Second Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong being Other Execution Case No. 5 of 1992.

<u>2. For the purpose of disposal of this leave petition it will be sufficient to notice that the learned Subordinate Judge passed an order on 14-3-95 in the execution proceeding requiring the defendant-judgment-debtor-petitioner to furnish a bank guarantee in favour of the plaintiff-decree-holder-respondent for an amount of Taka 12,82,000.00 before vacating the suit premises. This order was passed on the application of the petitioner for permission to vacate the suit premises. Being aggrieved by the said order the petitioner moved the High Court Division in revision but without any success. The Rule issued in the revision case No. 1896 of 1995 was discharged by a Division Bench by the impugned judgment and order dated 27 May, 1997.</u>

3. Mr Nazmul Huda, learned Counsel for the petitioner, submits that both the learned Subordinate Judge and the High Court Division upon a mistaken view of an earlier order of the High Court Division wrongly held that the petitioner was required to furnish security for the alleged dues (as to compensation) of the decree-holder-respondent. He submits that there cannot be any obstruction caused to vacating the suit premises by the petitioner which it is required to do under the decree on pain of paying a daily compensation. The decree-holder has been illegally preventing the petitioner from vacating the suit premises for undue enrichment as the decree provides for a daily compensation of Taka 2,000.00 in case of failure to vacate. The petitioner not only satisfied the decretal amount but also paid about Taka 7,00,000.00 on account of compensation. Mr Huda submits that the learned Subordinate Judge illegally put the condition of a bank guarantee before vacating the suit premises.

4. It appears that the petitioner's contention has always been that the decretal amount has already been paid to the decree-holder-plaintiff. The High Court Division also found in the impugned judgment that the judgment-debtor had already paid the entire decretal amount of Taka 32,14,976.00 as per schedule filed with the revisional application (Annexure "A" and "A1").

5. It is found that on 8-9-94 the petitioner made an application to the executing Court for installment admitting the dues of the decree-holder for an amount of Taka 11,29,272.00. The petitioner in that application stated that it had already paid Taka 39,48,132.00 to the decree-holder which not only included the entire decretal amount but also Taka 14,23,156 as compensation at the rate of Taka 2,000.00 per day for the occupation of the suit premises as decreed.

6. It appears that the decree-holder came to the High Court Division in revision, Civil Revision No. 3440 of 1994, impugning certain orders of the executing Court. By judgment and order dated 30 January, 1995 the Rule was disposed of in that case with the observation as follows:

The opposite party should be allowed by the executing Court to vacate the disputed premises by furnishing a security to the satisfaction of the executing Court up to the amount of the decree in execution within a month from the date of receipt of this order by the said Court. The amount of security will be excluding the quantum of compensation claimed for use and occupation of the premises by the judgment-debtor after the time fixed by the trial Court while decreeing the suit.

7. The learned Subordinate Judge put the condition of bank guarantee upon referring to the application of the petitioner dated 8-9-94 in which it had admitted that it was liable to pay Taka 11,29,272.00 to the decree-holder and prayed for installment. It will be seen from the same application that the said amount was not a part of the decretal dues but related to compensation payable to the decree-holder for subsequent use and occupation of the suit premises.

<u>8. Mr. Tofailur Rahman, learned Counsel entering Caveat for the respondent, does not dispute that the decretal amount has been fully satisfied as claimed by the petitioner and also found by the High Court Division. Mr Rahman, however, submits that any compensation which is payable under the decree is also a part of the decree and as such the amount for which the bank guarantee has been asked for is also a decretal amount. The learned Subordinate Judge has not committed any error in asking for a bank guarantee for the said decretal amount, he submits.</u>

9. Is the judgment-debtor-petitioner at all required to furnish security before vacating the suit premises by reason of the order of the High Court Division as quoted above? It has been made very clear in the said order that the amount of security will be excluding the quantum of compensation; in other words, there will have to be no security for any amount of compensation which may be due. Therefore having regard to the facts which are practically admitted, namely, that the decretal dues have already been satisfied and the dues referred to in the application dated 8-9-94 relate to compensation, the order requiring the judgment-debtor to furnish bank guarantee before vacating the suit premises was not legal and proper. There is substance in the contention of the petitioner that the order passed by the High Court Division in the earlier revision case was misconstrued by the learned Subordinate Judge as also by the High Court Division.

10. Mr Nazmul Huda has raised question as to the dues of the decree-holder on account of compensation because the decree-holder has prevented the petitioner from vacating the suit premises making undue demands. This is not the forum for raising the controversy with regard to the alleged claim of the decree-holder on account of compensation. The petitioner can take objection in the executing Court when demand will be made on account of compensation money.

11. Mr Nazmul Huda has then submitted that the judgment-debtor-petitioner being a Garments factory it will be difficult for winding up the factory all at once because there are already some orders from abroad which are to be complied with. The petitioner will vacate the suit premises within 6 months from date and for this period it is prepared to pay the compensation as under the decree, Mr Huda submits. He, therefore, prays that the petitioner may be allowed to continue in the suit premises for six months from date on the above term. The decree-holder can hardly have any objection because the petitioner wants to continue in terms of the decree. Even otherwise we think the prayer is quite reasonable.

12. It is, therefore, ordered that the petitioner will be permitted to remain in possession of the suit premises for six months from date as prayed for and the compensation for these 6(six) months at the rate of Taka 2,000.00 per day will be paid to the decree-holder-plaintiff for one month at a time and within seven days of the following month failing which the petitioner will be liable to eviction without furnishing security as demanded by the impugned order.

The petition is disposed of in the above terms.

End.

lawyer:
Syed Mahmud Hussain, Advocate —For the Petitioners. 
HK Abdul Hye with Abdul Hai Sarker, Advocates — For the Opposite Party No. 1
parties:
Yusuf Mia (Md) & others ------ Petitioners
Vs.
Shafiqul Islam ------ Opposite Party
full_judgment:
This Rule under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is directed against the judgment and decree dated 29-7-91 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Shahrasti, Chandpur, decreeing the suit in part under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act in Title Suit No. 49 of 1989.

2. Short facts, for the disposal of this Rule, are that, the opposite party as plaintiff filed the above suit against the petitioner as defendant for the recovery of land alleged to have been encroached by the defendants and also for a permanent injunction restraining the defendants from making any construction on the said land hereinafter referred to as the suit land.

3. The defendant Nos. 1 to 5 contested the suit by filing a written statement denying the material allegations made in the plaint.

4. The learned trial Court took the troubles of making a physical inspection of the suit land along with the learned Advocates for the plaintiff and the defendants. At the trial the plaintiff examined 5 witnesses including himself and the defendants examined 4 witnesses supporting their respective cases.

5. That on consideration of evidence and other materials on record, the learned trial Court dismissed the prayer for permanent injunction holding that in a suit for recovery of possession under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act prayer for permanent injunction is not maintainable. But the learned Court was pleased to decree the suit for the recovery of the land found to have been encroached by the defendant.

6. The suit was valued at Taka 5000.00 by the plaintiff, the defendants in the written statement stated that the suit had been under valued, however at the trial they did not press the point and the learned court accepted the valuation made by the plaintiff and accordingly found the court fees paid was sufficient and decreed the suit for recovery of the suit land found encroached. Hence, this Rule has been issued, at the instance of the defendant-petitioner.

7. Mr Syed Mahmud Hossain, the learned Advocate, appearing on behalf of the defendant-petitioners, submits that in view of section 3 of the Village Courts Ordinance the trial Court has no jurisdiction to entertain the suit. Village Courts Ordinance has clearly barred the plaintiff from filing the suit for the recovery of possession of immovable property if the valuation is upto Taka 5000.00. He has admitted that this is for the first time this point has been raised before this court but he argues that so far the point of jurisdiction is concerned, if the jurisdiction of the Court is specially barred by any provision of statute then the parties to the suit cannot invest such jurisdiction to the court by consent or otherwise. In support of his argument he referred to 3 cases, the case of Sirajul Hoque and others vs. Md. Shafiullah and another reported in BCR 1984 (HCD) 217, secondly, the case of Abul Kalam and others vs. Abdul Majid and others reported in 32 DLR 221 and lastly, the case of Senior Manager, Messrs. Dosta Textiles Mills Limited vs. Sudhanshu Bikash reported in 40 DLR (AD) 45.

8. First of all let me find out what section 3 of the Village Courts Ordinance, 1976 provides.

<u>9. Section 3 of the Village Courts Ordinance 1976 reads as follows:</u>

<u>"3. Cases triable by village Courts</u>

<u>(1) Nothwithstanding anything contained in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Act V of 1898), or in the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (Act V of 1908), all cases relating to offences specified in Part I of the Schedule and to matters specified in Part II thereof shall, save as otherwise provided hereinafter, be triable by Village Court, and no Civil or Criminal Court shall have jurisdiction to try any such case or suit.</u>

<u>(2) A village Court shall not try a case relating to an offence specified in Part I of the Schedule if the accused had previously been convicted of a cognizable offence or a case relating to any matter specified in Part II of the Schedule if—</u>

<u>(a) the interest of a minor is involved in the suit;</u>

<u>(b) provision for arbitration has been made in a contract between the parties to the dispute;</u>

<u>(c) the Government or a local authority or a public servant acting in the discharge of his duty is a party to the dispute."</u>

<u>Part II of the Schedule of the village Courts Ordinance reads as follows:</u>

<u>"1. Suit for the recovery of money due on contracts, receipts or other documents</u>

<u>2. Suit for the recovery of movable property, or for the value thereof.</u>

<u>3. Suit for the recovery of possession of immovable property within one year of dispossession.</u>

<u>4. Suit for compensation for wrongfully taking or damaging movable property.</u>

<u>5. Suit for damages by cattle trespass When the amount claimed or the price of movable property, or the value of immovable property involved does not exceed Taka 5,000</u>

<u>Reading of section 3 along with Part II of its Schedule will clearly appear that for suits for the recovery of immovable property valued up to Taka 5,000.00, Village Court is the only forum.</u>

10. In the case of Sirajul Hoque and others vs. Md Shafiullah and another reported in BCR 1984 (HCD) 217 the case is exactly on the point of jurisdiction of the Village Courts Ordinance wherein it has been observed that:

"When a Court suffers from inherent want of jurisdiction, no amount of consent or participation in the proceeding, without objection as to jurisdiction, can invest such Court with the jurisdiction".

11. In the case of Abul Kalam and others vs. Abdul Majid and others reported in 32 When the amount claimed or the price of movable property, or the value of immovable property involved does not exceed Taka 5,000 DLR 221 which was also on the point of jurisdiction but that relates to the criminal jurisdiction and the Village Court vis-a-vis any other criminal courts. However, in that case it has been held that no Criminal Court other than the Village Court can entertain a case where Village Court has been conferred with the jurisdiction.

12. In the case of Senior Manager, Messrs Dosta Textile Mills Ltd. vs. Sudhanshu Bikash Nath, reported in 40 DLR (AD) 45, their Lordships in the Appellate Division have observed : "The forum of ''Labour Court'' has been created by special statutes, as distinguished from a general law, the Civil Procedure Code; as such provision of special statute shall prevail over those of the general law."

<u>13. In view of the principles laid down in the aforesaid decisions and under the facts and circumstances of the present case I find that the trial Court had no jurisdiction to try the suit.</u>

14. Mr HK Abdul Hye, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-opposite party concedes that civil Court has no jurisdiction to try the suits for the recovery of possession of the immovable property if the valuation does not exceed Taka 5,000.00. But he submits that on the point of valuation the trial Court has not come to a definite finding as to whether the suit was over valued, Accordingly, he contends that the suit should be sent on remand to the trial Court for determining the valuation of the suit first and to decide its maintainability thereon.

15. I do not find much substance in his argument, because it is the plaintiff who has valued his suit at Taka 5,000.00. If on the face of the plaint the valuation appears to be such that the court has no jurisdiction to entertain the suit, the plaint is to be returned forthwith.

16. Accordingly, I hold the impugned judgment and decree as nullity. The plaint should be returned to the plaintiff for presenting it to the appropriate court.

<u>17. In the result, the Rule is made absolute, the judgment and decree passed by the learned Assistant Judge is set aside. The learned Assistant Judge is directed to return the plaint to the plaintiff for presentation of the same before the appropriate court.</u>

18. The order passed by this court earlier restraining the operation of the impugned judgment and order is hereby vacated.

19. There shall be no order as to costs.

Let the LC records be sent down at once.

End.

caseno:
Civil Revision Case No. 264 of 2000 
with 
Civil Revision Case No. 2588 of 1999
lawyer:
Abdul Quayyum with Tapas Kumar Biswas, Advocates -For the Petitioners (in Civil Revision 264 of 2000) 
AKM Ashiqul Hoque, Advocate -For the Opposite Party Nos. 1-9 (in Civil Revision No. 264 of 2000). 
Abdul Mannan Khan, Advocate -For the Petitioner (in Civil Revision No. 2588 of 1999).
Abdul Quayyum with Syed Jahangir, Advocates -For the Opposite Party No. 1 (in Civil Revision No. 2588 of 1999)
parties:
Kajol Das and others ------ Petitioners
vs.
Manowara Begum alias Marium Begum and ors ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
These two Rules were heard analogously and are disposed of by this Single Judgment as the connecting appeals and Suit were also heard analogously and disposed of by one judgment by the trial Court as well as by the appellate Court.

2. The short facts for disposal of the Rule in Civil Revision No. 264 of 2000 are that the petitioner as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 243 of 1997 for Specific Performance of Contract in respect of schedule property against the defendants-opposite parties 1-10, stating, in short, that the land under District Dhaka PS Demra Mouja Tara Bari, CS Khatian No. 306 CS Plot No. 647 1.04 acres land in which 0.02 acres was owned and possessed by late Mosleuddin by inheritance, the predecessor of opposite party Nos. 1-9 who executed a Bainapatra on 3-11-82 with the plaintiff-petitioner for sale of 0134 ajusangsha on consideration of value at Taka 13,000 out of which he paid Taka 3000 and the seller handed over vacant possession and thereafter, plaintiff filled up null land by earth and built a chapra house thereon by investing huge sum of money and leased the house on rent to one Md Hafiz on oral agreement and thereafter executed written agreement on 1-3-93 and that the predecessor of defendants as well as they refused to execute sale deed and lodged a complaint by wife of late Moslehuddin before Commissioner who on hearing both the parties directed defendants predecessor to execute sale deed in favour of plaintiff on 18-1-83 and thereafter predecessors of defendant died leaving successors defendant Nos. 1-9 who also avoided to execute sale deed and defendant No. 1 again lodged complaint against husband of plaintiff before the present Ward Commissioner who notified both the parties and upon hearing on 1-5-97 delivered judgment directing the defendants 1-9 to execute sale deed by taking rest dues of Taka 10,000 which was not complied with and defendants issued a legal notice under section 106 of TP Act for eviction and plaintiff replied to the same and filed the suit for Specific Performance of Contract.

3. The opposite party Nos. 1-9 as defendants contested the suit and filed written statement, moreover, they filed SCC Suit No. 16/97 for eviction denying the material allegations of the plaint of the said Title Suit.

4. The case of the defendants was as follows:

That the predecessor of the defendants being owner of 0.02 acres land including suit property, gave lease to plaintiffs husband on monthly rent of Taka 500 per month. The predecessor of defendants constructed a tin shed house thereon where sanitary goods were produced and said Mosleuddin was sick who was forced by husband of plaintiff to sign on some stamp papers on 10-1-83 and a GDE was lodged to that effect before Officer-in-Charge Demra PS Defendant No. 2 and that husband of plaintiff paid rent @ Taka 500 per month upto May, 1997 and refused to pay rent from June, 1997 and started to construct wall/tin shed in the Suit land and thereafter defendant lodged complaint to ward commissioner and made GDE with Demra Police and issued legal notice under section 106 TP Act and filed SCC Case No. 16 of 1997 which was heard analogously by trial Court.

5. The learned trial Court decreed the Suit in favour of the plaintiff, and defendants preferred Title Appeal No. 461 of 1998 before District Judge, Dhaka who transferred the same to First Sub-Judge, Dhaka for disposal who allowed the appeal dismissing the suit and decreed the SCC Suit. The opposite parties filed Civil Revision No. 2588 of 1999 against the said judgment of SCC Suit which is being heard analogously with Civil Revision No. 264 of 2000.

6. The short facts for disposal of Rule in Civil Revision No. 2588 of 1999 is that the defendant-opposite party (plaintiff in said Title Suit No. 243 of 97) took lease of the demised premises measuring 0.02 acres of vacant land on 1.2.83 from Mosleuddin (plaintiff No. 2, husband and father of rest plaintiffs) in presence of Ramijuddin, Abdul Hoshem, Dukhu Mia and other elites of the locality. Oral agreement of lease was made and it was stipulated that the defendant (plaintiff in Title Suit No. 243 of 1997) would construct a tin shed house at his own cost and deal in sanitary business therein, electric bill, holding tax to be paid by the tenant defendant in the name of the plaintiffs predecessor Mosleuddin, the owner landlord, of the case premises, but at the ill advice and instigation of the unscrupulous people of the locality with a view to grabbing the schedule premises on 10-1-83 the defendant and his accomplices confined the mentally retarded person (the predecessor of the plaintiffs) Mosleuddin in a place and took signatures on some unwritten stamp papers, on the next day of the incident the said Musleuddin through his son plaintiff No. 2 made a General Diary with the Local Thana dated 11-1-1983 (Exhibit Gha) and subsequently, Mosleuddin died on 22-5-84 in the Dhaka Medical College Hospital, the defendant paid rents upto May 1999 at the rate of Taka 500 per month according to stipulation, but the defendant defaulted payment of rent since June, 1997 in spite of repeated demands and takids of the plaintiffs and lastly, the defendant denied the ownership of the plaintiffs refusing payment of further rents, the defendant on 25-5-1977 tried to forcibly construct a tin shed and the matter was brought to the local Commissioner who served a notice for stopping construction work and GD Entry on 26-5-97 was made in the local thana, the premises in Schedule is bonafide required for use and occupation of the plaintiff and for development of case property, the defendant has become defaulter and that is why a legal notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was served upon the defendant determining the tenancy and for realisation of arrear rent, on receipt of notice by the said defendant the defendant hurriedly instituted Title Suit No. 243 of 1997 on 21-8-97 in the 6th Court of Assistant Judge for specific performance of contract in the name of his wife.

7. The defendant contested the said suit by filing a written statement stating the plaint case of Title Suit No. 243 of 1997.

8. Both the suits were taken up together for disposal analogously by the learned Assistant Judge.

9. The learned trial Court decreed Title Suit No. 243 of 1997 and dismissed SCC Suit No. 16 of 1997 by the judgment and decree dated 29-10-98. As against that the defendants in Title Suit No. 243 of 97 preferred Title Appeal No. 461 of 1998 and the learned appellate Court vide his judgment and decree dated 11-7-99 allowed the appeal.

10. Being aggrieved by the appellate judgment the plaintiff-petitioner obtained the Rule in Civil Revision No. 264 of 2000 and defendant-petitioner being aggrieved by the order passed by the SCC Judge obtained the Rule in Civil Revision No. 2588 of 1999.

11. Mr Abdul Quayyum with Mr Tapas Kumar Das, Advocates appearing on behalf of the petitioners in both the Rules, placed both the revisional applications,  impugned judgments and decrees passed by the Courts below. At the time of hearing of the revisional applications the petitioners in Civil Revision 264 of 2000 filed an application for amendment of the plaint, the copy of which was served on the learned Advocate of the opposite parties. It has been stated in the said application that plaintiff-petitioner since dead being in possession of the suit land since date of agreement dated 3-1-82, he acquired good title in the Suit land by adverse possession and that he is entitled to relief for continuation of possession and permanent injunction and, as such, he prayed for adding a relief No. Kha in the prayer portion of the plaint to the effect that,

“বাদীর চুক্তি প্রদানের দাবী তামাদি বলিয়া গণ্য হইলে বাদীকে স্থিরতর এর এবং চিরস্থায়ী নিষেজ্ঞার ডিক্রী দিবার”

12. The learned Advocate for the petitioner also submitted that the original plaintiff being in possession of the Suit land since date of agreement dated 3-11-82 and he having filed the suit on 21-8-97 the plaintiff and his heirs the petitioners acquired good title in the Suit land by adverse possession and, as such, entitled to get a decree at least for confirmation of possession as well as permanent injunction. The learned Advocate further submitted that in view of the decision in the case of Md Nurul Islam Patwari and others vs Abdul Awal Mia and others reported in 1996 BLD (AD) 169 there is no bar in allowing the amendment as prayed for before this Court.

13. Mr Abdul Mannan Khan along with Mr AKM Ashqul Huq appearing on behalf of the opposite parties in Civil Revision No. 264 of 2000 and on behalf of the petitioner in Civil Revision No. 2588 of 1999 opposed the amendment application submitting that the facts and circumstance of the case reported in 1996 BLD (AD) 169 being different on amendment at this stage cannot be allowed. The learned Advocate further submitted that the principle enunciated in the reported case is also not applicable in the present case and, as such, the Rule in Civil Revision 264 of 2000 is liable to be discharged and the Rule issued in Civil Revision 2588 of 1999 may be made absolute.

14. On perusal of the judgment it appears that the learned trial Court held that the suit is maintainable, that there is no defect of parties in Title Suit No. 243 of 1997, that the Suit is not barred, that the deed of agreement dated 3-11-82 has been duly executed by Mosleuddin, predecessor of the defendants, that the allegation by the defendants that the signatures of said Mosleuddin was obtained by force in blank stamp papers is not believable, that plaintiff is in possession of the Suit land since the date of the deed of agreement dated 3-11-82, that the defendants failed to prove that Ratan Das, husband of the plaintiff, is a monthly tenant under the defendants, that the SCC Suit No. 16 of 1997 is a counter-case of Title Suit No. 243 of 1997. On those findings the learned trial Court decreed the Title Suit No. 243 of 1997 and dismissed SCC Suit No. 16 of 1997.

15. The learned appellate Court, on the other hand, held that Title Suit No. 243 of 1997 is barred by limitation inasmuch as the plaintiff failed to prove the cause of action and accordingly, allowed the appeal dismissing Title Suit No. 243 of 1997.

16. Admittedly the plaintiff in Title Suit No. 243 of 1997 is in possession of the suit land and the defendant of that suit as plaintiff filed SCC Suit No. 16 of 1997 for eviction of the plaintiff alleging that he the defendant of SCC suit is a monthly bharatia and he is a habitual defaulter, The trial Court specifically found that the plaintiff is in possession of the Suit land since the date of agreement dated 3-11-82 but the learned appellate Court did not give any finding as to the date of possession of the plaintiff in Title Suit No. 243 of 1997. The plaintiff in the SCC Suit stated that the defendant in the SCC suit took lease of the Suit land with effect from 1-1-83 and the defendant paid rent upto May, 1997 @ Taka 500 per month and that subsequently, the defendant defaulted in payment of rent since June 1997, necessitating the filing of the Suit for ejectment. Thus it shows that that the defendant in the SCC Suit who is the plaintiff is Title Suit No. 243 of 1997 is in possession of the Suit land according to the plaintiff with effect from 3-11-82 and according to the defendant with effect from 1-1-83 which shows that the plaintiff is in possession of the suit land for more than 12 years when the present suit was filed on 21-8-97. The case of the plaintiff in Title Suit No. 243 of 1997 is that on the basis of the agreement dated 3-11-82 she is in possession of the Suit land. Since the learned trial Court decreed the suit but the learned appellate Court allowed the appeal holding that the plaintiff could not prove her cause of action for the Suit and accordingly, the Suit is barred by limitation as she failed to file the suit within 3 years from the date of cause of action as alleged by the plaintiff.

<u>17. The learned Advocate for the petitioner in Civil Revision No. 264 of 2000 having found it difficult to assail the finding of fact arrived by the learned appellate Court regarding the question of limitation thought it wise/proper to file an application for amendment of the plaint and accordingly, he filed an application for amendment of the prayer portion of the plaint. The plaintiff-petitioner thus prayed for a decree for confirmation of possession as well as for permanent injunction so that the defendant-opposite parties cannot disturb the plaintiff in her possession in the suit land.</u>

18. From the plaint case as well as from the depositions on record it appears that the plaintiff has been able to prove her possession in the Suit land for more than 12 years and since earlier the suit was a suit for Specific Performance of Contract the learned trial Court having found that the plaintiff was able to prove her case decreed the suit but the learned appellate Court having found that the suit is barred by limitation allowed the appeal dismissing the Suit for specific performance of contract.

19. The learned Advocate for the petitioner in Civil Revision No. 264 of 2000 has referred to the decision in the case of Md Nurul Islam Patwary and others vs Abdul Awal Miah and others reported in 1996 BLD (AD) 169 and submitted that there is no bar in allowing an amendment as prayed for in the revisional stage and that in a similar case in the said decision amendment of plaint was allowed in the revision.

<u>20. On perusal of the said decision, it appears that in a similar case application for amendment of the plaint was allowed wherein a suit for declaration of title by adverse possession was filed by the plaintiff and the defendant of the said suit also filed a SCC Suit for eviction of the plaintiff. In the said reported case, the original suit was for declaration of title by adverse possession on the basis of an agreement and subsequently, by amendment at the revisional stage the Suit was converted to a Suit for permanent injunction upon confirmation of possession and ultimately, in the said reported case the Suit was decreed which was affirmed upon the Appellate Division. Thus, in my opinion, the aforesaid decision reported in 1996 BLD is equally applicable in the present case as the facts and circumstances are similar to those of the reported case and accordingly, the amendment as prayed for by this petitioner in Civil Revision 264 of 2000 is allowed.</u>

<u>21. Since I have found as above the plaintiff in Civil Revision 264 of 2000 has been able to prove her possession in the suit land for more than 12 years, in my opinion she acquired a good title by adverse possession and she is entitled to get a decree in Title Suit No. 243 of 1997.</u>

<u>22. Since it has been found by the trial Court that the present plaintiff in Title Suit No. 243 of 1997 is in possession of the suit land by virtue of the agreement dated 3-11-82 and she or her husband is not a tenant of the (defendant in Title Suit No. 243 of 1997) plaintiff in SCC Suit No. 16 of 1997 said suit cannot be decreed and the learned appellate Court committed error in decreeing SCC Suit No. 16 of 1997 calling for interference by this Court.</u>

23. For the aforesaid discussions and reasons the Rule in 264 of 2000 is made absolute without any order as to cost and the judgment and decree dated 11-7-99 passed by the learned appellate Court in Title Appeal No. 461 of 1998 are set aside and those of the learned trial Court are restored but decree in modified form as per amendment of the plaint as stated above, i.e. Title Suit No. 243 of 1997 is decreed and the defendants are restrained permanently from disturbing the peaceful possession of the plaintiffs in the Suit land. Consequently, the Rule in Civil Revision No. 2588 of 1999 is discharged without cost and those passed by the learned trial Court in SCC Suit No. 16 of 1997 are maintained. The order of status quo granted at the time of issuance of the Rule in Civil Revision No. 264 of 2000 is vacated.

Send down the lower Court records.

End.

lawyer:

parties:
Karimon Nessa being dead her heir Chand Ali Pramanik and others ------ Petitioners
vs.
Sorab Ali and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule, arising out of an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, is directed against the judgment and decree dated 14-3-1996 passed by the learned District Judge, Pabna in Other Class Appeal No. 163 of 1987 setting aside those of the learned Subordinate Judge, Pabna, passed on 30-4-1987 in Other Class Suit No. 64 of 1975 which was decreed by the trial Court.

2. The relevant facts necessary for disposal of this Rule are that Karimon Nessa, deceased mother of the present plaintiff petitioners, instituted the above noted original suit for having a declaration of title in the suit land measuring 3.37 acres as described in the schedule "G" to the plaint. According to her case, 'ka' schedule land measuring an area of 5.00 acres including the suit land as recorded under CS Khatian No. 56 previously belonged to 3 sisters namely; Golejan Bibi and Sukjan Bibi in equal shares. Rupejan Bibi died leaving her heirs in 2 sisters. Thereafter, Golejan Bibi died leaving her husband Saimuddin and sister Sukjan Bibi, Subsequently, Sukjan Bibi died leaving the plaintiff Karimon Nessa as daughter, who also got the share of Saimuddin by purchase. That the plaintiff and Golejan Bibi previously transferred 0.87 acres of land to Ayet Ali who has also possession therein. SA Khatian in respect of the said transferred land along with the some other lands were prepared accordingly in the name of the plaintiff and Ayet Ali, which is shown in schedule 'Kha' to the plaint. That when the plaintiff was the actual owner and possessor of the remaining 'Ga' schedule land (suit land) it was once sold in auction on 21-11-1953 in Rent Execution Case No. 770 of 1953 and ex-landlord was shown to have purchased the land paper, but possession was never delivered to him after the said auction sale. Thereafter, the plaintiff filed the Miscellaneous Case No. 26 of 1959, in the 3rd Court of Munsif, Pabna for setting aside the auction sale under section 174(3) of the Bengal Tenancy Act. Accordingly, the disputed auction sale was set aside in the proceeding by the learned Munsif vide an order dated 23-5-1959. Therefore, the suit land remained under the ownership of the plaintiff as it was before. But subsequently, during SA operation, the suit land was wrongly recorded as khas land of the Government (defendant No. 1) on the basis of said wrong SA Khatian. Two lease cases were collusively started in the years 1970-71 and lease order was issued in favour of the defendant No. 2 Sobhan Ali Sheikh. On being aware of the aforesaid, settlement to the defendant No. 2 on 10-4-1975, the plaintiff filed the present suit for having a declaration of her title in the suit property. The defendant No. 1, Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, did not contest the suit. The defendant No. 2 Md Sorab Ali Sheikh contested the suit by filing a written statement contending, inter alia, that the 'Ka' Schedule land originally belonged to Kachir Mondal who died leaving 3 daughters namely, Golejan Bibi, Rupjan Bibi and Sukjan Bibi, one wife Moyful and 3 cousins (paternal) namely; Biru, Hiru and Miru. Rapjan Bibi died leaving her husband Gumani Mridha, mother Moyful and 2 sisters Golejan and Sukjan. Thereafter Sukjan Bibi died leaving her husband Pabna, mother Moyful, sister Golejan Bibi and daughter (plaintiff). Then Moyful died leaving her daughter Golejan Bibi, second husband Bina Mondal and daughter Elajan. Thereafter, Golejan Bibi died leaving her husband Saimuddin and Cousin Subid Mondal Miru Mondal was survived by his only son Subid Mondal. Hiru Mondal died unmarried leaving his brother Biru Mondal, Elajan, daughter of Biru Mondal, died leaving her father and 2 daughters in Sakina and Bashabi Bewa. Biru Mondal left his second wife Tolajan and nephew Mondal as heirs. Thereafter Subid Mondal, Tolajan Bibi and Pabna (husband of Sukja) sold 2.97 acres of land by 2 registered Kabalas dated 2-4-1968 and 12-4-1968. Subsequently, when the defendant No. 2 found that the suit land was sold in auction sale and the Government acquired ownership, he took lease from the Government vide Settlement Case No. 9 of 1970-71 and 14 of 1970-71 and continued possession in the suit property. The plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 410 of 1968 against the Government for correction of record, which was dismissed. So, the plaintiff has no right, title and interest in the suit property. The learned Subordinate Judge, on hearing both the sides and considering evidence adduced by the parties decreed the suit on contest on 30-4-1987 declaring plaintiffs title to the suit land. Against the said Judgment and decree the contesting defendant No. 2 filed an appeal, which was heard by the learned Additional District Judge, Pabna. The appellate Court on hearing both the sides allowed the appeal of the defendant No. 2 and reversed the judgment passed by the trial Court and consequently the original suit stood dismissed by his judgment dated 14-3-1996.

3. Being aggrieved, the plaintiffs side preferred this revisional application assailing the judgment of the appellate Court mainly on the ground that the learned Additional District Judge, Pabna, committed material illegality in reversing the findings of the learned trial Court and arrived at an erroneous decision resulting in failure of justice and, as such, the same is liable to be set aside.

4. The learned Senior Advocate Mr Rowshan Ali, appearing on behalf of the petitioner (plaintiff), has taken me through the judgments of both the courts below and the evidence on record. He submits that since the issue Nos. 2-3 relating to maintainability and limitation of the suit were not agitated before the trial Court, the appellate Court wrongly reopened the matters out of the way and took wrong decisions in respect of those issues uncalled for. It is submitted that the claim of the plaintiff is based on CS Khatian, which has got presumptive value as to its correctness but the learned Additional District Judge, discarded the said document at the instance of fictitious story introduced by the defendant No. 2 after a long span of time. That the defendant No. 2 never challenged the CS Khatian at any point of time in assertion of their interest. He submits that the defendant No. 2 also brought two conflicting stories of acquiring interest in the suit land, one from the alleged purchase from some fictitious co-sharers in the year 1968 and another by way of taking settlement from the Government admitting that he had no independent title in the land. It is further submitted that when the collusive auction sale was set aside, the ex-landlord or the successor Government did not acquire any interest in the said auction sale to hold its management and give settlement of the plaintiff's suit land. He has made further submission supporting the findings and decisions arrived at by the trial Court. It is submitted that the plaintiff petitioners, being the heirs of the original admitted owners, are in physical possession having title therein and they will suffer irreparable loss and injury if the impugned judgment and decree of the appellate Court are not set aside.

5. The learned Senior Advocate Mr Nazrul Islam, appearing on behalf of the opposite parties, submits that the findings and decision arrived at by the learned appellate Court are based on reasons and supported by the evidence on record. It is submitted that the plaintiffs were aware of the alleged wrong SA Khatian prepared in the name of the Government when a suit was filed by the plaintiff for correction of record under section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in the year 1968. So, the present suit having been filed after 6 years from the said knowledge of wrong record, was barred under Article 120 of the Limitation Act. It is further submitted that the cause of action of this suit, has not been proved. According to his submission, the judgment and decree passed by the appellate Court are based on evidence on record and there being instance of misreading and non-consideration of evidence, the said judgment does not call for interference.

6. Admittedly, the suit land measuring 3.37 acres of land (Ga-Schedule including some other lands were recorded in the names of 3 sisters namely, Golejan Bibi, Rupjan Bibi and Sukjan Bibi in equal shares during Cadastral Survey (CS Operation). Exhibit 5 CC Khatian No. 56 stands in support of the contentions as to the previous ownership of the suit land according to the plaintiff's case, Sale Certificate dated 12-1-1954 (Boinama) submitted by the defendant in connection with Rent Execution Case No. 720 of 1953 filed by the ex-landlord Raja Protiva Nath Roy Bahadur against the original plaintiff Karimon Nessa and another CS recorded owner Golejan Bibi (her Khala). It indicates clearly that said plaintiff Karimon Nessa was the owner of the suit land with Golejan Bibi in the year 1953-54 when the auction sale was held. None of the defendant No. 2's predecessors, according to his genealogy given in the written statement, was party to the execution proceedings of the connected Rent suit which he relied on. Had they any interest and possession in the suit land according to the defendant's case, their names ought to have appeared amongst the defaulter tenants against whom auction proceeding was initiated. The defendant No. 2 though set up a separate case stating genealogy of Kichir Mondal, father of the CS recorded tenants as previous owner, he has not been able to establish such contention by substantial evidence in view of consistency in the plaintiffs clear case on the basis of CS Khatian. So, the defendant's case so far his claim of independent ownership through reversion heirs of Kichir Mondal, cannot be acceptable. Further, it is evident that actually the case of the defendant stands on the second contention ie termination of plaintiffs tenancy right, in the suit land on the basis of auction purchase by the ex-landlord Raja Protiva Nath Roy Bahadur. The defendant No. 2 relying on the auction sale submitted Bainanama dated 12-4-1954, which is Exhibit I. After the promulgation of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the suit land, alleged to have been auction purchased by the ex-landlord, vested in the Government as non-retainable Khas land. So, the defendant No. 2 prayed that the suit land was correctly recorded in the name of the Government during SA operation giving a complete go-by to his earlier stand of independent claim of title. Accordingly, the defendant No. 2 took lease from the Government vide Exhibit 3 which shows that the lease was given showing the suit land as khas land of the Government in the year 1974. In such view of the matter, it must be held that the CS Khatian can be taken as the basis of asserting ownership of the suit land and the plaintiff Karimon Nessa was admitted to be owner of the suit land as she was shown as judgment debtor of the Execution Case through which the admitted auction sale took place on 21-11-1953.

7. Thus, it appears that if the auction sale on the basis of Exhibit 1 stands good, then the defendant No. 2 has a defendable case of claiming possessor right on the basis of lease deed executed by the Government treating the suit land as non-retainable khas case land of the ex-landlord. In other words, if the SA Khatian is found to be correct, then only the defendant No. 2 is entitled to effectively resist the claim of the plaintiff as a leaseholder under the Government, otherwise not. Exhibit 3 is the Certified Copy of a petition filed by the plaintiff on 2-2-1959 under section 174(3) of the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1849 for setting aside the auction sale, which was registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 26 of 1959 against the decree holder ex-landlord who was replaced by the Government, alleging that the auction was held in a fraudulent manner by suppressing notice on the plaintiff who was in physical possession. It appears that from Exhibit 4 that the said Miscellaneous Case was allowed setting aside the auction sale by the learned Munsif on 23-5-1959 and the plaintiff also paid arrears rent to the Government vide challan dated 17-4-1959 which is marked as Exhibit 2. In view of the order setting aside the prior auction sale in respect of the suit land, the plaintiffs title and possession cannot be said to have been terminated. Had she not been in physical possession, the application for setting aside the auction sale need not have been brought by her in the year 1959. It may be mentioned here that the decree holder auction purchaser did not take delivery of possession in the suit land in pursuance of the said auction sale, which had been subsequently set aside by the competent Court. No writ of delivery of possession is available. So, there is no reason to record the disputed land in the name of the Government as Khas land during SA Operation which was done after setting aside the auction sale in the year 1959. It is therefore, apparently a wrong record of right and the said Khatian in respect of the suit land ought to have been recorded in the name of original plaintiff Most. Karimon Nessa. So, the petitioners being admitted heirs of Karimon Nessa appear to have acquired good title in the suit land by way of inheritance. So far possession in the suit land is concerned, the plaintiff's side produced some Government dakhilas (Exhibit 1 series) and adduced 5 witnesses. They also paid arrear rent by a challan (Exhibit 2). All the PWs gave testimony in support of the plaintiffs possession, whereas 4 DWs said about possession of both the parties in the suit land. So, the assertion of plaintiffs possession gets affirmation by many DWs at least in respect of some portion of the suit land. The learned trial Court appears to have elaborately discussed evidence of possession and arrived at a proper finding in support of the plaintiff's possession. The appellate Court appears to have taken erroneous view in the matter of ascertaining possession due to misreading and non-consideration of material evidence on record, which I have already discussed above.

<u>8. Mere knowledge about wrong recording of SA Khatian does not give rise to the cause of action to bring any suit, if the plaintiff does not bring such cause of action in the plaint. Limitation shall start running from the date of given cause of action. The learned Additional District Judge, Pabna, appears to have taken a wrong view in holding that since the plaintiff knew about the alleged wrong SA Khatian at the time of filing the suit bearing No. 410 of 1968 the present suit filed in the year 1975 was barred by limitation. He did not see that the plaintiffs cause of action in the present suit arose on 10-4-1975, when she came to know about the lease granted in favour of the defendant No. 2 by the Government. It appears from the lease deed that it was executed and registered on 16-7-1974. So, the plaintiff appears to have filed the suit in time from given cause of action and, as such, the suit cannot be said to have been barred by limitation under Article 120 of the Limitation Act. I have carefully gone through the judgment passed by the appellate Court along with the evidence on record and it is evident that the learned Additional District Judge has failed in error in taking decision in the appeal reversing the findings of the trial Court on the main question of acquisition of title and possession in the suit land. When some of the PWs admitted possession of the plaintiffs in some portion of the suit land, the learned Additional District Judge was totally wrong to find that the suit was not maintainable under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. Moreover, the findings arrived at by the learned trial Court on the question of possession appears to be sound and proper. Therefore, I hold the view that the findings and decision arrived at by the trial Court were not liable to be set aside in the appeal.</u>

9. After the reconsideration of all the materials, facts, circumstances and evidence on record, I am inclined to hold that the appellate Court has fallen in error of law due to the misreading and non-consideration of the evidence on record and, as such, it resulted in an error of law in the decision occasioning failure of justice. Accordingly, the impugned judgment and decree cannot legally be sustained.

10. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and decree passed by the Court of appeal are set aside and those of the trial Court restored.

Send down the lower Court records at once.

End.

lawyer:
Md Muzibur Rahman with Chowdhury Nasima, Advocates — For the Petitioner. 
Abdul Zalil Gazi, Advocate — For the Opposite
parties:
Shahjahan (Md) ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Hamdon Nessa ----- Opposite-Party
full_judgment:
ABM Khairul Haque J : This Rule arises out of the judgment and decree dated 4-6-2005, passed by the District Judge, Dhaka, in Civil Revision No. 26 of 2005, in setting aside the judgment and order dated 15-1-2005, passed by the Joint District Judge, Arbitration Court, Dhaka, in Review Miscellaneous Case No. 18 of 2004, rejecting the application for review.

2. The facts, in brief, are that the opposite party No. 1 filed a suit on 25-7-2002 in the Court of Joint District Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka, being Title Suit No. 15 of 2002, renumbered as the Title Suit No. 3 of 2004 after being transferred in the Court of Joint District Judge, Arbitration Court, Dhaka, praying for declaration of title in respect of the disputed land.

3. After a contested hearing the learned Judge by his judgment and decree dated 12-10-2004 dismissed the suit. Being aggrieved the plaintiff filed a review application under Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, being Review Miscellaneous Case No. 18 of 2004. After hearing the said review, miscellaneous case was also dismissed by the order dated 15-1-2005 Being aggrieved by the said order passed by the learned Joint District Judge, the plaintiff obtained a Rule in the Court of District Judge, under section 115(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure. After hearing he Rule, the learned District Judge, by his Judgment and decree dated 4-6-2005 in allowing the revisional application, set aside the order dated 15-1-2005, passed in Review Miscellaneous Case No. 18 of 2004 and also set-aside the Judgment and decree dated 12-10-2004, passed by the trial Court and decreed the suit. Accordingly, a decree in the said Civil Revision was drawn under Order XLI, rule 35 of the Code. Being aggrieved, the defendant obtained the present Rule under section 115(4) of the Code.

4. This Rule was opposed on behalf of the opposite party No. 1 by filing a counter-affidavit sworn on 27-8-2005.

5. Mr Md Muzibar Rahman, Advocate, papers with Ms Chowdhury Nasima, Advocate, on behalf of the petitioner while Mr Abdul Zalil Gazi, Advocate, appears on behalf of the plaintiff-opposite party.

6. Mr Md Muzibur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submitted that in the facts and circumstances of this case, the judgment and decree passed by the learned District Judge, is misconceived as he dealt with the issues as a first appeal in ignoring the specific provisions of Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code. He further submitted that since there is no error apparent on the face of the record in the impugned judgment and decree passed in the trial Court in Title Suit No. 3 of 2004, the learned District Judge, Dhaka, erred in law, apparent on the face of the record and, as such, the said judgment and decree are to be set aside.

7. On the other hand, Mr A Zalil Gazi, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-opposite party, submitted that the learned Joint District Judge erred in law in disposing of the review miscellaneous case as his order was not a speaking order and the learned Judge failed to appreciate the errors apparent on the face of the record as envisaged in Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code, as such, the learned District Judge, under section 115(2) of the Code rightly set aside the said order passed by the learned Joint District Judge.

8. We have heard the learned Advocates of both the sides, perused the provisional application, counter-affidavit, etc. We have gone through the judgment and order dated 12-10-2004 passed in Title Suit No. 3 of 2004 and the order dated 15-1-2005 passed in the Review Miscellaneous Case No. 18 of 2004, passed by the Joint District Judge.

9. It is true that the Order of the learned Joint District Judge in disposing of the review miscellaneous case, is a short one but at the same time the judgment and decree passed by the learned District Judge in disposing of the revisional application in respect of the legality of the said order passed in review, appears to be a judgment in appeal from the decree in the suit and not on a review miscellaneous case. The principle of review has been spelt out in rule 1 under Order XLVII of the Code of Civil Procedure.

10. It appears that three conditions, among others, are required to be fulfilled in order to allow an application for review under Order LXVII, rule 1 of the Code. Those are : (i) firstly, discovery of new and important matter or evidence which could not have been done earlier even by exercising due diligence. (ii) secondly, mistake or error apparent on the face of the record, (iii) thirdly, any other sufficient reason.

11. In the instant case admittedly no new document was sought to be produced on behalf of the plaintiff-opposite party. The question of some substantive cause was also not argued. But it was argued that the petition for review raised various errors which are apparent on the face of the record and those are sufficient reasons for allowing the petition and, as such, the learned District Judge rightly decreed the suit.

12. Let us first understand what is an error apparent on the face of the record. This has been explained in the case of AHM Mustain Billah vs Bangladesh 2005 BCR (AD) I = 57 DLR (AD) 41. The concept of error apparent on the face of the record has been explained by Md Fazlul Karim, J at paragraphs 27-28 at p. 11 :

"27. Mere error of fact or law is no error on the face of the record. It is such obvious error of law, which has either crept through Court's oversight or Counsel's mistake and failure to explain the legal position by the learned Counsel for the party. The error must be such which at a glance can be detected without advancing elaborate argument.

28. Though there is no hard and fast rule as to what is an error apparent on the face of the record but the same depends on the facts and circumstances of each case. But there could not be an error apparent on the face of the record merely because two possible views as to the interpretation or application of law vis-a-vis the particular facts of a case, one view accepted by the Court though may be erroneous but could not be the ground of review even if a decision or order is erroneous in law or on merits, the same shall not amount to an eror apparent on the face of the record.

13. The scope of review has also been lucid-ly explained by his Lordship at para 19, page 9 :

"19. A decision of this Court should not be reopened on a cloak of review as the same is never meant for rehearing of the matter closed by a judgment but could be reported to under exceptional circum-stances. Generally, a review will only be exercised consistently with the nature of review jurisdiction and with due regard to the principles that there must be an end of litigation. Law does not allow any court to sit over an appeal against its own decision but allows its own decision to be reviewed under its very limited scope and limitation set for in the law and rules. And the said jurisdiction should not be exercised or abused sitting over the decision, as if, it is an appeal."

<u>14. The ratio decidendi of the above decision shows that the purpose of the review is not the rehearing of the suit in order to correct the earlier findings of the concerned Judge himself. It appears that the learned District Judge interfered with the order of review passed by the trial Court on the ground that the said order is a non-speaking order. Thereafter, the learned District Judge elaborately examined the judgment passed by the Joint District Judge, in the suit considering the evidence on record as if he was dealing with a first appeal but without deciding the errors apparent on the face of the record. Apparently, the learned District Judge missed the scope of review under Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code.</u>

<u>15. The scope of review, as we have already pointed out earlier above, is very narrow and the learned Judge is not allowed to re-open the case all over again in considering a petition for review. In considering such a petition, a Judge needs to identify the errors and other sufficient reasons, if any.</u>

<u>16. In considering a revisional application from an order passed in review, the learned District Judge is first required to see whether an interference in the order passed in review is at all called for. If he finds that no interference is required, the matter ends there. But if he finds the petition for review as maintainable, still then he shall not act as an appellate Court but confine himself in the four corners of Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Code and decide the review petition as if he is the Judge before whom the review petition had earlier been filed.</u>

<u>17. We have asked the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite party to pinpoint from the judgment of the learned District Judge and ascertain such an error which is apparent on the face of the record but he failed to do so. On scrutiny of the records, it appears that the learned District Judge very laboriously scrutinised the judgment passed in the suit, taking into consideration the evidence on record, as such, traveled far beyond the scope of rule 1 of Order XLVII of the Code. The learned District Judge dealt with the matter as if it was a First Appeal, as such, committed an error of law.</u>

18. As such, the contention raised on behalf of the learned Advocate for the defendant-petitioner has got substance.

<u>19. Under such circumstances, the judgment and decree passed by the learned District Judge in exercise of his jurisdiction under section 115(2) of the Code, requires to be set aside.</u>

20. In that view of the matter, the judgment and decree passed by the learned District Judge, Dhaka, in Civil Revision No. 26 of 2005, is set aside.

In the result, the Rule is made absolute but without any order as to costs.

End.
