parties:
Anwar Hossain ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Shahadat Hossain and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
M.M. Ruhul Amin, J: This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party Nos. 1-5 to show cause as to why the judgment and order dated 28-2-91 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka Sadar in Title Suit No. 395 of 1986 allowing the prayer for addition of party under Order I rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure should not be set aside or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. Facts relevant for the purpose of disposal of the Rule are as follows :

The present petitioner as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 395 of 1988 in the 1st Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka alleging, inter alia, that the respondent No. 6 Offeaed 0210 land described in the schedule of the plaint to this petitioner by a registered Hiba-bil-Ewaz deed dated 16-8-84 and delivered possession of the land in favour of the petitioner and since then the plaintiff-petitioner has been in possession of the land and residing therein with other members of his family. The respondent No. 6 is a foster mother of the petitioner who at the instance of some motivated persons filed Title Suit No. 70 of 1988 in the 1st Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka for cancellation of the said Hiba-bil-Ewaz deed dated 16-8-84. It was disposed of on compromise but this petitioner was not aware of the terms of compromise. Hence the petitioner has filed the present suit for setting aside the compromise decree dated 26-6-88 passed in Title Suit No. 70 of 1988 brought by the respondent No. 6. During pendency of the suit Opposite Party Nos. 1-5 purchased the suit land from opposite party No. 6 by 5 registered kabalas dated 4-3-90. The opposite party Nos. 1-5 filed an application on 6-3-91 under Order 1 rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure for being added as defendants. The learned trial Court in spite of objection raised by the present petitioner allowed the prayer for addition of party by the impugned judgment and order.

3. Mr Mojibur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, submits that the transfer by the kabalas dated 4-3-90 in favour of added opposite party Nos. 1-5 were made during pendency of the suit and, as such, the transfer is hit by the doctrine of lis pendens as provided in section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act and, as such, the opposite party Nos. 1-5 had no locus standi to be added as party but still the learned trial Court allowed their prayer for addition of party without assigning any reason by the impugned order. He next submits that the transferees cannot apply under Order I rule 10(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure to be impleaded as party to the suit. In support of his contention the learned Advocate has placed reliance upon the case of Jamaluddin vs. Rabeay Begum, reported in 32 DLR 63. In that case it was held that since the transfer was made by the defendant No. 1 during the pendency of the suit, the petitioners are bound by the results of the suit under section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act. Their title, if any, is subject to the result of the suit. In such circumstances their presence is neither necessary nor proper for effectually and completely to adjudicate upon and settle all the questions involved in the suit. In that case it was further observed that the transferees during pendency of the suit do not come within the category of persons whose presence before the court may be necessary in order to enable the court effectually and completely to adjudicate upon and settle all the questions involved in the suit.

4. Mr Fazlul Karim, the learned Senior Advocate appearing for the opposite parties, submits that the case reported in 32 DLR was a suit for Specific Performance of Contract and in a suit for Specific Performance of Contract only the parties to the contract are necessary parties. He further submits that this is on the principle that the scope of a suit for Specific Performance of Contract ought not to be enlarged and the suit turned also into a title suit between one of either of the parties to the contract and a stranger to the contract. In that case it was also held that section 27 of the Specific Relief Act does not contemplate a suit for adjudication of title between a party to the contract and a purchaser pendente lite from one of the parties to the contract.

5. Mr Fazlul Karim next submits that the facts of the case reported in 32 DLR 63 are quite distinguishable from the facts of the present case and the present case has some distinguishing features. The present suit was filed for setting aside a compromise decree dated 26-6-88 passed in Title Suit No. 70 of 1988 between the parties. He further submits that there was an agreement for sate between opposite party No. 6 and opposite party Nos. 1-5 prior to the institution of the present suit ana in pursuance of that agreement, the kabalas in favour of Opposite Party Nos. 1-5 were executed during pendency of the suit. So, the transfer in favour of the opposite party Nos. 1-5 having been made on the basis of an earlier agreement executed prior to the institution of the suit are not hit by the doctrine of lis pendens and the transferees were rightly added as defendants in the suit for proper adjudication of the dispute between the parties. Mr Karim also relied upon the case reported in 27 DLR (AD) 129. In that case it was observed that in the absence of a necessary party a decree cannot be made in favour of the plaintiff. In that case it was held as follows: The position in law undoubtedly is that, in the absence of a necessary party a decree cannot be made in favour of the plaintiff. Of course, the question as to what parties are necessary is often not easy to determine. One test which has been recognised as of great importance is that when in the absence of a party the court cannot give an effective remedy, that party is a necessary party. Besides, in order that a party may be considered a necessary party two conditions must be satisfied, first, that there must be a right to some relief against him in respect of the matter involved in the suit and second, that his presence should be necessary in order to enable the court effectively and completely to adjudicate upon and settle the question involved in the suit."

<u>6. It may be mentioned here that in order to enable the court effectually and completely to adjudicate upon and settle all the questions involved in the suit, the court may allow an amendment at any stage of the suit and a belated prayer is no ground for refusal of such a prayer.</u>

7. In view of the discussion above, in my opinion, the learned trial Court did not commit any illegality by allowing the prayer for audition of party by the impugned order. Accordingly, I have nothing to interfere with.

The Rule is accordingly discharged without any order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
Shafique Ahmed, Advocate — For the Petitioner
AY Salehuzzaman, Deputy Attorney-General — For Opposite Parties
parties:
Ansurul Hoque ----- Petitioner.
vs.
Secretary, Ministry of Public Works and Urban Development of Bangladesh and another ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
AM Mahmudur Rahman J : This Rule calls in question an order of the Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka setting aside an ex parte decree made in Title Suit No. 167 of 1983.

2. The aforesaid suit was started upon filing an award dated March 23, 1983 by Arbitrator under section 14 read with section 17 of the Arbitration Act, 1940/1 and the court fixed June 5, 1983 for service of summons and order. The petitioner appeared on June 5, 1983 by filing an application for making the award as Rule of the court. Thereafter the court adjourned the hearing of the suit from time to time on the prayer of the opposite parties for filing written objection. Ultimately on 24-11-1983 the court passed the Owing order. The learned Advocate for the 2nd party prays for time for filing objection. Prayer is allowed for ends of justice as a last chance. No further time will be given for filing objection; to 29-12-83 for filing objection indefalt for ex parte hearing. "On 29-12-1983 the opposite parties, although filed an application for time to file written objection, the application was not moved and the court decreed the suit ex parte and made award "part of the decree. The petitioner, thereafter, started Money Execution Case No. 11 of 1984 against the opposite parties for realisation of the decretal amount as per the award.

3. The ex-parte decree was followed by an application filed under Order 9, rule 13 CPC read with section 151 CPC on March 11, 1984 for setting aside ex parte decree along with an application under section 5 of the Limitation Act for condonation of delay in filing the application for setting aside ex parte decree resulting in starting the Miscellaneous Case No. 208 of 1984. By the impugned order dated June 27, 1984 the court allowed Miscellaneous Case on contest and restored the suit on setting aside the ex-parte decree giving rise to the present Rule.

4. It is contended by the petitioner that the court below committed an error of law in its decision occasioning failure of justice in condoning the delay inasmuch as the grounds stated for condonation do not constitute sufficient causes as there was no explanation offered by the opposite parties for each day's delay in filing the application beyond 2 months and 13 days after signing of the decree. The learned Advocate for the petitioner referred us to the decision in the case of. Province of East Pakistan vs. Abdul Hamid Darjee, 21 DLR 824 wherein a Division Bench of the High Court of East Pakistan held that law does not make any discrimination between the Government and a private litigant in respect of condoning the delay under section 5 of the Limitation Act. Considering the circumstances of that case it was found by the learned Judges that negligence was well established in that case and held that negligence of an agent or a servant of the Government was not a sufficient cause to condone the delay. In that case the delay in filing the appeal was 442 days. In the petition under section 5 it was stated that although the Additional Deputy Commissioner sent proposal for filing the appeal to the Legal Remembrance on 28-12-67 and there were correspondences regarding filing of appeal on "a number of times but unfortunately, nothing could be traced out and the correspondences with respect to the proposal has been misplaced." In considering the question of condonation of delay the learned Judges took these circumstances into consideration and came to the findings that there were "utter callousness and gross negligence of the servants of the petitioners, Government of East Pakistan" and upon such findings the delay was not condoned. But in the instant case we do not find such circumstances as were found in that case. Accordingly, we held that the principle laid down therein has no application in the instant case. The petitioner also referred us to the decision in the case of Province of East Pakistan vs. Suboda Kumar Dey Das, 25 DLR 280 to argue that the Government has a great responsibility in the matter of filing an appeal and the laches on the part of the Government is very serious and the court has always looked at it with disfavour. The proposition of law admits of no doubt. The Single Bench of the then High Court of East Pakistan in that case held that in filing appeal any laches on the part of the Government is very serious and the court has always looked at it with disfavour and the Government must come before the Court at an earliest opportunity within the statutory period of limitation. The learned Deputy Attorney-General also invited our attention to the following observation of the learned Judge.

"There is still another aspect of the matter. The different links of the Government are so connected that one cannot work without the co-operation and assistance of the other".

contends that in the instant case the opposite parties were to take step in the matter after collecting necessary papers and there was no laches on the part of the opposite parties. He also submits that in condoning the delay the special feature of a given case are to be taken into consideration and section 5 of the Limitation Act is to be interpreted liberally. He submits that the case condoned the delay and in so doing, as the court acted according to the discretion to secure the ends of justice, the order does not call for any interferences by this court under section 115(1) CPC. He also placed reliance on the case of Bangladesh vs. jaharuddin, 1986 BLD (AD) 180. In that case the learned Chief Justice in delivering the judgment of the report observed:

"In matters of condonation of delay Government does not enjoy any special privilege, but the fact remains that due to the necessity to obtain opinions on various authorities concerned before filing an appeal, some time may reasonably be expected to elapse which in the case of an individual does not happen. Some consideration in appropriate circumstances may therefore be extended to Government appearing as a litigant. In saying so, no rule is being laid down for not observing strictness of the proof of substantial and reasonable cause in making such delay. Standard of acceptance must, however, remain the same in case of both citizens and State."

The learned Chief Justice has cautioned that in matters of conditions of delay the Government does not enjoy any special privilege. In our opinion the words 'sufficient cause' contemplated an enquiry as to whether the person claiming indulgence has been so negligent or that there has been a serious lack of bonafide and to uphold the plea of sufficient cause the court is to see whether it will result in injustice to the opposite party. And unless such situation arises the expression" sufficient cause" calls for a liberal construction so as to advance the cause of substantial justice and the court of law should look at the plea of sufficient cause "in a practical way" and should not adopt "any doctrinaire approach to the question".

5. Now, we are to find out and give our opinion as to whether in the instant case there was any laches or negligence on the part of the opposite parties. This Rule has been opposed by filing an affidavit-in-opposition wherefrom it appears that the delay was caused not for the negligence and laches on the part of the opposite parties. In the petition under section 5 it has been stated that after obtaining the copy of the ex parte decree the matter was referred to the concerned Ministry for necessary action for want of which they could not take any step against the ex parte decree in time and there was no laches on the part of the opposite parties to file the application for setting aside the ex parte decree. From examining the order impugned we also find that the learned Judge in passing the impugned order has also adverted to the aforesaid statements of the opposite parties. Thus, it seems to us that the court after having had considered the circumstances stated in the application and hearing both the parties found that there were sufficient causes in not filing the applications in time and set aside the ex parte decree.

<u>6. The order dated 24-11-83 as quoted earlier shows that 29-12-83 was fixed both for filing written objection and for ex parte hearing of the suit. Taking into consideration the nature of the order we cannot conclusively hold that the suit was fixed for ex parte hearing only on that date. When a court fixes a date for filing written objection, it ought not have fixed that date for expert hearing also as fixing the same date for both filing written objection and for ex parte hearing gives sufficient scope for confusion. Looking from this angle it also seems to us that the impugned order was legally made. In view of the observations made in the cases cited at the Bar we are of the opinion that section 5 requires a liberal interpretation and as we find that in this case there was no laches on the part of the opposite parties there is no wrong in condoning the delay taking into consideration the entire facts as emerged from this case. In this respect the case of Punjab Province vs. Sultan Kha, PLD 1959 (Lah) 500 cited at the Bar may also be referred to Section 115(1) CPC contemplates interference with an order only where there is an error of law committed by a court in its decision occasioning failure of justice. Mere error of law cannot be a ground for interference unless such error has led to injustice. In the instant case, we are of the opinion, by the impugned order rather the ends of justice has been advanced by setting aside the ex parte decree and restoring the suit giving both parties an opportunity to contest on merit. The decision cited by Mr. Shafique Ahmed reported in 21 DLR 824 speaks that the Government as a litigant does not stand on a different footing from the ordinary litigant. But on the strength of the observation made in the case of Bangladesh vs. Jaheruddin 1986 BLD 180 by the Appellate Division we are of the opinion that in this case the opposite parties are entitled to privilege of section 5 of the Limitation Act as we find that there was no laches or negligence on their part to proceed with the instant case.</u>

7. In the result, we discharge the Rule but without any order as to cost.

The court below is to proceed with the suit in accordance with the law.

End.

lawyer:
Mihir Kanti Majumder, Advocate—For the Petitioner. 
Hasan Foez Siddique with M Habibullah, Advocates—For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Khoda Baksh Biswas ----- Petitioner
vs. 
Nabirunnessa and others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party, No. 1 to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 19-3-98 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Jessore, in Title Appeal No. 204 of 1991 reversing the Judgment and decree dated 30-7-91 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Additional Court, Jessore, in Title Suit No. 645 of 1977 dismissing the suit should not be set aside.

2. The short fact of the case is, that the defendant-respondent-opposite party No. 1 as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 645 of 1977 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Sadar, Jessore praying for preliminary decree of partition for her alleged share of seven annals sixteen gandas two kares in Ka schedule land out of an area of 1.95 acres of land appertaining to CS khatian No. 94 and SA khatian No. 101 and for establishment of title and preliminary decree of partition for her share of four annas one ganda three kares two karanties ten tiles share in the 'kha' schedule land out of an area of 12.11 acres appertaining to CS khatian Nos. 198, 206 and 697 corresponding to SA khatian Nos. 222, 234, 235 and 76.

3. The further case of the plaintiff-opposite party, in short, is that the suit land of 'ka' schedule originally belonged to Asmani Bibi who died leaving behind one son Hajer Mollah and while Hazer Mollah was the exclusive owner and possessor of the suit land died leaving behind his wife Nurjahan Bibi (defendant No. 4) and two sons Osman Mollah and Atiar Mollah and two daughters Amena Khatun and defendant No. 12 Ahurunnessa. Under the said circumstances at first Atiar Mollah died at the age of 12/13 years during the lifetime of his mother Nurjahan Bibi, Brother Osman Mollah and two sisters Amena Khatun and defendant No. 1. Thereafter, Osman Mollah died at the age of 18 years leaving behind his mother Nurjahan Bibi and his two sisters Amena and defendant No. 1. Thereafter Amena Khatun died leaving behind her mother Nurjahan Bibi, sister defendant No. 1 and her husband defendant No. 3 Abdul Malek as the ultimate surviving heirs in the 'ka' schedule properties of Hazer Mollah defendant No.4 and thus Nurjahan became the owner of five annals nineteen ganders three kares two warranties as her share and defendant No. 1 became the owner of eight nanas three gandas two karas share and defendant No.3 became the owner of two annas four ganders two karas and one karanties as his share.

4. That in the 'kha' schedule land Khoda Box Biswas was owner of nine annas share and Fulzan Bibi was owner of seven annals share. That Fulzan Bibi was the 2nd wife of Tafazuddin Biswas and defendant Nos. 2 and 5 was the son of Hazratullah Biswas who was the owner of the share of said Tofazzuddin Biswas by his first wife and one Asia Khatun was the daughter of Fulzan and Tofazuddin. That while Fulzan was in ejmali possession of her share in 'ka' schedule land she settled five annas share in favour of Hazer Mollah by a registered patta dated 7-12-1932 AD and delivered the possession thereof and thereafter Fulzan Bibi gave marriage of her daughter Asia Khatun with Hazer Mollah who began to live in the family of Fulzan as "gharzamai" and used to possess his acquired land along with land of his mother-in-law Fulzan Bibi in ejmali with the petitioner. Under these circumstances Asia Khatun died issueless and after the death of Asia Khatun, Hazer Mollah was being treated as son of Fulzan Bibi and for that reason Fulzan Bibi gave marriage to Hazer Mollah with present defendant No. 4 Nurjahan Bibi allowing them to live in the homestead of Fulzan Bibi. For this reason the defendant No. 4 had great regard and love for her mother-in-law Fulzan Bibi. Thereafter, during the lifetime of Fulzan Bibi, Hazer Mollah died leaving the persons referred to paragraph 1(a) of this petition in the same chronological order entitling defendant No.4 for one anna fifteen gandas one karanti share and defendant No.1 for two annals eleven gandas one karanti share and defendant No. 3 for thirteen gandas three Karas two karanties share in the 'kha' schedule land.

5. Then Fulzan Bibi having no other heirs and out of love and affection orally gifted her remaining two annas share in favour of the defendant No. 4 and then Fulzan Bibi died. Thereafter, the defendant No. 4 married Ibrahim Mollah and in that wedlock the plaintiff was born and afterwards defendant No. 4 gifted her share of 'kha' schedule land in favour of the plaintiff by a registered deed of Heba-bil-ewaz dated 28-7-72 and defendant No. 3 transferred his share in the 'ka' schedule land in favour of the plaintiff by a Heba-bil-ewaz deed 30-9-72 and the defendant No. 4 gifted her share in the 'kha' schedule land in favour of the plaintiff by a registered Heba deed dated 28-10-75 and defendant No. 3 transferred half of his share of the 'kha' schedule land in favour of the plaintiff by a registered kabala dated 8-4-78 and the remaining half annas share was sold to another wife of the husband of the plaintiff namely, Rabeya Khatun.

6. The defendant No. 1 collusively filed the partition suit No. 79 of 1993 in the same Court against the present plaintiff and her husband Abu Bakar and defendant Nos. 3 and 4 impleading present 'ka' schedule land of the plaint and excluding the present 'kha' schedule land and in that suit the present plaintiff-opposite party appeared and filed written statement which was ultimately withdrawn with the permission to sue afresh regarding 'kha' schedule land present defendant No. 2 (herein the petitioner) filed Title Suit No. 206 of 1962 which was renumbered as Title Suit No. 12 of 1964 against defendant No. 1 which was decreed in terms of codename as a collusive resort to defraud the co-sharers and as the defendant-petitioner refused amicable partition of the said 'kha' schedule land the present suit has been filed for partition of the 'Kha' schedule land.

7. That the 'Ga' schedule land has been settled jointly by Fulzan and defendant-petitioner in favour of Tanai Ram and others (predecessors of defendant No. 7) by registered Kabuliyat dated 24th of April, 1947 and by subsequent transfer now the defendant No. 2 (petitioner) Khurshed and Shahidul Islam acquired the same.

8. The petitioner as defendant No. 2 contested the suit by filing written statement denying the case as described in the plaint by the plaintiff as regards the 'kha' schedule land stating, inter alia, that the land of CS chitin No. 198 had been owned and possessed and recorded in the name of defendant-petitioner for nine annas and Fulzannessa Bibi for seven annas. Fulzannessa Bibi gave her daughter in marriage with Hazer Ali Mollah and kept him in her house as "gharzamai" and after the death of her daughter she again gave him in marriage with defendant No. 4 and conditionally gave a written patter about some land in favour of Hazer Mollah. Thereafter, their relationship has been deteriorated and when it became impossible to live together Hazer Mollah left the house of Fulzan Bibi giving an unregistered Istafa Patra dated 27th Chaitra, 1344 BS in favour of Fulzan who thereafter used to possess her land through defendant-petitioner. During the liberation war many documents including the said Istafa Patra were burnt and at the time of furnishing Istafa Patra Hazer Mollah also returned the patter dated 7-12-32 which was ultimately handed over to defendant-petitioner at the time of execution of Kabala dated 12-2-46 and the husband of the plaintiff while employed as servant in the house of the petitioner he heed stolen the said patta and kabuliyat and thereafter, when Fulzan Bibi proposed to sell her property, the petitioner purchased the share of Fulzan in the 'kha' schedule land by registered kabala deed dated 14-2-46 and during the last settlement operation the defendant No. 1 collusively got recorded her name as daughter of Hazer Mollah and on that basis while threatened the petitioner's possession he filed Title Suit No. 206 of 1962 renumbered as Title Suit No. 12 of 1964 of Additional Court of Munsif, Jessore and ultimately, the said suit was decreed in terms of Solenama against the defendant No. 1 and the third schedule of land by registered kabuliyat dated 24-4-37 was settled with Foni Rui Das and others among whom Foni Rui Das sold his 1/3 share to the petitioner by a registered kabala dated 21-3-59 and in the said Kabuli at the name of Hazer Mollah was wrongly omitted as landlord and plot No. 909 was wrongly omitted and though the land of CS khatian No. 206 was in exclusive possession of the petitioner but the same was wrongly inserted in the kabala dated 14-2-46 and at the time of preparation of the written statement of this case the petitioner further came to know that part of the land of CS kalian No. 206 was wrongly recorded in the name of the defendant No.1 for which the petitioner separately filed Title Suit No.12 of 1964 in- the 3rd Court of Assistant Judge, Jessore earlier Title Suit No. 206 of 1962 and got compromise decree on 16-7-64 and acquired good title by ouster and adverse possession of the plaintiff's claim of title from defendant Nos. 3 and 4 is totally false and the alleged pasta deed dated 7-11-52 was never acted upon and in such, view of the facts, prayed for dismissal of the suit.

9. The defendant Nos. 5 (ka), 5(kha) and 6 herein opposite party Nos. 5, 6 and 22 by fling separate petition praying for their Saham in the 'ka' schedule land on the basis of their purchase of registered deeds which have been admitted by the plaintiffs also.

10. That on perusal of the pleadings the learned trial Court framed the following issues:

a) Is the suit maintainable in its present form?

b) Is the suit barred by limitation?

c) Is the suit bad for defect of parties?

d) Is the plaintiff entitled to get the decree as prayed for?

11. The learned trial Court after considering the evidence on record and document produced by both the parties and materials on record and after assessment of the evidence was pleased to dismiss the suit by his judgment and decree dated 30-7-91.

12. Being aggrieved by the judgment and decree passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Jessore, the plaintiff preferred an appeal before the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Jessore, being Title Appeal No. 204 of 1991. The learned Subordinate Judge on consideration of the evidence on record and documents produced by both the parties and after proper assessment of the evidence and registered deeds came to a finding that the learned trial Court was in error in law as well as on facts, as such, the judgment and decree passed by the learned trial Court was reversed. The learned Subordinate Judge allowed the appeal after hearing both the parties and reversed the judgment of the trial Court by his judgment and decree dated 19-3-98.

13. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Jessore, the defendant-respondents as petitioner preferred the instant revisional application before the High Court Division stating, inter alia, that the lower appellate Court without considering the evidence on record and by misreading and non-considering the material evidence reversed the judgment and decree of the trial Court and allowed the appeal which calls for interference by this Court.

14. The learned Counsel Mr Mihir Kanti Mazumder, appearing on behalf of the defendant-respondent-petitioner, submits that the lower appellate Court without applying his judicial mind and proper assessment of the evidence on record allowed the appeal which should be interfered by this Court. The learned Counsel further submits that the defendant-respondent petitioner purchased the share of Fulzan in 'kha' schedule land by a registered kabala dated 14-2-47 and since the purchase of the land he was in peaceful possession but the learned appellate Court totally ignored the title deed which was exhibited as Exhibit Umma (ঙ) by the defendant as DW 1 which was manifestly perverse. He also submits that the appellate Court without applying his judicial mind and proper assessment of the evidence on record and the registered deeds passed the judgment and decree allowing the appeal and reversing the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court. The learned Counsel next submits that although the plaintiff claimed that they were enjoying the suit land in 'kha,' schedule on the basis of the registered patta given by Fulzan Bibi to Hazer Mollah on 7-12-32 but after the death of Fulzan Bibi Hazer Mollah returned the patta by a unregistered Istafa Patra dated 27th of Chaitra, 1344 BS, though the plaintiff could not prove this fact before the learned trial Court as well as the appellate Court but the subsequent conduct of the plaintiff with regard to the possession of the suit land obviously proves the fact the patta was surrendered by Hazer Mollah through Istafa Patra.

15. He further submits that thereafter the defendant purchased the suit land of 'ka' schedule from Fulzan Bibi by a registered deed dated 12-2-46 and was enjoying the suit land peacefully. The learned lower appellate Court without considering this material aspect of the case allowed the appeal and reversed the judgment and decree passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Jessore. Finally, he submits that the observation made by the learned lower appellate Court is absolutely erroneous, that the plaintiff was also in possession of the 'ka' schedule land as both plaintiff and defendant were enjoying the suit land jointly. The learned lower appellate Court misread and did not consider the material evidence affecting the merit of the case, as such, the judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge should be reversed by this Court.

16. The learned Counsel Mr Hasan Foez Siddique with Mr M Habib Ullah, appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-appellant-opposite party, submits that the lower appellate Court is absolutely justified in allowing the appeal by reversing the judgment and decree of the trial Court because the learned trial Court totally misread the evidence of DW 1 who admitted in cross-examination that after the death of Hazer Mollah his property was enjoyed by Nurjahan and Nurjahan married Ibrahim after the death of Hazer Mollah. The DW 1 admitted in his evidence that the plaintiff also was enjoying the suit land, as such, the story that Hazer Mollah returned the patta by a Istafa Patra became falsified. If the patta remained valid which was registered and executed by Fulzan Bibi on 7-12-32 the subsequent claim of the plaintiff to the effect that he purchased the suit land from Fulzan Bibi by a registered deed dated 12-2-46 was a nullity. The learned Counsel next submits that the lower appellate Court elaborately discussed the evidence on record and examined the registered deed produced by both the parties and also applying his judicial mind and considering the evidence on record allowed the appeal which does not call for any interference by this Court. He finally, submits that the finding of facts passed by the lower appellate Court is final unless it is manifestly perverse or there is serious non-reading or misreading of the evidence, but in the instant case there is no error of finding and non consideration and misreading of the evidence, as such, the Judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Jessore do not call for any interference.

<u>17. On a meticulous examination of the judgment of lower appellate Court, as well as the trial Court and evidence on record and also the Exhibits, it transpires that the lower appellate Court carefully and clearly discussed the evidence on record and after proper assessment of evidence on record came to his finding reversing the judgment and decree passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Jessore.</u>

<u>18. By now the settled principle of law in exercising the provisional power under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure has been laid down in the several judicial pronouncements of our Appellate Division, that the finding of facts, whether concurrent or not, arrived at by the lower appellate Court is final unless it is manifestly perverse. In this connection I like to rely on the decision in the case of Khurshed Ali and others vs Nurjahan Bewa and others reported in 1995 BLD (AD) 82 wherein it has been held that when the appellate Court as the final Court of fact decides question of fact and records its findings on consideration of evidence on record, the High Court Division while exercising the revisional jurisdiction cannot interfere with the findings of facts unless the High Court Division is satisfied that the said findings are perverse. When the material findings of the appellate Court are upheld by the High Court Division and in doing so it commits no error of law. The decision of the High Court Division calls for no interference by the Appellate Division.</u>

19. Another decision can also be cited in the case of Hazari Bala Sana and another vs Niron alias Niranjan Mandal and others reported in 1997 BLD (AD) 295 wherein it is stated that it is a settled principle that the findings of facts, whether concurrent or not, arrived at by the lower appellate Court, which is the final Court of facts, is binding on the High Court Division, as a provisional Court except in certain well-defined exceptional circumstances, such as non-consideration or misreading of the material evidence affecting the merit of the case.

<u>20. The judgment of lower appellate Court transpires that in arriving at its finding the said Court carefully considered the material facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record both oral and documentary including the registered deeds.</u>

21. The learned Counsel for the defendant-respondent-petitioner could not point out any error or illegality or infirmity of law in the Judgment passed by the lower appellate Court.

<u>22. The discussion made above and the facts and circumstances of the case, the impugned judgment and decree dated 19-3-98 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Jessore reversing the judgment and decree dated 30-7-91 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Jessore and the case having been concluded on finding of facts, as such, no interference is called for in revision under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure.</u>

23. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. The order of stay earlier granted by this Court is hereby vacated.

Lower Court's records be sent down at once with a copy of the judgment.

End.

lawyer:

parties:
Asia Bewa and others ------ Petitioners
Vs.
Md Bachchu Fakir and anr ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Md Abdur Rashid J: The plaintiffs obtained the Rule upon making a revision application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure against the Order No. 128 dated 17-11-2002 passed by Joint District Judge, Court No.1 at Bogra in Miscellaneous Case No.73 of 1999, which set aside the decree dated 8-2-99 and restored the suit to its original file and number.

2. It is stated that on 2-2-1992 petitioners Nos. 8 to 12 and the predecessors of the petitioners Nos. 1 to 7 and 13 to 17 as plaintiffs instituted partition suit No. 31 of 1992 against 44 defendants, out of the defendants; defendant Nos. 2 to 6 and 9 only contested the suit.

<u>3. The suit was first decreed in the preliminary form on contest against said defendants and ex parte against the rest by Judgment and decree dated 8-2-99. After the report of the Advocate Commissioner effecting partition of the joint property was filed, the preliminary decree was made final on 19-8-99. In execution of the decree in other Execution No. 1 of 2000, the plaintiff got possession of his shares and on 24-10-01, the execution proceeding was finally disposed of on full satisfaction.</u>

<u>4. Meanwhile, on 20-6-99 defendant Nos. 40 and 41 jointly made an application under Order IX rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restoration of the suit to its original file and number after setting aside the decree mainly on the ground that no summons was served upon them. The application was registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 73 of 1999.</u>

5. Opposite party No. 10 of said application opposed the application by filing a written objection.

6. In support of the case, defendant No. 40, Bachchu Fakir alone was examined on behalf of himself and on behalf of defendant No. 41 while on behalf of the plaintiffs four witnesses were examined including the process server and two witnesses who witnessed the services.

7. On 8-2-99 by the impugned order, learned joint District Judge allowed the application with cost of Taka 2000 and restored the suit to its original file and number by setting aside both the preliminary decree and final decree.

8. It appears from the record that the process server returned the process with the report that he went to the house of defendant Nos. 39, 40, 43 and 44, found defendant No. 41 present. When he asked him to receive the summons with acknowledgment, he refused. Consequently, he served the summons by affixing copy at the door of the house. The return was duly verified by statutory declaration. Upon the aforesaid return, the Court found that the summons was duly served and proceeded to hear and disposes of the suit.

9. Opposite party No. 2 of Miscellaneous Case No. 73 of 1999, Md Moksed Ali examined him as OPW 1 on behalf of opposite party Nos. 1 to 10. He deposed that the process server served the summons upon defendant Nos. 40 and 41 in presence of witnesses, namely, Md Abdus Suttar Mandal and Md Abu Bakkar Siddique.

10. Process server, Sheik Sultan Ali as OPW 2 testified that on 18-4-92 he served summons upon defendant No. 40 Bachchu Fakir and 41 Dulu Fakir. Reaching the address, he found defendant No. 41 Dulu Fakir and explained the contents of the summons and asked him to receive them. But he refused to receive them. Then, he served the summons by hanging at the main door of their house. At the time, Md Abdus Sattar Mandal, son of defendant No. 7 and Md Abu Bakkar Siddique, son of defendant No. 8 were present there. They signed the return as witnesses. He proved the return as Exhibt 'K' and identified his signature as Exhibit 'K' 1.

11. Both Md Abu Bakkar Siddique and Md Abdus Sattar Mandal as OPW 3 and OPW 4 corroborated OPW 2 process server Sheikh Sultan that they took the process server to the house of Bachchu and Dulu. Dulu was present. The peon asked him to receive the summons after reading that over. Dulu refused to receive it. Then, the peon hanged the summons at the door of their house. They also singed the return, which they identified.

12. Defendant No. 41 did not appear. Defendant No. 40 claimed that they did not receive any summons. They could not, however, claim that they did not live in the house at the door of which the summons was served by hanging.

13. After careful scrutiny of the evidence of said OPWs 1 to 4, we have no hesitation to say that the summons was rightly found to have been duly served upon said defendant Nos. 40 and 41. Learned Joint District Judge also could not say that the summons was not served.

<u>14. Mr Md Khorshid Alam, learned Advocate for opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 read entire evidence of the witnesses and submitted that the witnesses contradicted with each other. But the inconsistency in the depositions of the witnesses as mentioned by Mr Khorshed Alam could not displace the proof that the summons was duly served by hanging at the door of the house of defendant Nos. 40 and 41 who are full brothers.</u>

<u>15. Under Order IX rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the trial Court has got discretion to set aside a decree passed ex parte but such discretion could only be exercised on either of the grounds, namely, (a) summons was not duly served or (b) absentee defendant was prevented by sufficient cause from appearing when the suit was called on for hearing. In the absence of any of such findings, the trial Court has no jurisdiction to set aside on ex parte decree.</u>

<u>16. In the case at hand, the learned Joint District Judge allowed the application on the view that it was reasonable to give them opportunity to contest. He, however, did not say a wrong how he found it to be reasonable, upon such assumption, exercise of the discretion by the learned Joint District Judge, resulted in serious indiscretion, which no doubt occasioned failure of justice in the facts and circumstances of the case.</u>

<u>17. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without however, any order as to cost. Order of stay granted at the time of issue of the Rule on 18-1-2003 is hereby recalled and vacated. Impugned order dated 17-11-2002 is hereby set aside.</u>

Send down the record at once.

End.
