full_judgment:
Md. Abdur Rouf J: These two appeals, Civil Appeal Nos. 35 and 36 of 1997, following leave, having been preferred by the plaintiff, in respect of the same suit property and in between the same parties, are being disposed of by this judgment.

<u>2. Civil Appeal No. 35 of 1997, is from the judgment and order dated 19-6-96 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 175 of 1996 discharging the Rule and refusing thereby to interfere with the order dated 6-1-96 passed by a Senior Assistant Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Title Execution Case No. 19 of 1995 rejecting the appellant's prayer to stay further proceeding of the said execution case pending disposal of Title Suit No. 210 of 1991 (originally numbered as Title Suit No. 294 of 1982) of the Court of Subordinate Judge, First Court, Dhaka.</u>

<u>3. Civil Appeal No. 36 of 1997, has arisen from the judgment and order dated 18-6-96 passed by the above mentioned same Bench of the High Court Division, in Civil Revision No. 3532 of 1995 making the Rule absolute and setting aside thereby the judgment and order dated 12-8-95 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Second Court, Dhaka in Miscellaneous Case No. 17 of 1995, under Order 9, rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure, allowing the same and restoring thereby the aforesaid Title Suit No. 210 of 1991, which was dismissed for default on 4-6-94.</u>

4. The relevant facts for disposal of these appeals are, briefly, as follows:

Late Al-haj Duliluddin Ahmed (died on 6-2-82), the predecessor-in-interest of the defendant-respondents of both the appeals instituted on 8-9-78 Title Suit No. 243 of 1978 in the court of then Munsif, 6th Court, now Assistant Judge, Dhaka for khas possession of the suit premises, against the custodian of vested property as defendant No. 1 and the present plaintiff-appellant, the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) Dhaka, as defendant No. 2 alleging, inter alia, that on 26-12-61 he has auction purchased, in a certificate case under the Public Demands Recovery Act, the suit properties comprising of Municipal Holding Nos. 26 and 26/1, Kali Charan Shaha Road, within Sutrapur police station, District Dhaka. The auction sale was confirmed on 9-9-66 and formal symbolical possession was given to him on 22-7-71. But the defendants illegally kept the suit property under their possession. The suit was decreed ex parte on 3-6-80. The decree-holder then filed Title Execution Case No. 14 of 1981. The present appellant filed Miscellaneous Case No. 47 of 1981, under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the said ex-parte decree, which, however, was dismissed for default on 15-6-81 and then his application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restoration of the said Miscellaneous case was also rejected on 27-2- 82. One MA Khaleque, who claimed himself as a monthly tenant in respect of the suit premises under the present appellant, on 11-5-81 instituted Title Suit No. 509 of 1981 in the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka for declaration that the aforesaid ex-parte decree was illegal, void, etc. making the present appellant as well as the Government of Bangladesh as defendant No. 5 and 3 respectively and on 13-7-81 got an order of temporary injunction restraining the decree-holder-respondent from proceeding with the said title execution case pending disposal of the suit. The suit was dismissed and the same was maintained by the High Court Division by its judgment and order dated 10-3-83 passed in Civil Revision No. 116 of 1982. On 26-6-82 the present appellant filed Title Suit No. 294 of 1982, subsequently renumbered as Title Suit No. 210 of 1991, for setting aside the aforesaid ex parte decree passed in Title Suit No. 243 of 1987 and the same was dismissed for default on 4-6-94. Against which the appellant filed Miscellaneous Case No. 33 of 1994, renumbered as Miscellaneous Case No.17 of 1995, under Order 9 rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restoration of the suit alleging, inter that on 4-6-94 the learned Advocate had been engaged in another court and accordingly, he filed an application for adjournment but the court dismissed the suit before noon without considering the prayer for adjournment.

5. The defendant-respondents opposed the aforesaid miscellaneous case by filing a written objection contending, inter alia, that the suit itself being barred by the principle of res-judicata the miscellaneous case was not maintainable as the ex parte decree passed in Title Suit No. 243 of 1978 had already reached its finality and conclusiveness against the plaintiff, because of dismissal of his Miscellaneous Case No. 47 of 1981, filed under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the said decree and rejection of his subsequent application filed under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and, as such, in view of the final, conclusive and binding character of the said ex parte decree upon the parties, if the Title Suit No. 210 of 1991 is restored the defendants will be driven to fruitless litigation and unnecessary harassment. It was also alleged that the Misc. Case had been brought upon making absolutely false statements that the plaintiff's concerned Advocate had been engaged on 4-6-94 in another court in connection with another case and that the plaintiff was prevented by sufficient cause from appearing in the suit when the same was taken up for hearing.

6. The plaintiff examined two PWs and exhibited the copy of the application for adjournment of the suit, Ext. 1 and the case diary of the plaintiffs advocate Ext. 2. On behalf of the defendant-opposite parties the present respondent No. 1 as their attorney was examined as OPW 1.

7. Upon hearing the parties the learned Subordinate Judge allowed the said Miscellaneous case by his judgment and order dated 12-8-95 and accordingly, Title Suit No. 210 of 1991 was restored to its original file and number.

8. The aggrieved respondents then moved the High Court Division in revision, and obtained Rule, Civil Revision No. 3532 of 1995. A learned Single Judge of the High Court Division by the impugned judgment and order dated 18-6-96 upon making the Rule absolute reversed the judgment and order of the learned Subordinate Judge and dismissed the Miscellaneous case holding, inter alia, that the plaintiff could not prove that he had been prevented by sufficient cause from not appearing in court when the suit was called on for hearing and that in the facts and circumstances of the case restoration of Title Suit No. 210 of 1991 would lead the parties to a fruitless litigation. Against the said judgment of the High Court Division Civil Appeal No. 36 of 1997 has been preferred.

9. The plaintiff-appellant also filed an application in the court of the Senior Assistant Judge, Dhaka in Title Execution Case No. 19 of 1995 (original execution case was Title Execution Case No. 14 of 1981) to stay its further proceeding till disposal of the aforesaid Title Suit No. 210 of 1991. But the same was rejected on 6-1-96. Against which the plaintiff moved the High Court Division and obtained another Rule, Civil Revision No. 175 of 1996. By a separate judgment dated 18-6-96 the same learned Judge of the High Court Division discharged the Rule holding, inter alia, that in view of his decision given in the other Rule, noted earlier, the latter Rule became infructuous, which has given rise to Civil Appeal No. 35 of 1997.

10. In connection with Civil Appeal No. 36 of 1997 leave was granted to consider whether the learned Singled Judge of the High Court Division was justified in dismissing the Miscellaneous Case No.17 of 1995 without setting aside the findings of fact arrived by the learned Subordinate Judge that on the date fixed for hearing of Title Suit No. 210 of 1991 the plaintiff had sufficient cause for his non-appearance and that whether the learned Judge did consider the evidence and materials brought on record in the said Misc. Case and that whether the learned Judge has travelled beyond his revisional jurisdiction upon tracing the history of litigation between the parties in passing the impugned Judgment and that whether the learned Judge by terming the appellant's suit as a "fruitless litigation" has condemned appellant and sealed the fate of the suit without hearing its merit.

11. In connection with Civil Appeal No. 35 of 1997 leave was granted to consider that in the facts and circumstances of the case whether the" earned Judge of the High Court Division was justified in discharging the Rule issued in Civil Revision No. 175 of 1996 treating the same as "infructuous".

12. Mr. Shahidul Alam, learned Advocate appearing for the appellant in both the appeals, submitted that the learned trial Judge on consideration of the evidence of PWs 1-2, OPW 1 and the documentary evidence namely, Ext. 1, the copy of the application for adjournment of hearing of the suit, Ext. 2 the case diary of the plaintiff''s advocate, Ext. 3, the gazette notification that the suit premises is a recorded evacuee property, held that the plaintiff had sufficient cause for his non-appearance in court on 4-6-94 and that for the dismissal of the suit for default the plaintiff suffered irreparable loss. Accordingly, the learned trial Judge allowed the Misc. Case set aside the order of dismissal of the suit for default and restored the same to its original file and number. Mr Alam then submitted that the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division acted illegally beyond his revisional jurisdiction by superimposing his appreciation of evidence in reversing the judgment of the trial Court without even reversing the finding of fact of the trial Courts, as noted above. The learned Advocate further submitted that the trial judge in consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case and the materials on record rightly held that whether Title Suit No. 210 of 1991 is maintainable or not and whether the same has been brought to harass the defendant will be considered by the trial Court itself upon the evidence to be adduced by the parties in support of their respective cases but in the disposal of a proceeding under Order 9 rule 13, the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division has travelled beyond his jurisdiction in holding that the said title suit is a "fruitless litigation" and thereby has, in fact, condemned the plaintiff and prejudged the fate of the suit before being heard on merit. The learned Advocate also submitted that the learned Single Judge upon misapplication of the decision reported in 1989 BLD (AD) 1, Sanatannessa Bewa vs Hipatullah Sarker & ors misdirected himself in holding that the decree dated 3-6-80 of Title Suit No. 243 of 1978 having already become final and conclusive the plaintiff's Title Suit 210 of 1991 is nothing but a fruitless litigation.

13. On the other hand, Mr. A Rab-1, the learned Advocate and constituted attorney of the contesting defendant-respondents, appearing-in-person, submitted that the learned Judge of the trial Court had failed to consider the material facts on record viz (i) Mr Md Abdul Khaleq, PW 1, the learned Advocate of the plaintiff, made false statement before the trial Court that on 4-6-94 he had been engaged in another court in connection with another case and, as such, he could not move the application filed for time in the instant suit and that he made false entry in his diary (Ext. 2) to prove his engagement in another court on the relevant day, (ii) the application filed under Order 9 rule 9 CPC was not signed by the plaintiff and the affidavit sworn in support thereto by one Narayan Chandra, was neither the clerk of the learned Advocate of the plaintiff nor even he was authorized by the plaintiff to swear the said affidavit on his behalf nor in any capacity he was attached with the office of the plaintiff; (iii) even in the said petition it was not disclosed in which court and in connection with which specific case PW 1 had been engaged on 4-6-94, (iv) PW 2 Khondaker Yasin Siddique did not support PW 1 that after filing the application for time he went to another court to conduct another case; (v) neither the plaintiff himself nor any legally authorized person deposed in court in support of the application for restoration of the suit.

14. Mr Rab, thus, submitted that the learned judge of the High Court Division on consideration of the above mentioned materials on record rightly held that the trial Court had failed to apply its judicial mind on the facts and circumstances of the case and the materials on record in holding that the plaintiff could prove that he had been prevented by sufficient cause from appearing at the time of hearing of the suit, and, as such, the learned Judge is justified in holding that the impugned order having suffered from legal infirmity the same was not sustainable in law. Mr. Rab further submitted that the trial judge himself in his order No. 87 dated 4-6-94 noted that after the order of dismissal of the suit for default had been passed, the plaintiff at about 12-30 PM filed an application for time, which fact negative the case of the plaintiff that after filing the application for time PW 1 went to another court to conduct another case and that without disposing of the time petition, the trial Court wrongly dismissed the suit for default. Mr. Rab also submitted that there being no scope of preferring an appeal against the order of allowing an application under Order 9 rule 9 CPC the High Court Division, in the instant case with a view to preventing the causing of injustice, in its revisional jurisdiction has rightly considered the above noted materials on record in holding that the trial Court had failed to apply its judicial mind in allowing the Misc. Case. Mr. Rab lastly, submitted that in consideration of the finality and conclusiveness of the decree passed in Title Suit No. 243 of 1978 the High Court Division held in Civil Revision No. 116 of 1982, arising out of the Title Suit No. 509 of 1981, instituted by one MA Khaleque impleading the present appellant as a defendant, that the said suit was not maintainable and as such, the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division in the instant case has rightly relied upon the principles of law enunciated in 1989 BLD (AD) 1 in holding that the restoration of Title Suit No. 201 of 1991 will drive the parties to a fruitless litigation.

15. It appears that the learned Subordinate Judge after taking note of all the relevant facts on record and believing the evidence of PWs 1 and 2 upon assigning reasons therefor and on consideration of Exts. 1, 2, 3 held that the plaintiff had sufficient cause for his failure to appear in Court on 4-6-94 and thereby the suit in question was dismissed for default and he also suffered loss for dismissal of the suit. In passing the impugned judgment the learned Subordinate Judge also took note of the impugned ex parte decree, which has been challenged in Title Suit No. 210 of 1991 and rightly held that whether the said title suit is a fruitless litigation or not and whether it is barred by the principle of res judicata will be decided by the trial Court after hearing the same on merit upon the evidence to be adduced by the parties. In that view of the matter the learned Subordinate Judge in the interest of justice restored the suit for setting aside the order of dismissal for default.

<u>16. The learned Judge of the High Court Division appears to have misdirected himself in weighing much of the back history of the instant litigation and upon taking unnecessarily a serious view of the alleged not inexcusable negligence of PW 1, the engaged Advocate of the plaintiff, and unexpectedly failed to consider the real and legal aspect of the matter, what had rightly been done by the trial Court, whether the plaintiff himself being the victim of the circumstances had failed to appear in court when the suit was called on for hearing and dismissed for the default for his non-appearance.</u>

<u>17. In exercise of its revisional jurisdiction the High Court Division should not ordinarily sit as a court of appeal and superimpose its appreciation of evidence upon the trial Court's appreciation of evidence in interfering with the findings of fact arrived at by the trial Court, inasmuch as the trial court had the initial advantage of seeing the very demeanor of the witnesses, unless appreciation of evidence of the trial judge is perverse and unfounded.</u>

<u>18. In the instant case the learned Judge of the High Court Division did not virtually reverse the finding of the trial Court that the plaintiff had sufficient cause for his non-appearance in the suit, which caused its dismissal for default. It is true that in the order sheet, the learned Subordinate Judge noted that after he had passed the order of dismissal of the suit, at about 12-30 PM an application for its adjournment was filed on behalf of the plaintiff. It is in the evidence of PW 1 that he had filed the petition earlier but collusively the same was not placed before the court before the order of dismissal was passed. The trial Court, however, on consideration of the evidence on record, noted earlier, and the other attending circumstances believed the evidence of PW 1 and the case of the plaintiff that he had sufficient cause for non-appearance in the suit at the relevant time.</u>

<u>19. Mr. Rab's submission in support of the High Court Division's observation that the restoration of the suit will drive the parties to a fruitless litigation is also not acceptable in the eye of law, being uncalled for at this stage of the instant legal proceeding for the simple reason as has, profitably been recorded by the trial Court.</u>

<u>20. Moreover, in the facts and circumstances of the instant case, the High Court Division was not justified in relying upon the case of Sanatannessa Bewa vs Haipatullah Sarker & ors, 1989 BLD (AD) 7, inasmuch as in that case plaintiff-appellant's second appeal, preferred against the concurrent findings of fact, was dismissed for default and the High Court Division refused to restore the same having held that the appellant had failed to show any sufficient cause which had prevented her from appearing when the appeal was taken up for hearing and found little merit of the said second appeal having concluded upon the concurrent findings of fact. This Division, however, maintained the judgment of the High Court Division.</u>

<u>For the reasons recorded earlier we find substance in these appeals. Accordingly, both the appeals are allowed without any order as to costs. The judgments appealed from are set aside. In consequence thereof the trial Court's order of restoration of Title Suit No. 210 of 1991 be restored and further proceeding of the Title Execution Case No. 19 of 1995 pending in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka be stayed pending disposal of the aforesaid title suit.</u>

End.

lawyer:
Abul Kalam Azad, Advocate — For the Petitioner.
No one — For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Mohammad Hussain ------ Petitioners
Vs. 
Abul Kashem and ors ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule arising out of a suit for declaration of title and confirmation of possession is directed against a judgment of reversal passed by learned District Judge, Cox's Bazar in Other Appeal No. 8 of 1989 reversing the judgment and decree passed by learned Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar Cox's Bazar in Title Suit No. 482 of 1982.

2. For the disposal of the Rule it is necessary to set out the brief history of the case as emerges from the pleadings of the parties before the court below. The petitioner as plaintiff instituted Other Suit No. 482 of 1982 in the Court of Munsif (now Assistant Judge) for declaration of title and confirmation of possession in respect of the suit land measuring 0.20 acre of land impleading opposite parties Nos. 2 and 3 as defendants. One Abul Khair took settlement of the suit land from the Government and a settlement khatian No. 1230/55 under Jote No. 237 was opened in his name. He exercised ownership and possession over the suit land by constructing dwelling house. During the Second Great War the land of Abul Khair along with other land of other persons was acquired by the then British Government and after the Great War he again got back his possession over the suit land and also got compensation for his damaged house. On the death of Abul Khair, the said suit land was inherited by his two daughters Julmas Khatun and Saira Begum. The plaintiff is the son of Julmas Khatun. Julmas Khatun and Saira Begum gifted the said property by registered deed of gift on 2-9-81 in favour of the plaintiff and possession was handed over to the plaintiff. The suit land was recorded in the name of Julmas Khatun in the last MRR Survey. The defendants being very much powerful and influential got the suit land recorded in MRR and BS Khatian in the name of Cox's Bazar Airport Authority. The defendants got no right, title and possession on the suit land. The defendants claiming title on the suit land on the basis of MRR and BS Khatian threatened to dispossess the plaintiff and hence the suit.

3. The defendant Nos. 1 and 2 Airport Manager, Cox's Bazar and the Government of the People''s Republic of Bangladesh represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Cox's Bazar respectively entered appearance and contested the suit by filing joint written statement denying all material allegations made in the plaint and taking the stand that the suit land measuring 0.20 acre had been claimed from 39.86 acres of land of Revisional Settlement Plot No. 265 recorded in Revisional Settlement Khatian No. 965 and the entire 39.86 acres along with other adjacent lands were transferred to the Civil Aviation Authority in LA Case No. 5 of 1957-58 for the future development and extension of the Airport. Cox's Bazar Airport services was inaugurated in the year 1856 and since then the defendant Airport Authority have been in continuous and uninterrupted possession of the suit land along with other lands. The Civil Aviation Department paid compensation of the acquired land which has been assessed at Taka 1,56,394.00 in the year 1962-63. The defendants totally denied of granting of any settlement of the suit land in favour of the predecessor of the plaintiff Abul Khair and opening of a Settlement Khatian No. 1230 of 1955 under Jote No. 237 in the name of Cox's Bazar Airport Authority having been in ownership and possession of the suit land the same was recorded in the name of the Airport very correctly both during MRR and BS operation.

4. One Abul Kashem by way of an application under the provisions of Order I rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure was impleaded as defendant No. 3 in the suit. The added defendant No. 3 also contested the suit by filing a separate written statement contending that on the death of Abul Khair his wife Salma Khatun and daughter Saira Begum on receipt of Taka 900.00 sold 0.11 acre of land to him and granted two receipts on 7-3-72 and 10-3-72 and handed over possession of the said 0.11 acre of land in his favour but they did not execute and register any kabala deed rather made a gift of the entire 0.20 acre of land in favour of the plaintiff. The defendant No. 3 acquired title by adverse possession.

5. The defendant No. 3 filed Other Suit No. 110 of 1984 in the court of Munsif (now Assistant Judge), Cox's Bazar for declaration of title over the said 0.11 acre of land.

6. Learned Assistant Judge, Cox''s Bazar heard both the suits analogously and disposed of the same by a common judgment. Learned Assistant Judge decreed Title Suit No. 482 of 1982 and dismissed Title Suit No. 110 of 1984.

7. There were appeals preferred by defendant No. 3 of Other Suit No. 482 of 1982 and plaintiff of Other Suit No. 110 of 1984 being Other Appeal No. 8 of 1989 and 7 of 1989 respectively. Learned District Judge, Cox''s Bazar heard both the appeals analogously and disposed of the same by a common judgment allowing Other Appeal No. 8 of 1989 arising out of Other Suit No. 482 of 1982 and dismissing Other Appeal No. 7 of 1989 arising out of Other Suit No. 110 of 1984 and dismissed both the suits.

8. Learned trial judge in awarding judgment in Title Suit No. 482 of 1982 and dismissing Other Suit No. 110 of 1984 held that the title and possession of the plaintiff of Title Suit No. 482 of 1982 had been proved and the defendant No. 1 could not file any paper in support of its claim and the defendant No. 3 also could not produce any documentary evidence in support of his alleged acquisition of title by adverse possession. In view of those findings learned trial judge declared title over the suit land and confirmed possession thereon of the plaintiff in Title Suit No. 482 of 1982 and also granted decree of permanent injunction.

9. Learned District Judge in reversing the judgment of the learned Assistant Judge held that the plaintiffs of both the suits claimed title on plot No. 2918 under Jote No. 237 recorded in Jamabandi Khatian No. 1230/55 but in the Revisional Settlement Khatain there is no mention of the said plot and the plot No. 265 of revisional khatian No. 956 has been described as Government khas land and the same had been recorded in MRR and BS Khatian in the name of Cox's Bazar Airport. Learned District Judge further held that the plaintiff in the plaint did not even state the date of alleged settlement in favour of Abul Khair nor did file any rent-receipts in support of the said settlement and, as such, the acquisition of title by Abul Khair on the basis of alleged settlement remained disproved. Learned District Judge further found that the certified copy showing the Bandabasta Khatian in the name of Abul Khair is nothing but a forged and created document and Abul Khair''s acquisition of title followed by possession could not be proved. Learned District Judge finally found that the plaintiff of both the suits did not acquire any title and possession over the suit land.

<u>10. Mr. Abul Kalam Azad, learned Advocate, appeared in support of the Rule. None appeared to oppose the Rule. The only argument advanced by learned Advocate is that, though the trial Court decreed suit with the finding that the plaintiff proved title and possession over the suit land the defendant No. 1, Airport Authority, did neither file any appeal against the said decree nor any cross objection and the lower appellate Court committed a serious error of law in dismissing both the suits on allowing Other Appeal No. 8 of 1989 and dismissing Other Appeal No. 7 of 1989. Preferred by defendant No. 3 learned Advocate referred to the provisions contained in Order 41 rule 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure in support of his contention and placed reliance on a decision in the case of Prahalad Chandra Mahato and others vs. The State of Bihar and others reported in AIR 1976 Patna 109.</u>

<u>11. In order to appreciate the contention raised from the side of the plaintiff petitioner it will be appropriate to extract Order 41 rule 33 of the Code Civil of Procedure so far as it is relevant for the purpose which runs as follows:</u>

<u>"The appellate Court shall have power to pass any decree and make any order which ought to have been passed or made and to pass or make such further or other decree or order as the case may require and this power may be exercised by the court notwithstanding that the appeal is as to part only of the decree and may be exercised in favour of all or any of the respondents or parties although such respondents or parties may not have filed any appeal or objection."</u>

<u>On a plain reading of this Rule it is manifestly clear that the power conferred is of the widest amplitude to enable an appellate Court to pass decree according to the justice of the case. The language used is affirmative and the rule is further strengthened by non obstante clauses giving the clear impression that the intention is beneficial so that no legal right should be denied which the appellate Court considers should be allowed within the framework of the suit. The rule frees the court from the tentacles of the procedural law and empowers it to do complete justice.</u>

12. Now let me consider whether the appellate Court was justified in reversing the decisions arrived at by the trial Court in allowing the appeal filed by defendant No. 3 and not by defendant Airport Authority and dismissing both the suits filed by the plaintiff and defendant No. 3.

13. The alleged settlement is the sheet anchor of the plaintiff's claim. The plaintiff did neither produce the alleged deed of settlement nor did file any Dhakhilas showing payment of rents to the Government in recognition of the settlement granted by Government in favour of Abul Khair. No date of the said settlement had been stated in the plaint. The plaintiff simply submitted Jamabandi Khatain No. 1230/55 under the Jote being 237 and one rent receipt alleged to have been granted by a Revenue Collector for the year 1364 BS and these two documents had been exhibited as Exhibit Nos. 1 and 3 for the plaintiff. On perusal of the said Jamabandi Khatian Exhibit-1 it appears that in the remarks column the following remarks had been stated: “১২৩০/৪২ খতিয়ানের আদেশ মতে ১-৪-৩৫ হইতে পুনঃজরিপ পর্যর্ন্ত । স্বাক্ষর অস্পষ্ট ৩১-৩-৭৬” From this remark the point becomes very much clear that the process of the said Jamabandi Khatian had been made on 31-3-1976 but the predecessor of the plaintiff Abul Khair claimed to have got the settlement before the Second Great War broke out. The process of the preparation of Jamabandi Khatian in the year 1976 on the basis of an alleged Settlement long before the second Great War speaks a volume about the legal existence of the alleged settlement of the plaintiff as well as of the Jamabandi Khatian. The court of appeal as, the last and final court of fact considered this aspect of the matter.

14. It is admitted that the disputed 0.20 acre of land is within the land of defendant-Airport Authority measuring 137.32 acres of land which was a khas land. The defendant Airport Authority claimed to have acquired ownership and possession. On the basis of a transfer made by the Government to the Civil Aviation Department in Miscellaneous Case No. 5 of 1957-58 and the entire land had been recorded in the name of Defendant-Airport Authority in MRR and BS Khatians. It is the case of the plaintiff that the British Army took possession of the suit land along with other lands during the Second Great War and after the Great War Abul Khair took over possession of the said land and also got compensation for the damage caused to the house constructed by him on the suit land but no papers had been produced before the court below to show that after the Second Great War Abul Khair took possession over the disputed land and got compensation for the damaged house. In the absence of legal evidence it is difficult to hold that Abul Khair went into possession over the suit land on the basis of settlement from the Government. Learned Trial Judge based his decision on discussion of factum of possession of the plaintiff ignoring the vital aspect that the plaintiff failed to produce any document showing settlement from the Government in his favour.

15. The lower appellate Court on consideration of the legal evidence and materials on record found that the alleged Jamabandi Khatian had not been proved and the claim of title on the basis of certified copy of a Jamabandi Khatian is not at all acceptable. The appellate Court further found that the acquisition of title on the basis of alleged settlement having not at all been proved by legal evidence, the acquisition of title by the plaintiff on the basis of a danpatra deed from two daughters of Abul Khair did not also arise and thus reversed the decisions arrived at by the trial Court awarding decree in favour of the plaintiff.

16. In the case of Prahalad Chandra Mahato and others vs. The State of Bihar and others reported in AIR 1976 Patna 109 as referred to by Mr Abul Kalam Azad the fact is that the plaintiffs filed a suit for declaration that the tank with its embankment, the homestead and khas property of the plaintiffs and the proforma defendants No. 6-10 have no title to the suit property and their recognition as tenants by the state is illegal. There was also a further prayer for permanent injunction restraining the defendants from interfering with the possession of the plaintiffs. The suit was contested by the defendant Nos. 1-5 who were State of Bihar and its officers. The trial Court dismissed the suit with the finding that the plaintiffs were never in possession of the disputed property and appeal was preferred by all the plaintiffs and the lower appellate Court dismissed the suit with the finding that the entire tank vested in the Government and modified the decree of the trial Court to the effect that the defendant Nos. 6-10 got no right in the disputed property as the same vested in the State of Bihar. Thereafter, second appeal has been preferred by the defendant Nos. 6-10. The second appeal was allowed. The judgment and decree of the appellate Court in so far as it interfered with the decree passed by the trial Court which was in favour of the defendant-appellant Nos. 6-10 were set aside and those of the trial Court restored. In the said case all the plaintiffs preferred an appeal as because the suit was dismissed. But in this instant case plaintiff's suit was decreed and against that added defendant No. 3 preferred an appeal being aggrieved by the decree passed by the trial Court. So, the facts and circumstances of the cited case are quite distinguishable and got no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of this present case.

<u>17. In this instant case the decree was before the appellate Court no matter whether the appeal was preferred by added defendant No. 3 or by defendant-Airport Authority. The non-obstante clause is directly relevant, for it totally avoids any condition that a party seeking the benefit of the rule should itself have filed an appeal or objection. Thereafter, the mere fact of defendant-Airport Authority having not filed any appeal would not by itself be sufficient to justify refusal to exercise the power under Order 41 rule 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The question before me came up for consideration before the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of SM Yousuf and Brothers vs. Mirza Mohammad Mahadi Pooya and another reported in 16 DLR (SC) 619. The Supreme Court held relying upon good number of decisions the principle that in the absence of a counter appeal being filed a decree against another defendant cannot be given not only constitutes a fetter upon the extremely wide power given to the appellate Court by the Code, but may also be thought to be in direct contravention of a clear provision in the rule". This question also came up for consideration before the Appellate Division of our Supreme Court in the case of Md Osman Gani vs. Mst Kulsum Bibi and others reported in 37 DLR (AD) 63. The Appellate Division in the said case held: "The wording of the rule shows that the appellate Court may pass any order to do complete justice in disposing of the appeal. This power must be exercised in the interest of and to further ends of justice".</u>

18. The principle of law enunciated by Pakistan Supreme Court and Appellate Division of our Supreme Court is a complete answer to the contention raised by the learned Advocate for the petitioner. The contention of the learned Advocate is therefore, devoid of any substance.

<u>19. The lower appellate Court on a due consideration of all aspects of the case rejected the claim of the plaintiff of his suit. Law is settled that plaintiff must succeed on his strength and cannot have any reliance on the weakness of the defendant. In this instant case the plaintiff-petitioner signally failed to prove acquisition of title and possession over the suit land on the basis of the alleged settlement. The appellate Court does not appear to have committed any error of law in dismissing the suit and no failure of justice has been occasioned by the judgment under challenge and the same does not warrant any interference by this court in the exercise of revisional jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure.</u>

20. Finally, learned Advocate for the petitioner submitted that the suit may be remanded to the trial Court to enable the plaintiff to produce documents in support of title. I do not think there is any substance in this contention. It is not understood what type of documents may be produced in the trial Court since documents of title were neither filed in the trial Court nor in the appellate Court. It is too late in the day for the petitioner to wake up at this stage for taking steps to prove title. There exists no reason, no ground to send the suit back on remand to the trial Court. The prayer for remand is not acceptable and hence rejected.

21. In the result, the Rule is discharged. The judgment of the appellate Court is maintained.

22. Having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case I make no order as to costs.

Send down the LC Record at once.

End.

lawyer:
Sigma Huda with Eaqub Ali Howlader & Shawkat Ara Begum, Advocates -For the Petitioner. 
Md Mostafa, Advocate -For the Opposite Parties
parties:
SAM Mahbub Elahi, represented by Md Jahangir Alam ------ Petitioner
vs.
Md Shah Alam and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Upon an application under section 116 of the Code of Civil Procedure filed by the petitioner, this Rule was issued calling upon the Opposite Party No. 1 to show cause as to why the impugned order No. 2 dated 30-4-2001 passed by the District Judge, Jhalakati in Title Appeal No. 42 of 2001 admitting the appeal and staying the operation of the judgment and decree dated 26-2-2001 passed by the Assistant Judge, Rajapur, in Title Suit No. 63 of 1999 shall not be set aside.

2. The petitioner as plaintiff filed a suit being Title Suit No. 63 of 1999 on 10-11-1999 under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act in the Court of Assistant Judge, Rajapur, against the defendant-opposite parties praying for a decree of recovery of possession of the Kha schedule land contending, inter alia, that Ananta Kumar, Madhusudhan and Rahini Kumar were owners and possessors of 1.30 acres of land of SA Khatian No. 1354, Plot No. 4103 of Mouza Rajapur, PS Rajapur, district Jhalakati, and that Madhusudan died leaving his cousin Ananta Kumar as his heir, that Ananta Kumar sold 0.21 decimals of land to the plaintiff petitioner vide registered deed No. 4209 dated 25-11-1969 and delivered possession of the said land from the northeastern portion of plot No. 4103, and that the plaintiff petitioner mutated his name and paid rents and has been possessing the same, that the plaintiff dug out a pond from the western portion of the land and filled earth and created a passage from the eastern portion to flow water and made east facing road and planted different, kinds of trees, constructed tinshed house with wire surrounding for more than 30 years. It was further contended that Rajapur Pilot High School has no right, title, interest and possession on the suit land and the defendant-opposite party Nos. 2-4 teachers of the said school used to reside towards the southern Plot No. 4099 of Plot No. 4103. But the defendant-opposite party No. 1, headmaster of the said school, for the benefit and advantage of defendant opposite party Nos. 2-4 by using the name of Rajapur Pilot High School illegally threatened to grab the Suit land, the plaintiff-petitioner filed Miscellaneous Petition Case No. 263 of 1999 in the Court of learned Magistrate, 1st Class, Jhalakati, and that during pendency of the said case, the threat was continued and on 15-4-1999 GD Entry No. 514 was made with the Rajapur, Police Station. Thereafter, on 17-4-1999 under the leadership of the defendant -opposite party No.1 along with other defendant opposite parties forcibly dispossessed the plaintiff petitioner from the 0.8 decimals of land described in the schedule 'kha' of the plaint. The defendant opposite party No. 1 in order to legalise his illegal activities of dispossession of the plaintiff petitioner from the suit land made a statement in the Daily Ajker Barta dated 18-4-1999 and thereafter, under the leadership of defendant opposite party No. 1 some hired people broke an old tin shed adjacent to the main building of the school and reconstructed the said tin shed on the eastern portion of the land of the plaintiff petitioner and created obstacle to the access of the house of him. Thereafter, the defendant opposite party No. 1 cut earth from the southeast portion of the suit plot and filled up the floor of the newly constructed tin shed and changed the nature and character of the land of the plaintiff petitioner. Thereafter, on 12-5-1999 while the defendant opposite parties started unfinished work of the newly constructed tin shed, the plaintiff petitioner informed the matter to the police of Rajapur Police Station and the police issued warning notice but the defendant opposite parties completed the unfinished work disobeying the warning notice. The defendant opposite parties having no right, title, interest and possession of the suit land and being completely strangers, caused damage to the plaintiff petitioner amounting to Taka 50,000 by dispossessing him from the suit land and changing the nature and character of it. The plaintiff petitioner requested the defendant opposite parties to hand over the possession of the suit land after removing the tin shed structure but the defendant opposite parties refused and, as such, the suit under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act was filed.

3. The defendant opposite party No. 1 contested the suit by filing written statement denying all the material allegations made in the plaint and contending, inter alia, that Ananta Kumar, Madhusudan and Ruhini were the owners and possessors of the Suit land, and that Madhusudan transferred his entire share to Rajapur Pilot High School and delivered possession and the said school is 100 years old and its main building is situated on 9.30 acres of land, and after transfer of the share of Madhusudan, the school has been possessing the same for 50 years and Madhusudan is a Life Member of that school and the vocational branch of the school is situated in the suit land and there are trees of different kinds in the suit land. It was also contended that during liberation war, all the documents were lost and the then Headmaster died, and taking advantage, the plaintiff-petitioner created some forged and fraudulent documents and claimed the suit land of the school. The plaintiff although filed Miscellaneous Petition Case No. 263 of 1999 the enquiry report shows the possession of the defendant opposite parties for which the said case was dismissed on 8-8-1999 against which Criminal Revision No. 76 of 1999 was preferred before the learned Sessions Judge, Jhalakati which is pending for disposal and, as such, as the plaintiff petitioner filed this false case, it is liable to be dismissed.

4. The learned assistant judge, Rajapur, at Jhalakati, heard the case and was pleased to decree the suit for khas possession by his judgment and decree dated 26-2-2001, directing the defendant opposite party No.1 to shift the house from the suit land. Against this judgment and decree, the opposite party No.1 filed Title Appeal No. 42 of 2001 in the Court of District Judge, Jhalakati. The applications one for exemption of the service of notice upon the respondent Nos. 2-5 and for staying the operation of the judgment and decree dated 26-2-2001 passed in title Suit No. 63 of 1999 by the trial Court were also filed. The learned District Judge, Jhalakati, by order on 30-4-2001 admitted the appeal, rejected the prayer for exemption of the service of notice upon the respondent Nos. 2-5 and allowed the application for stay of the operation of the judgment and decree dated 26-2-2001. Against the said order dated 30-4-2001, regarding the admission of the appeal and staying the operation of the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court, the plaintiff petitioner filed this revisional application and obtained the Rule.

5. Ms Sigma Huda along with Mr Eaqub Ali Howlader, the learned Advocates appeared for the petitioner while Mr Md Mostafa, the learned Advocate appeared for the opposite party No. 1.

6. Ms Sigma Huda, the learned Advocate, appearing for the petitioner, took me to the revisional application, annexed documents, the impugned order, the affidavit-in-opposition filed by the petitioner and submitted that section 9 of the Specific Relief Act clearly debars the aggrieved party to file appeal against the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court. As such, the appeal filed by the defendant opposite party No. 1 in the Court of District Judge was not maintainable and the admission of the said appeal and stay order passed in the appeal are also not maintainable and have been passed committing error of law resulting in error in the decision occasioning failure of justice and hence liable to be set aside. Mrs, Huda then submitted that the impugned order passed by the Court of appeal and the filing of the appeal by the appellant and his learned Advocate having knowledge that the appeal is not maintainable and causing serious hardship to the respondent petitioner calls for action to be taken by this Court. She submitted that section 9 of the Specific Relief Act mentions that no appeal and review can be filed against any judgment and decree passed, but by filing the appeal the learned Advocate has and by admitting the appeal and passing orders, the learned Judge has not only showed disrespect to law but it is a proof of their inefficiency and misconduct for which proper action should be taken against them.

7. On the other hand, Mr Md Mostafa the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party, submitted that although section 9 of the Specific Relief Act does not authorise any party to file appeal against the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court but the aggrieved party is entitled to file a revisional application against the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court. He then submitted that in this case also, the defendant opposite party should be allowed to file the revisional application in this court on finding that the appeal as filed by the said defendant opposite party is not maintainable. He then submitted that when it is palpably clear that the appeal is not maintainable, the petitioner without coming to this Court with the revisional application against the order passed by the Court of appeal, could very well agitate and submit this point before the court of appeal and get the proper order, and in that case the harassment caused to the parties could well be avoided. But the petitioner having not done so, he submitted that the Rule should be disposed of directing the petitioner to go to the court of appeal with the prayer, he is claiming by way of this revisional application.

8. I have heard the learned Advocates for both the parties and perused the materials on record. Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act states us follows:

"If any person is dispossessed without his consent of immovable property otherwise than in due course of law, he or any person claiming through him may, by suit, recover possession thereof, notwithstanding any other title that may be set up in such suit.

Nothing in this section shall bar any person from suing to establish his title to such property and to recover possession thereof.

No suit under this section shall be brought against the Government.

No appeal shall lie from any order or decree passed in any suit instituted under this section, nor shall any review of any such order or decree be allowed."

<u>9. The Suit was filed under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act and the trial Court decreed the suit directing the defendant No. 1 to shift the house from the suit land and if the defendant No. 1 became aggrieved by that order, he could very well fight his grievance by filing revisional application. The defendant opposite party No. 1 could also file a fresh suit to establish his title to the property and to recover possession thereof. But the defendant opposite party No. 1 without availing the opportunity authorised by law, went to file appeal and got it admitted by the Court of appeal and also got an order of stay of the operation of the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court which under the law was totally barred. When a decree has been passed under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act in favour of the petitioner, it is binding upon the opposite party No. 1 unless it is set aside/varied by an order passed under revisional jurisdiction and any order passed by the Court of appeal will be without jurisdiction and not sustainable in law. This view finds support from the decision of Nawabzada Mohammad Umar Khan vs Mohammad Asif and others reported in 16 DLR (WP) 164, wherein it has been held that</u>

<u>"Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act 1877 provides a quick remedy for the recovery of possession where a person is dispossessed of immovable property. In other words, the object of the section is clearly to discourage forcible dispossession. The last part of this section expressly prohibits an appeal from or review of any order or decree passed in any suit under this section A party adversely affected under this section has an alternative remedy by was of a regular suit for establishing title and recovering possession or by way of revision, but any order passed in appeal against the express provision of law as contained in the last part of section 9, Specific Relief Act must be held to be without jurisdiction and a nullity in the eye of law."</u>

<u>10. As such, it is clear that as the appeal filed is not maintainable the order passed by the Court of appeal admitting the appeal staying the operation of the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court are also not maintainable and without jurisdiction and, as such, nulity in the eye of law. And the court of appeal committed error in law resulting in error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in passing the impugned order which is liable to be set aside.</u>

11. The submission made by the learned Advocate for the opposite party No. 1 that the petitioner in this revision application could very wall agitate his submissions before the court of appeal also does not merit consideration. It is already established that the appeal filed before the Court of appeal was not maintainable and the impugned order passed by that court was without jurisdiction. The petitioner moved this court rightly in its revisional jurisdiction. He cannot be asked to go to the Court of appeal to submit his submissions as because the Court of appeal has got no authority to hear and pass order in the appeal filed against the judgment and decree passed in a suit under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act as all orders passed by the Court of appeal will be without jurisdiction. A party cannot be asked to go to a court which has no legal authority to hear and pass orders. Moreover, when the petitioner has preferred this forum against the order passed by the Court of appeal and this forun being legal one, I am of the view that the petitioner need not go to the court of appeal for setting aside/vacating the order passed by that court when admittedly, that order was without jurisdiction.

12. The last submission made by the learned Advocate for opposite party No. 1 to the effect that as the appeal is not maintainable, the opposite party No. 1 should be given a chance to file revisional application against the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court need not be considered here as because if the opposite party No. 1 desires to file revisional application in this respect, and if it is not otherwise barred, he is at liberty to file it in this Court and for this no order is required to be passed there.

13. On consideration of the materials discussed hereinabove, I am of the view that the Rule merits consideration.

<u>14. Before parting with this Rule, I feel inclined to consider the last submission advanced by Mrs Huda in respect of the action of the learned District Judge and the learned Advocates for the appellant. Mrs, Huda submitted that it is clearly mentioned in section 9 of the Specific Relief Act that no appeal lies against any decree or order passed under this section. As such, it involves the moral and professional quality of the District Judge and the learned Advocates who admitted the appeal and filed the appeal. It is contended that this being a primary question of law that appeal is not maintainable, it is clear that by filing the appeal and admitting it, the learned Advocates and the learned Judge have acted against their morality. Ignorance of law cannot be a defence even by the general people and, as such, the learned judge and the learned advocates cannot be given any benefit for ignorance of law. This action of theirs is open to serious exception from both the moral and professional points of view inasmuch as not only that therein the ignorance of a litigant has been exploited but it is also evident that they did not properly advert to the case before filing and admitting the case and thus failed to discharge their professional obligations. I wonder as to how with such performance may any of them be able to justify their service and conscious and professional fees. As such, it is a fit case for the Bar Council concerned to deal with the cases of inefficiency of the learned Advocates who filed appeal against the judgment and decree passed in a suit under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act. This finds support from the view taken in a decision reported in PLD 1987 Lahore 415 in the case of Hasan Mohammad vs Munshi Khan and two others. The aggrieved party ie the opposite party No. 1, or the petitioner against whom the appeal was filed, may take the recourse to file a case against the concerned Advocates Mr AY Sayeed and Mr SM Fazlul Huq of Jhalakati Bar Association in the Bar Council for redress for their inefficiency and illegal harassment committed to them by filing wrong appeal which may tantamount to professional misconduct if facts and circumstances established that. Even the Bar Council may suo moto start a proceeding against the learned Advocates in this respect. As regards the District Judge, it cannot even be imagined that a District Judge shall not know the law that under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act, no appeal lies. As such, agreeing with the above decision, it is directed that the District Judge of Jhalakati who passed the order dated 30-4-2001 in Title Appeal No. 42 of 2001 Mr Md Abdul Hannan is asked to show cause as to why legal action shall not be taken against him for passing the said impugned order which is apparently not maintainable and for putting the parties in utter harassment which tantamounts to inefficiency to the greatest extent. The reply of the show cause shall have to reach this Court within two months ie 10-7-2003.</u>

15. With the above finding and observations, the Rule is made absolute with cost of Taka 1000 to be paid to the respondent-petitioner by the learned Advocate for the appellant mentioned hereinabove who filed the appeal in the Court. The order dated 30-4-2001 passed by the District Judge Jhalakati in Title Appeal No. 42 of 2001 admitting the appeal and staying the operation of the judgment and decree dated 26-2-2001 passed by the Assistant Judge, Rajapur, Jhalakati in Title Suit No. 63 of 1999 is hereby set aside.

Inform the Courts below at once. Let copies of the judgment be sent to the Bangladesh Bar Council, and Mr Md Abdul Hannan, District Judge, Jhalakati (posted on 30-4-2001) through the Secretary, Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs for necessary action. The matter is fixed on 15-7-2003 for orders.

End.

AFM Mesbahuddin, Senior Advocate, instructed Md Nawab Ali, Advocate-on-Record—For Respondent Nos. 1 & 2. 
Not Represented—For Respondent Nos. 3-6.
parties:
Rupali Bank Ltd, Dhaka ----- Appellant 
Vs.
Brick Linkers Ltd & other ----- Respondent
full_judgment:
SK Sinha J: <u>Only point involves in this appeal is whether the Artha Rin Adalat can draw up a final decree beyond the statutory period of three years from the date of preliminary de involves in this appeal is whether the Artha Rin Adalat can draw up a final decree beyond the statutory period of three years from the date of preliminary decree.</u>

2. To decide this point let us recapitulate short facts out of which this appeal has arisen. Appellant Rupali Bank Limited instituted a suit in the Artha Rin Adalat, Dhaka shortly, the Adalat, for realization of Taka 48,68,970.270 against the respondents by selling the mortgaged property. The Adalat ultimately by judgment and order dated 5th February, 1997 decreed the suit in preliminary from with interest. The Adalat thereupon drew up the preliminary decree. As the judgment debtors did not pay the decreetal amount within the stipulated time, the decree holder Bank filed an application under Order XXXIV, rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure for drawing up the final decree, which prayer was allowed and the Adalat drew up the final decree on that date. Thereupon the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 moved the High Court Division a writ petition challenging the said order of drawing up the final decree on the ground that the Adalat erred in law in drawing up the final decree after the expiry of three years from the date on the preliminary decree. The High Court Division accepted the contention and quashed the order.

3. Mr Harun-or-Rashid, learned counsel appearing for the appellant contended that the High Court Division erred in law in interfering with the order of the Adalat in exercise of its Writ jurisdiction in failing to consider that the said order is appealable and that since there is alternative remedy, the writ petition is not maintainable.

4. The appellant simply stated in its petition made on 24th April, 2003 that the suit was disposed of on 27th February, 1997 and thereafter, the defendants did not repay the total amount as per direction of the Adalat and, as such, with a view to sell the mortgaged property on auction, a final decree should be drawn up. The preliminary decree was made on 27th February, 1997 and in the operating portion of the judgment the Artha Rin Adalat directed the judgment-debtors to pay the decreetal amount by 28th February, 1994 and interest at the rate of 21% within four months from 1st March, 1990. The appellant did not assign any reason whatsoever in its application for not taking steps for drawing up the final decree despite that the judgment-debtors did not pay the decreetal amount within the specified time.

5. Now the moot question is whether a final decree can be drawn up by the Adalat after the expiry of the period of limitation provided in Article 181 of the Limitation Act. The Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 shortly the Ain was amended by the Artha Rin Adalat (Amendment) Ain, 1997 and by this amendment, section 6Ka had been added wherein it is provided that the decree passed by the Adalat be executable by the Artha Rin Adalat. Section 5(4) provides that the Artha Rin Adalat shall be deemed to he a civil Court and the powers and jurisdiction of a civil Court under the Code of Civil Procedure will be applicable to the Artha Rin Adalat subject the Ain. Section 5(5) provides that the Artha Rin Adalat shall follow the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure so far as they are not inconsistent with the provisions of the Ain. The Ain does not provide the procedure to try a suit and executed a decree passed by it, and in the absence of any provision for executing the decree, there is no dispute that the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure will apply.

6. In the preliminary decree there was direction to pay the decreetal money within a specified time and if the judgment-debtors failed to pay the decreetal amount, the decree-holder was authorized to sell the mortgaged property for recovery of the money. Therefore the provisions of Order 34 will be applicable in this matter.

7. Sub-rule (1) of rule 4 of order 34 provides that in a suit for sale, if the plaintiff succeeds, the Court shall pass a preliminary decree to the effect mentioned in clause (a), (b) and (c) of sub-rule (1) of Rule 2, and further directing that, in default of the defendant paying as therein mentioned, the plaintiff shall be entitled to apply for a final decree directing that the mortgaged property or a sufficient part thereof be sold, and the proceeds of the sale be paid into Court and applied in payment of what has been found or declared under Or by the preliminary decree due to the plaintiff, together with such amount as may have been adjudged due in respect of subsequent costs, charges, expenses and interest, and the balance, if any, be paid to the defendant or other persons entitled to receive the same.

8. Sub-rule (2) provides "The Court may, on good cause shown and upon terms to be fixed by the Court, from time to time, at any time before a final decree for sale is passed, extend the time fixed for the payment of the amount found or declared due under sub-rule (1) or of the amount adjudged due in respect of subsequent costs, charges, expenses and interest."

9. Under these provisions the judgment-debtor has been given an opportunity to pay the decreetal amount which such period as may be fixed by the Court. If he fails to satisfy the decree, the Adalat may extend the time fixed for payment of mortgaged money if he can satisfy the Adalat the cause for nonpayment of the decreetal amount before a final decree for sale of the mortgaged property is dawn up. Sub-rule (2) is intended for the benefit of the mortgagor. The respondents did not seek extension of time to pay the decreetal amount before the expiry of the time fixed by the Adalat. Under such circumstances, the decree holder Bank ought to have prayed for drawing up the final decree before the expiry of four months from 1st March, 1994. The decree holder-Bank did not assign any reason whatsoever as to why it did not pray for drawing up the final decree after expiry of the time fixed in the preliminary decree or within a period of three years from the date of expiry of the time mentioned in the preliminary decree as per Article 181 of the Limitation Act.

<u>10. A preliminary decree for sale of mortgaged property can be enforced only by applying for an order for a final decree in accordance with Order 34 Rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the limitation for such application will be governed by Article 181 of the Limitation Act. Time for an application for a final decree to starts when the right to apply accrues, that is to say, from the date when the default occurred. It is the date which is fixed in the decree which is relevant under this provision. Admittedly the decree-holder did not file the application within 3 years from the date of default.</u>

11. Learned counsel appearing for the appellant fails to explain the reason for not filing proper application in time rather he remains silent when his attention has been drawn in that regard. His contention is that the writ petition is not maintainable since there is alternative remedy for appeal is available to the judgment-debtors. In this connection earned counsel has drawn our attention to section 6 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, wherein it is provided that for filing an appeal under section 7, no question could be raised to any authority other than the provisions provided therein against any order, judgment and decree of the Artha Rin Adalat. Section 7 provides that any person aggrieved by a judgment for decree may prefer an appeal within 30 days in the High Court Division subject to deposit of 50% of the decreetal amount in the Adalat. In proviso, it is stated that no appeal shall lie from any interlocutory order. This provision shows that an appeal lies only from a decree or judgment and no appeal lies from any interlocutory order. Though there is reference or 'order' in section 6, but the language used therein is clear that this section should be read along with section 7 in which it is specifically provided that an appeal lies against the judgment and decree only.

12. Mr AFM Mesbahuddin, learned counsel appearing for the respondents contended that since the writ petitioner did not challenge the judgment of the Artha Rin Adalat or the decree on merit, no appeal is maintainable under section 7 against the impugned order. We find force in the contention of the learned Counsel. There is no dispute that the writ petitioner did not challenge the judgment or the decree of the Adalat on merit. He has challenged an order of the Adalat allowing the decree holder's application for drawing up final decree.

<u>13. It sometimes happens that there is repugnancy between enacting clauses and the question then arises, how the Act, taken as a whole, to be construed. The generally accepted rule with regard to the construction where there are two sections dealing with the same subject matter, one section being unqualified and the other containing a qualification, effect must be given to the section containing the qualification. In Maxwell's Interpretation of Statutes, 12th Edition, it is stated that the meaning of section may be controlled by other individual sections of the same Act. "So too, the apparently general language of a schedule may be restricted by the more specific provision of one of the sections of the statute. If one section of an Act, for instance, required that 'notice, should be 'given' a verbal notice would generally be sufficient; but if another section provided that it should be 'served, on a person, or 'left' with him , or in a particular manner or place, it would obviously show that a written notice was intended."</u>

14. The question whether an appeal lies against an order of the Artha Rin Adalat has been considered in Sarder Jan-e Alam vs Arab Bangladesh Bank Ltd, 4 BLC (AD) 178. In that case the facts are that in pursuance of an ex-parte decree, the decree holder-Bank put the decree into execution for realization of the decreetal amount. The Adalat ultimately sold the mortgaged property in auction. The judgment-debtor filed application in the executing Court praying for shifting a date for sale on the ground that a country wide strike was called on the day fixed for auction sale. The Adalat sold the property in auction despite such objection. Thereafter the judgment-debtor filed application for setting aside the sale under Order XXI, rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure on the ground of material irregularity in conducting the sale. The Adalat upon hearing the parties dismissed the petition. Thereafter the judgment-debtor challenged the order by filing a writ petition. The High Court Division set aside the order of the Adalat in an appeal from the said judgment, it was argued on behalf of the auction-purchaser that the writ petition was not maintainable since there was alternative remedy for appeal. This Division repelled the objection and maintained the judgment of the High Court Division observing as under:

"Although in section 7 is provided that a judgment or decree of Artha Rin Adalat is appealable yet a judgment which does not result in a decree but results only in an order is not appealable under the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990. If any other meaning is given to section 7, then this section will mean that the judgment is appealable but the operative portion of the judgment, namely, the order, will have to be challenged otherwise than by way of appeal. Such an incongruous result cannot be contemplated in any law."

<u>15. Furthermore, apparently the Adalat drew up the final decree long after the expiry of three years. Even if an appeal was to file, it would have been allowed since the final decree was drawn up after the expiry of the period of limitation and in that case, the writ petitioner would have unnecessarily deposited 50% of the decreetal amount. He did not challenge the judgment or the decree of the Adalat on merit and therefore, if he deposited 50% of the decreetal amount, that would serve no purpose. On a combined reading of section 6 and 7, we are of the view that the expression "order" used in section 6 is superfluous in view of the clear language used in section 7 that an appeal lies from judgment and decree, and that no appeal lies from any order passed by the Adalat. Section 6 should be read subject to the provisions of section 7. In the premises, the High Court Division is perfectly justified in quashing the order dated 24th April, 2003 of the Adalat</u>

<u>16. On perusal of the materials on record, particularly the preliminary decree and the application for drawing up final decree, we have reason to believe that the concerned staff of the Rupali Bank Limited, Hajaribagh Branch and its lawyers deliberately did not take steps for drawing up the final decree within the period of limitation in collusion with the judgment-debtors so that the preliminary decree render in fructuous being barred by limitation. This is evident from the application made in the Adalat wherein the decree holder made superficial statements without explaining the reasons for not filing it in time. They simply performed a routine work by filing an application after long lapse of time. The Adalat passed a decree for over forty eight lakh with interest at the rate of 21% in February, 1997. We failed to understand why the concerned officials did not take any step for selling the mortgaged property after expiry of four months from the date of passing of the preliminary decree? This fact proved that they in collusion with the judgment debtors allowed the decree to die a natural death so that the decree could not be executed. By reason of this intentional latches huge amount of decreetal money could not have been recovered from the judgment debtors. Thereafter, the decreetal amount with interest should be recovered from those officials who are responsible for the default. Accordingly, we direct the Managing Director, Rupali Bank Limited to hold an enquiry into the matter and if it is detected that the concerned officials intentionally did not take step for drawing up the final decree with a view to give undue advantage to the judgment-debtors, recover the decreetal amount with interest from them.</u>

The appeal is dismissed with the above observations without any order as to costs.

End.

Md Nurul Mostafa, Advocate—For the Petitioners.
