parties:
Abdul Khaleque Dewan and others ----- Petitioners
vs.
Sheikh Md Tajuddin and others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party No. 1 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order dated 8-6-1999 passed by the Additional District Judge, Third Court, Dhaka, in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 68 of 1999 dismissing the appeal and affirming the judgment and order dated 14-3-1999 passed by the Assistant Judge, 6th Court, Dhaka, in Preemption Miscellaneous Case No. 7 of 1996 should not be set aside.

2. The short fact of the case is, that pre-emptor-respondent-opposite party No. 1 filed the above pre-emption case against the pre-emptee petitioner and others for getting an order for pre-emption on 12-2-1996 in respect of the case land of Mouza Dhania appertaining to CS Khatian No. 139, SA Khatian No. 154 in Plot No. 1409, measuring an area of land 1.16 acres out of which 0.33 acre is the case land for pre-emption. Pre-emptor further stated that he is a co-sharer in the case holding and as well as a tenant in holding, land contiguous to the case land. The further case of the pre-emptor is that one Kalimuddin, the great grandfather of the pre-emptor opposite party No. 1 was the original owner of the case holding and the CS record was prepared in sole name of Kadam Ali, the younger son of Kalimuddin. But the sons of said Kalimuddin by mutual agreement partitioned the case property and enjoying and possessing the case land holding among themselves and in consequence Sk Syed Ali transferred the case land along with other lands to one Sk Nizam Uddin, the father of the petitioner by a deed of gift dated 27-3-1954. The SA Khatian in respect of 1.00 acre of land out of the total case land was prepared in the name of Salim Meah and others and SA Khatian No. 155 for the rest portion of the case land was prepared in the name of the heirs of Kadam Ali. But when the recent RS record was prepared the case land was recorded correctly in the name of the father of the pre-emptor opposite party No. 1. The pre-emptor of the case land obtained the land from his father by way of Heba-bil-Ewaj dated 4-1-1978 and he was also owner and possessor of the land in Plot Nos. 1412 and 1413 contiguous to the case land. The seller opposite party No. 2 sold out the case land to the preempted-petitioner Nos. 1-3 behind the back of the pre-emptor without serving any notice upon the heirs including the pre-emptor about 21/2 months ago and the opposite party No. 2 disclosed to the locality that she sold out the case land. Thereafter, he on search obtained the certified copy of the sale deed on 31-12-1995 and became sure about the transfer of the case land beyond his knowledge and hence the case.

3. The preempted-petitioners contested the case by filing written objection denying the material allegations of the pre-emption petition contending, inter alia, that the entire case land in CS Khatian jote belonged to Kadam Ali who while owning and possessing the same died leaving behind son Golam Mostafa and daughter Basirunnessa now opposite party No. 2 who sold out the case land to the pre-emptee petitioners by a registered kabala No. 5685 dated 29-8-1992 and transferred the possession of the case land to them. After the purchase the pre-empted petitioners raised the land by filling earth and then constructed semi-pica building and thereafter the opposite party Nos. 1 and 3, now petitioner Nos. 1 and 2, transferred the case land in favour of Sheikh Raisuddin, Dalilur Rahman and Nur Mohammad by a registered power of Attorney on 8-11-95. The said Attorney made further development of the case land by constructing semi-pucca house and have been residing therein peacefully. The opposite party No. 1 being allured by the increased value of the case land filed the instant case with false statement in order to grab the case land and to harass the purchaser petitioners. The pre-emptor is a stranger in the case land and did not sell the property secretly to the preempted. The petitioners' case is false and hence the Miscellaneous Case is liable to be dismissed with cost.

4. During the course of hearing of the case pre-emptor examined two witnesses and, on the other hand, opposite party pre-emptee examined as many as three witnesses in this case. Pre-emptor Sk Md Tajuddin was examined as PW 1 who categorically stated that originally Kadam Ali, son of Kalimuddin, was the owner and possessor of the case land measuring 1.16 acres of land in CS Khatian No. 139, Kalimuddin had four sons namely, Mainuddin, Samaruddin, Syed Ali and Kadam Ali, they were possessing and enjoying the property by amicable partition. The pre-emptor Tajuddin was the grandson of Sk Syed All who is a co-sharer by inheritance. During the RS settlement operation the name of four brothers i.e. Mainuddin, Samaruddin, Sk Syed Ali and Kadam Ali were rightly recorded in Khatian No. 391 measuring 16 decimals in the name of Golam Mostafa, Abed Ali and Bashirunnessa, sons and one daughter of Kadam Ali and bearing Khatian No. 417 measuring one acre in the name of heirs of Mainuddin, Samaruddin and Syed Ali. The PW 1 exhibited both the RS Khatian as exhibit 6 series and also exhibited the CS Khatians as Exhibit 1. The pre-emptor-petitioner further stated in his evidence that pre-emptee-opposite party secretly purchased 33 decimals of land from Bashirunnessa, daughter of Kadam Ali in CS Plot No. 1409. The PW 1 further stated that he was the owner and possessor of CS Plot Nos. 1412 and 1413 which were contiguous to CS Plot No. 1409, as such, the pre-emptor was co-sharer by inheritance and also owner and possessor of land contiguous to case land. He also stated in his evidence that the pre-emptee-opposite party is a stranger and also stated that he was absolutely ignorant about the sale of the case property and subsequently, in the locality seller Bashirunnessa disclosed that she had sold out the case land to the preempted-opposite party.

5. Thereafter, the pre-emptor-petitioner went to the sub-registrar's office and on search obtained the certified copy of the sale deed on 31-12-1995. This witness further stated in his evidence that prior to the sale of the case land, the preemptive-opposite party did not serve any notice under section 89 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Hence, the petitioner filed the instant pre-emption case on 12-2-1996.

6. The foster son of Kadam Ali was examined as PW 2, who is also a co-sharer, and fully corroborated the PW 1 in his evidence and further stated that the co-sharers including the pre-emptor were absolutely in the dark about the sale of the property. The preemptive-opposite party, on the other hand, examined three witnesses. OPW 1, Abdul Halim was examined as OPW 1 for himself and as well as for two witnesses, who stated in his evidence that while the case land was purchased pre-emptor was very much aware of the sale of the property and after the lapse of three and half years when the value of the land has been in-creased to a great extent pre-emptor came forward with this pre-emption case only to grab the case land. The OPW 1 Abdul Halim further stated that he has developed the land by filling earth, erecting a semi-pucca house and also restored gas and electricity connections in that house. The OPW 1 also stated in his deposition that the pre-emptor is not a co-sharer and at the time of the purchase of the suit land pre-emptor was aware of the fact that the case land was going to be sold. Aftabuddin and Fakiruddin were examined as Opus 2 and 3 respectively who supported the evidence of OPW 1 and stated in their evidence that during the purchase of the land the pre-emptor was very much aware of the sale.

7. The learned trial Court on consideration of the evidence on record, exhibits, documents and other connected papers, framed as many as six issues.

1. Whether the suit is maintainable in its present form.

2. Whether the suit is barred by limitation or not.

3. Whether the case is bad for defect of parties or not.

4. Whether the pre-emptor-petitioner is a co-sharer in the suit holding and whether the pre-emptor has got any contiguous holding land to the case land.

5. Whether the case land was disclosed or not.

6. Whether the pre-emptor-petitioner is entitled to get pre-emption decree.

8. Thereafter, the learned trial Court elaborately discussed the issues framed by him earlier and came to the finding that the pre-emption case was not barred by limitation because no notice was served under section 89 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act by the pre-emptee-opposite party and thereafter long lapse of 31/2 years when Bashir-un-nessa, one of the pre-emptee-opposite party, disclosed herself that she sold the case property, then the pre-emptor-petitioner obtained the certified copy end came to know about the transfer of the case land and instituted the instant pre-emption case which is very much time i.e. within 4(four) months, from the knowledge of the pre-emptor-petitioner. Thereafter, the learned trial Court further held that the pre-emptor-petitioner successfully proved that he was a co-sharer and owner and possessor of the contiguous land to the suit property and no defect of parties could be proved by the pre-emptee-opposite party. The learned trial Court after a meticulous examination of all the evidence oral and documentary came to his case. On the other hand, the pre-emptee-opposite party could not prove anything according to their written statement and hence the pre-emption case was allowed by the judgment and order dated 14-3-1999 in favour of the pre-emptor-petitioner.

9. Being aggrieved by the judgment and order dated 14-3-1999 the pre-empt-opposite party filed a pre-emption Miscellaneous Appeal being No. 68 of 1999. The learned Additional District Judge, Dhaka stating, inter alia, that the trial Court by applying his judicial mind and considering the evidence on record, carefully passed the judgment and order in favour of the pre-emptor-petitioner. The learned Additional District Judge after hearing the appeal and considering the judgment of the learned trial Court dismissed the appeal and affirmed the judgment of the learned trial Court by his judgment and order dated 8-6-1999.

10. Being aggrieved by the judgment and order dated 8-6-1999 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Third Court, Dhaka, the pre-emptee purchaser appellant-petitioner, filed the instant revisional application before the High Court Division.

11. The learned Counsel Mr Kabiruddin, appearing on behalf of the pre-emptee-appellant-petitioners, submits that both the trial Court as well as the lower appellate Court failed to apply their judicial mind and came to a wrong finding and allowed pre-emption case in favour of pre-emptee. The learned lower appellate Court as well as the trial Court, without discussing the evidence on record and also applying their judicial mind, came to wrong finding of the case. The learned Judge of the trial Court failed to appreciate the most important aspect of the case, that the pre-emptor-petitioner filed the pre-emption case long after 3 and half years. The OPW 1 who stated in his evidence that while the case land was purchased by them the pre-emptor-petitioner was fully aware of the fact and he did not take any interest to purchase the land. Thereafter, when the pre-emptee-opposite parties purchased the land and developed the land by filling earth and restored electricity and constructed semi-pucca houses and also when the value of the land has been increased to a great extent the pre-emptor-petitioner filed the pre-emption case only to harass and grab the property. The learned Counsel also submits that the lower appellate Court without exercising his independent opinion supported the finding and verdict of the learned Judge of the trial Court. The learned Counsel further submits that both the courts below are in error in law as well as in the facts and both the courts failed to appreciate the evidence on record and also the facts and circumstances of the case. Both the lower appellate Court and the trial Court due to non-consideration and misreading of the evidence came to a wrong finding and allowed pre-emption case in favour of the pre-emptor-petitioner which is liable to be interfered by this court.

12. On the other hand, the learned Counsel Mr SRM Lutfor Rahman Akhand, appearing on behalf of the pre-emptor-petitioner respondent-opposite party, submits that the learned trial Court as well as the lower appellate Court after discussing the evidence on record and also considering the exhibits, documents and other connected papers and the facts and circumstances of the case, passed the judgment and order which is absolutely justified and there is no legal infirmity nor the courts below acted illegally in passing the judgment and order in favour of the pre-emptor-petitioner. The pre-emptor-petitioner Tajuddin examined two witnesses including himself, Tajuddin, as PW 1 who categorically stated that he was a co-sharer by inheritance and also he has got contiguous land situated with the case land. He further disclosed in his evidence that while the case land was sold out no notice was served under section 89 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. He also stated that he was absolutely in the dark about the transfer of the land and long after while Bashir-un-nessa after 3 and a half year disclosed in the locality that she sold 33 decimals of land to the pre-emptee-opposite parties then he came to know. Thereafter, he rushed to the Sub-Registrar Office and obtained the certified copy of the sale deed to become sure about the transfer of the land. He further disclosed in his evidence that the pre-emptor-petitioner was in the possession of the suit property. He was cross-examined by the lawyer of the adverse party but he could not be shaken in cross-examination. The learned Counsel also submits that the pre-emptor-petitioner exhibited CS Khatian as exhibit-1 and RS Khatian as exhibit-6 showing that petitioner was a co-sharer by inheritance. Next he submits that the lower appellate Court elaborately discussed the evidence on record, also the exhibits and documents and came to a correct finding and observation in his judgment that admittedly the pre-emptor-petitioner was not served with any notice of the transfer of the case land as required under section 89(4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, which was required to be served upon him in the status of his being a co-sharer of the case holding and, as such, he filed the pre-emption Miscellaneous Case within 4(four) months from the date of his knowledge of the transfer under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The learned Counsel finally submits that since both the courts below committed no error and illegality in finding of the facts and circumstances of the case it should not be interfered by this court.

<u>13. On a meticulous examination of the evidence on record, exhibits, registered deed, the judgment of both the courts and other connected papers, it transpires that the learned Judge of the trial Court and the lower appellate Court in their judgment discussed the evidences and also perused exhibits and registered deed produced by both pre-emptor-petitioner and the pre-emptee-opposite parties and observed that the petitioner is a co-sharer by inheritance and admittedly, no notice was served upon him, as such, the ground of limitation from the date of knowledge of the pre-emptor-petitioner will be of no avail. The pre-emptor-petitioner successfully proved the date of knowledge and institution of the pre-emption case within 4(four) months as required under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.</u>

14. By now the settled principle of the law in exercising the revisional power under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure has been laid down in several judicial pronouncements of our Appellate Division that the concurrent finding of facts should not be disturbed unless it is manifestly perverse. The principle which has been laid down by our Appellate Division is that when the appellate Court as the final court of finding facts affirms or reverses the judgment of the trial Court on a proper assessment of the evidence on record and the findings do not suffer from any error of law and the case is concluded by finding of facts, no interference is called for under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure. In this connection I rely on the case of Khurshed Ali and others vs Nurjahan Bewa and others reported in 1995 BLD (AD) 82 where it was held, that the finding of facts and when can be disturbed when the appellate Court as a final court of fact decides question of facts and records its finding on consideration of the evidence, the High Court Division cannot interfere with the findings of facts in revision unless the said findings are found to be perverse. When the material findings of the appellate Court are upheld by the High Court Division to be correct no interference is called for by the Appellate Division unless a substantial error of law is proved.

15. Another decision in this connection can be cited in the case of Hazari Bala Sana and others vs Nira alias Niranjan Mondal and others reported in 1997 BLD (AD) 295 wherein it was stated that it is settled principle that the findings of fact, whether concurrent or not, arrived at by the lower appellate Court is binding on the High Court Division as a revisional Court except in certain well defined exceptional circumstances, such as non-consideration or misreading of the material evidence affecting the merit of the case.

16. The Judgment of the lower appellate Court transpires that in arriving at its finding the said Court carefully considered the material facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record, both oral and documentary including the registered deeds. The learned Counsel for the pre-emptee (purchaser)-appellant-petitioners could not point out any error, illegality or infirmity of law in the judgment passed by the lower appellate Court.

17. In view of the facts and circumstance of the case, I do not find that the lower appellate Court in affirming the judgment and order of the trial Court committed any error of law or acted illegally. From the discussion made above and the facts and circumstances of the case, the impugned judgment and order dated 8-6-1999 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 68 of 1999 affirming the Judgment and order dated 14-3-1999 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Sixth Court, Dhaka in pre-emption Miscellaneous Case No. 7 of 1996 decreeing the case in favour of pre-emptor do not call for any interference.

18. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

The lower court's record be sent down at once with a copy of the judgment.

End.

parties:
IFIC Bank Ltd ----- Appellant 
Vs.
Mariner Fashions Wear Pvt Ltd and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
ABM Khairul Haque J: This appeal arises in respect of an order dated 5-4-2004 passed by the Judge, Artha Rin Adalat No. 3, Dhaka, in Artha Rin Execution Case No. 1 of 2003, rejecting an application under Order XXI, rule 98 of the Code of Civil Procedure read with section 57 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003, praying for deployment of law enforcing agency for handing over the possession of the suit property in favour of the decree-holder petitioner.

2. It appears that the International Finance Investment and Commerce Bank Ltd. (IFIC) obtained a money decree against Mariner Fashions Wear Pvt. Limited and 5 others for an amount of Taka 1,26,25,902.40. In due course, the decree holder filed an execution case being Money Execution Case No. 1 of 2003 in the Third Court of Artha Rin Adalat, Dhaka, when the judgment-debtor failed to satisfy the decree in accordance with the direction of the Court but in spite of the best efforts taken on behalf of the decree-holder, the properties of the judgment-debtor could not be sold in auction, as such, the decree-holder filed an application under sub-section 7 of section 33 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003, ('the Act' in short), praying for an order vesting the title of the concerned properties in favour of the decree-holder and issue a certificate to that effect which would be treated as the title deed of the concerned properties in favour of the decree-holder.

3. It also appears that in pursuance to the said application the learned Judge by his order dated 10-11-2003 allowed the necessary certificate of title in respect of the concerned property in favour of the judgment debtor. But when the decree-holder bank went to the premises of the said property for taking its formal possession as directed in the Order dated 10-11-2003, they were resisted by the main judgment debtor, as such, they could not take the possession of the said property. Being aggrieved, they filed an application under Order XXI, rule 98 of the Code read with section 57 of the Act, praying for deploying a contingent of law enforcing agency for helping them to get the possession of the suit property but the learned Judge by his order dated 5-4-2004 rejected the said application on the grounds, inter alia, that since by his order dated 10-11-2003, the execution case had already been disposed of after passing the necessary order allowing a certificate of title in favour of the decree-holder, no further order can be made, in the said execution case.

4. Mr Md Zafor Ali Khan, Advocate, appears on behalf of the decree-holder while none appears on behalf of the judgment-debtor respondents.

5. Mr Md Zafor Ali Khan, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the decree-holder-appellant, submits that although the execution case was disposed of, furnishing a certificate of title in favour of the decree-holder but the decree-holder is entitled to further legal assistance under the ambit of Order XXI, rule 98 read with section 57 of the Act, effecting actual delivery of possession in its favour but the learned Judge erred in law in not allowing its such prayer for assistance to get such physical possession of the concerned properties.

6. Under such circumstances, the learned Advocate submits that for ends of justice and in exercising its jurisdiction as envisaged under Order XXI, rule 98 of the Code, the necessary orders should be passed, allowing assistance by deployment of police force so that the decree-holder bank can take over physical possession of the concerned properties of the Judgment-debtor in satisfaction of the decree as well as the certificate of title, executed in its favour by order of the Court itself.

7. It appears that section 26 of the Artha Rin Act, provides that notwithstanding anything which is not repugnant to the Act relating to the execution of the money decree, the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure shall be applicable under the Act. But from the said provision, it is obvious that when necessary provisions are already in the Act, the provisions of the Code would not normally be applicable.

8. Let us first look at the relaxant provisions in respect of the execution of the decree passed by an Artha Rin Court.

9. The provisions in respect of execution of the decree has been provided in Chapter Six of the Act. Section 28 provides for the period of limitation for filing of an execution case.

10. Section 33 provides for sale of the properties of the judgment-debtor. Sub-sections 1,2,3 and 4 of section 33, narrates the various steps and procedure leading to the sale of the properties of the judgment-debtor by public auction.

11. If the property could not be sold in auction under the above provisions, then under sub-section 5, the right to possess and enjoy the said property can be vested upon the decree-holder and the decree-holder again can take the steps as mentioned in sub-sections 1, 2, 3 and 4 to sell the said property in satisfaction of the decree.

12. If the decree-holder desires to get the ownership of the property in spite of sub-sections 4 and 5, it may file an application under sub-section 7. This provision is now under our consideration in this appeal. Sub-section 7 reads as follows:

ধারা-৩৩। নিলাম বিক্রয়ঃ

(১) - - - - -

(৭) উপ-ধারা (৪) ও (৫) এর বিধান সত্ত্বেও ডিক্রিদার উল্লেখিত সম্পত্তি মালিকানাসত্ত্বে পাইতে আগ্রহী মর্মে আদালতের নিকট লিখিতভাবে আবেদন করিলে আদালত উপ-ধারা (১), (২) ও (৩) এর বিধানাবলীর কোনরুপ হানি না ঘটাইয়া, উপ-ধারা (৪) ও (৫) এর কার্যক্রম অনুসরন করা হইতে বিরত থাকিবে; এবং ডিক্রিদারের প্রার্থিতমতে উল্লেখিত সম্পত্তির স্বত্ত্ব ডিক্রিদারের অনুকুলে ন্যস্ত হইয়াছে মর্মে ঘোষনা প্রদান পূর্বক তৎমর্মে একটি সনদপত্র জারী করিবে এবং জারীকৃত এইরুপ সনদপত্র সত্ত্বের দলিল হিসাবে গণ্য হইবে এবং আদালত উহার একটি অনুলিপি সংশ্লিষ্ট স্থানীয় সাব-রেজিষ্টারের অফিসে নিবন্ধনের জন্য প্রেরণ করিবে।

<u>13. This provision enables the Court to vest the ownership of the property of the judgment debtor upon the decree holder and also to issue a certificate to that effect. In English language the meaning of the words মালিকানাসত্ব or স্বত্ব means ownership. It envisages both title and possession to the property. As such, sub-section 7 enjoins upon the Court to vest not only the title but also the possession of the property. Besides, an application under sub-section 7 does not depend upon sub-section 5, rather, when an application is filed under sub-section 7, the Court will refrain from following the procedure under sub-sections 4 and 5. The relevant portion of sub-section 7 reads as follows:</u>

<u>“....মালিকানাসত্ত্বে পাইতে আগ্রহী মর্মে আদালতের নিকট লিখিতভাবে আবেদন করিলে, আদালত, উপ-ধারা (১), (২) ও (৩) এর বিধানাবলীর কোনরুপ হানি না ঘটাইয়া, উপ-ধারা (১), (২) ও (৩) এর বিধানাবলীর কোনরুপ হানি না ঘটাইয়া, উপ-ধারা (৪) ও (৫) এর কার্যক্রম অনুসরণ করা হইতে বিরত থাকিবে.........."</u>

<u>14. It appears that the decree-holder appellant filed an application praying for an order to put the decree-holder into possession of the concerned property as it was allegedly obstructed by the judgment-debtor but the learned Judge, Artha Rin Court, dismissed the petition on the ground that on the issuance of the certificate of title in favour of the decree-holder, the execution case had already been disposed of and the Court has got nothing further to do in this respect.</u>

15. With respect, we are unable to agree with the said views of the learned Judge, Artha Rin Court.

<u>16. Sub-section 7 envisages vesting of ownership of the property of the judgment-debtor upon the decree-holder. The said vesting of ownership includes delivery of possession of the property. Without the delivery of possession, the execution case cannot be disposed of.</u>

17. Sub-section 9 would make the position clearer, Sub-section 9 reads as follows:

“(৯) উপ-ধারা (৫) এর অধীনে সম্পত্তির দখল ও ভোগের অধিকার অথবা উপ-ধারা (৭) এর অধীনে সম্পত্তির স্বত্ব ডিক্রিদারের অনুকুলে ন্যস্ত হইলে, ধারা ২৮ এর বিধান সাপেক্ষে, উক্ত ডিক্রিজারী মামলার চুড়ান্ত নিষ্পত্তি হইবে।”

<u>18. From a plain reading of the above provision it would be clear that only with the total vesting upon the decree-holder, the execution case would be disposed of, otherwise not.</u>

19. As such, in the instant case, the learned Judge ought to have taken necessary steps to put the decree-holder in physical possession of the concerned property of the Judgment-debtor as prayed for.

<u>20. Since specific provision is not available in the Act enabling the Artha Rin Court to put the decree-holder into possession, the Court may exercise its such jurisdiction as provided in rules 97 and 98 under Order XXI of the Code read with section 26 of the Act, and give necessary directions to execute its order.</u>

21. Under such circumstances, the order dated 5-4-2004, passed by the learned Judge, Artha Rin Court, is set aside. He may pass necessary orders to put the decree holder in possession of the concerned property of the judgment-debtor, if necessary, by deploying police force and other measures as provided in the Code.

In the result, this appeal is allowed but without any order as to costs.

End.

SM Ziaul Haque Advocate, instructed by Md Nawab Ali, Advocate-on-Record—For Respondent No.1. 
Not represented — Respondent Nos. 2 & 3.

Vs.

case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated 9-7-95 passed by the High Court Division, Dhaka in Civil Order No. 3744 of 1995)
full_judgment:
Latifur Rahman J: This appeal by leave at the instance of the plaintiff-appellant is against the judgment and order dated 9-7-95 passed by a Single Judge of the High Court Division in Civil Order No. 3744 of 1995 affirming the judgment and order dated 20-5-95 passed by the Assistant Judge. 1st Court, Dhaka in Misc. Case No. 60 of 1991 under Order 9 rule 13 CPC allowing the said Misc. Case and setting aside the ex parte decree dated 25-4-85 and restoring original Title Suit No. 257 of 1994 to its file and number.

2. The plaintiff-appellant filed Title Suit No. 257 of 1994 in the Court of Assistant Judge, First Court Dhaka for specific performance of contract. The suit was decreed ex parte on 25-4-85. Against that ex parte judgment and decree defendant respondent filed on 25-9-91 Miscellaneous Case No. 16 of 1991 under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex parte decree stating, inter alia, that the plaintiff by suppression of all notices obtained the ex parte decree on 25-4-85, which he came to know by filing information slip on 23-4-91 through an Advocate, Shunil Ranjan Biswas; that thereafter by obtaining necessary papers he filed the case and that no summons was served upon him and the report of the serving peon is false.

3. Plaintiff appellant contested the Miscellaneous Case by filing written objection contending, inter alia, that after taking the entire proposed money the agreement for sale was executed on 14-2-70 and possession was handed over along with the lease deed of the Housing Estate and all other documents; that thereafter another agreement was executed on 8-10-77; that the plaintiff was residing in the said house all through; that notice was served in the original suit as well as at the time of registration of the document; that the defendant had full knowledge about the construction of the building and the living of the tenants; that the alleged knowledge dated 23-4-91 is absolutely false and the application is liable, to be dismissed; that the information slip stands in the name of one Shahabuddin Ahmed and not in the name of defendant No. 1. Plaintiff further asserted that the plaintiff's name has been duly mutated in the office of the Housing Estate, Ministry of Works, Municipality, WASA, WAPDA, Titas Gas, etc. and due notices were served upon defendant No. 1 for those mutation proceedings. The defendant had full prior knowledge of the decree and the pucca construction and, as such, the Miscellaneous case that was filed long after six years without any application for condemnation of delay is liable to be dismissed.

4. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division found that there was no due service of summons upon defendant No. 1 and consequently affirmed the order of the trial Court allowing the miscellaneous case under Order9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

5. Leave was granted to consider the following submissions of the learned Advocate for the appellant.

(1) The ex parte decree was passed on 25-4-85 and the Miscellaneous case for setting aside the ex parte decree was filed on 25-5-91 long after six years without any explanation for condemnation of delay.

(2) The defendant respondent also failed to prove his initial knowledge of the ex parte decree by examining Shahabuddin Ahmed through whom he came to know about the ex parte decree and the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division acted wrongly in not at all considering that the application was barred by limitation.

(3) The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division did not also consider that summons and registered notices were duly served upon the defendants and, as such, the learned Judge wrongly affirmed the order of the trial Court allowing the Miscellaneous Case for setting aside the ex parte decree.

(4) The defendant respondent having not examined any witness to prove his definite date of knowledge of the ex parte decree, the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division acted wrongly in allowing the application for setting aside the ex parte decree when the Miscellaneous Case was admittedly filed after six years.

6. Before entering into the question whether defendant No. 1- respondent No. 1 could prove his definite date of knowledge of the ex parte decree we would consider whether there was due service of summons on the defendants. If it is found from the materials on record that summons and notices as prescribed under the law were duly served upon the defendants, then of course, a heavy burden lies upon defendant No. 1 to prove his initial knowledge of the ex parte decree by adducing independent and cogent evidence.

7. From the order sheet it appears that the suit was filed on 25-4-84. From Order No. 8 dated 24-11-84 it appears that summons upon defendant No. 1 returned duly served as per peon's report and summons on defendant Nos. 2 and 3 did not return after service. Plaintiff also filed postal requisites and the court ordered for issuance of the same by registered post. From order No. 9 dated 10-12-84 it appears that acknowledgment due did not return by that time. From order No. 10 it appears that the court on 18-12-84 found that summons has been duly served and defendants filed no written statement. Next date was fixed for filing written statement and the defendants did not file any written statement and the case was fixed for ex parte hearing on 5-1-85. From 5-1-85 to 25-4-85 the defendant did not appear nor file any written statement nor took any steps. Ultimately, the suit was decreed ex parte on 25-4-85.

8. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division found fault with the service of summons as the acknowledgment due was not received by the court and nothing was known about the said acknowledgment receipt. The learned Single Judge also found fault with the court for giving the declaration that summons has been served. The learned Single Judge further found fault for fixing the case on 26-11-84 for ex parte hearing without affording the defendants the statutory period of two months notice under Order 8 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure to file the written statement. From these above facts the learned Single Judge went on to hold that there was no due service of summons upon defendant No. 1. The report of the process server states that he has returned the summons and he also made a declaration to the effect that he served the summons by affixing the same on the door of defendant No. 1 under rule 17 as defendant No. 1 refused to receive the summons. The process server as a serving officer of the court has also given a declaration to the effect that he has served the same in the same manner as indicated in the report.

<u>9. A reference to Order 5 rule 19 A of the Code of Civil Procedure shows that the declaration of the serving officer shall be received as evidence of the fact as to the service or attempted service of the summons. In the present case there was a declaration to the effect that the process server went to defendant No. 1's house with the summons but defendant No. 1 having refused to receive the same he served it by hanging on defendant No. 1's door in presence of three witnesses of the locality, namely, Shahed Ali, Azizuddin and Alauddin. In that view of the matter, the trial Court accepted such service as duly made under the law and the service of summons is to be construed as a valid service in law.</u>

<u>10. Mr SS Halder, learned Advocate for the appellant, cited the case of Santosh Kumar Chakraborty and others vs MA Motaleb Hossain and others reported in 36 DLR (AD) 248 wherein the declaration of the process server was accepted by this court as evidence of that fact as to the service or attempted service of the summons. Mr SS Halder has also cited the case of Md Insan Ali vs Mir Abdus Sobhan, 40 DLR (AD) 193 to show, that there being declaration of the process-server as per rule 19A of Order 5 of the Code, the onus is shifted to the defendant to prove that the summons was not served upon him. Apart from this, rule 19B(2) of Order 5 speaks that if the acknowledgment due is lost or mislaid or for any other reason has not been received by the court within 30 days from the date of posting of the letter the court issuing the summons shall declare that the summons has been duly served on the defendant. In that view of the matter, the postal acknowledgment due in respect of service upon defendant Nos. 2 and 3 having not returned within 30 days there was no legal bar on the part of the court to proceed with the case after holding that the summons has been duly served on the said defendants. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division was not correct in holding that the suit could not be fixed for ex parte hearing without return of the acknowledgment due. It further appears from the order sheet that on 18-12-84 the court made a declaration that the summons has been duly served and the suit was decreed ex parte on 25-4-85. So there was sufficient time for the defendants either to file a written statement or to take any steps for hearing. But no such step was taken by the defendants. As a matter of fact, ex parte hearing of the case was fixed on 26-12-84 and the ex parte decree was passed on 25-4-85, thereby more than two months time was afforded to the defendant-respondent to file a written statement or to take steps for the hearing of the suit. The materials on record show that there was valid and legal service. In view of the above finding by us, it is incumbent upon the defendants to show why the application for setting aside ex parte decree was filed long after six years of the ex parte decree and that too without any explanation of such long delay. We also find that Shahabuddin Ahmed through whom the defendant got his initial knowledge of the ex parte decree was not examined. The defendant did not examine any witness to prove his definite date of knowledge of the ex parte decree. As we find that summons and registered notices were validly and legally served upon the defendants it was the duty of the defendants to prove his initial date of knowledge of the ex parte decree. The defendants having failed to do so we hold that the defendant failed to prove his case.</u>

<u>For the reasons stated above, the appeal is allowed without any order as to costs and Miscellaneous Case No. 60 of 1991 of the Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka is dismissed.</u>

End.
